chapters.title: Chapter 1. In which Phileas Fogg and Passepartout Accept each Other, the One as Master, the Other as Man
paragraphs: Mr. Phileas Fogg lived, in 1872, at No. 7 Saville Row, Burlington Gardens—the house in which Sheridan had died in 1814. He was one of the most conspicuous members of the Reform Club, though he seemed to do everything he could to avoid attracting attention: an enigmatic figure about whom little was known, except that he was a polished man of the world. People said he resembled Byron—at least his head was Byronic; but he was a bearded, tranquil Byron, the sort who might live a thousand years without growing old.

An Englishman, certainly. Whether he was a Londoner was less clear. He was never seen on ’Change, nor at the Bank, nor in the counting-rooms of the “City”; no ships ever came into London docks of which he was the owner; he held no public office; he had never been entered at any of the Inns of Court—not the Temple, not Lincoln’s Inn, not Gray’s Inn—nor had his voice ever sounded in the Court of Chancery, or the Exchequer, or the Queen’s Bench, or the Ecclesiastical Courts. He was certainly no manufacturer, no merchant, no gentleman farmer. His name was unknown to the scientific and learned societies, and he had never been seen taking part in the deliberations of the Royal Institution, the London Institution, the Artisan’s Association, or the Institution of Arts and Sciences. He belonged, in short, to none of the countless societies that swarm in the English capital, from the Harmonic to that of the Entomologists, founded chiefly to abolish pernicious insects.
Phileas Fogg was a member of the Reform Club, and that was all.
How he had managed to gain admission to this exclusive club was simple enough.
He had been recommended by the Barings, where he held an open line of credit. His cheques were paid regularly on sight from his account, which was always flush.

Was Phileas Fogg rich? Without a doubt. But how he had made his fortune, even those who knew him best could not guess, and Mr. Fogg himself was the last person to whom one would put the question. He was not extravagant, nor, on the other hand, miserly; whenever he learned that money was needed for some noble, useful, or benevolent purpose, he supplied it quietly, sometimes anonymously. He was, in short, the least communicative of men. He spoke very little, and seemed all the more mysterious for his taciturn manner. His daily habits were entirely open to view, yet whatever he did was so exactly the same thing he had always done before, that the wits of the curious were thoroughly baffled.

Had he travelled? It seemed likely, for no one appeared to know the world more familiarly. There was no spot so remote that he did not seem on intimate terms with it. He often corrected, with a few clear words, the thousand conjectures advanced by club members about lost or unheard-of travellers, pointing out the true probabilities and seeming gifted with a kind of second sight, so often did events confirm his predictions. He must have travelled everywhere, at least in spirit.

What was certain, at least, was that Phileas Fogg had not absented himself from London for many years. Those who knew him better than the rest declared that no one could claim to have seen him anywhere else. His only pastimes were reading the papers and playing whist. He often won at this game, which—being a silent one—harmonised with his nature; but his winnings never went into his purse, being set aside as a fund for his charities. Mr. Fogg played not to win, but for the sake of playing. The game was, in his eyes, a contest, a struggle with a difficulty, yet a motionless, unwearying struggle, congenial to his tastes.

Phileas Fogg was not known to have either wife or children, which may happen to the most honest of men; nor relatives or close friends, which is certainly more unusual. He lived alone in his house in Saville Row, where no one ever penetrated. A single servant was enough to look after him. He breakfasted and dined at the club, at hours mathematically fixed, in the same room, at the same table, never taking his meals with the other members, much less bringing a guest along; and he went home at exactly midnight, only to retire at once to bed. He never used the cosy chambers the Reform provides for its favoured members. He spent ten hours out of the twenty-four in Saville Row, either sleeping or making his toilet. When he chose to take a walk, it was always with a regular step in the entrance hall with its mosaic flooring, or in the circular gallery with its dome supported by twenty red porphyry Ionic columns and illumined by blue painted windows. When he breakfasted or dined, all the resources of the club—its kitchens and pantries, its buttery and dairy—combined to crowd his table with the finest fare; he was served by the gravest waiters, in dress coats and shoes with swan-skin soles, who offered the dishes on special porcelain and on the finest linen; club decanters of a long-lost mould held his sherry, his port, and his cinnamon-spiced claret; while his beverages were cooled with ice brought, at great cost, from the American lakes.
If to live in this style is to be eccentric, then it must be confessed there is something good in eccentricity.

The mansion in Saville Row, though not lavish, was extremely comfortable. The habits of its occupant demanded little of the single servant, but Phileas Fogg required him to be almost superhumanly prompt and regular. On this very 2nd of October he had dismissed James Forster, because the luckless youth had brought him shaving-water at eighty-four degrees Fahrenheit instead of eighty-six; and he was awaiting his successor, who was due at the house between eleven and half-past.

Phileas Fogg sat squarely in his armchair, his feet close together like a grenadier on parade, his hands resting on his knees, his body straight, his head erect; he was watching, steadily, a complicated clock which indicated the hours, the minutes, the seconds, the days, the months, and the years. At exactly half-past eleven Mr. Fogg would, as he did every day, leave Saville Row and walk to the Reform.
A rap at this moment sounded on the door of the cosy apartment where Phileas Fogg was seated, and James Forster, the dismissed servant, appeared.
“The new servant,” he said.
A young man of thirty stepped forward and bowed.
“You are a Frenchman, I believe,” asked Phileas Fogg, “and your name is John?”

“Jean, if monsieur pleases,” the newcomer replied, “Jean Passepartout—a surname that has stuck to me because I have a natural knack for slipping out of one business and into another. I believe I’m honest, monsieur, but to speak plainly, I’ve had a number of trades. I’ve been a wandering singer, a circus-rider who used to vault like Leotard and dance on a rope like Blondin. Then I became a professor of gymnastics, to make better use of my talents; and then I was a sergeant fireman in Paris, and helped at many a great fire. But I left France five years ago, and, wanting to taste the sweets of domestic life, took service as a valet here in England. Finding myself out of place, and hearing that Monsieur Phileas Fogg was the most exact and settled gentleman in the United Kingdom, I have come to monsieur in the hope of living a tranquil life with him, and of forgetting even the name Passepartout.”
“Passepartout suits me,” replied Mr. Fogg. “You are well recommended; I hear a good report of you. You know my conditions?”
“Yes, monsieur.”
“Good! What time is it?”
“Twenty-two minutes past eleven,” returned Passepartout, drawing an enormous silver watch from the depths of his pocket.
“You are too slow,” said Mr. Fogg.
“Pardon me, monsieur—it is impossible—”
“You are four minutes too slow. No matter; it’s enough to note the error. From this moment, twenty-nine minutes past eleven, a.m., this Wednesday, 2nd October, you are in my service.”
Phileas Fogg got up, took his hat in his left hand, set it on his head with an automatic motion, and went off without a word.

Passepartout heard the street door shut once; that was his new master going out. He heard it shut again; that was his predecessor, James Forster, departing in his turn. Passepartout was left alone in the house in Saville Row.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. In which Passepartout is Convinced that He Has at Last Found His Ideal
paragraphs: “Good Lord,” Passepartout muttered, a little disconcerted, “I’ve seen people at Madame Tussaud’s with as much life in them as my new master!”
The “people” at Madame Tussaud’s, it should be explained, are made of wax and attract many visitors in London; only the power of speech is needed to make them human.

Throughout his short interview with Mr. Fogg, Passepartout had studied him closely. He looked about forty, with handsome, finely drawn features and a tall, well-proportioned body; his hair and whiskers were fair, his forehead neatly shaped and unlined, his complexion rather pale, and his teeth superb. His face displayed to an exceptional degree what readers of character call “repose in action,” a quality found in people who act instead of talking. With his calm, unruffled manner and clear eyes, Mr. Fogg seemed the perfect embodiment of that English self-possession which Angelica Kauffmann has captured so skilfully in her paintings. In every aspect of his daily life, he appeared perfectly balanced, keeping time as precisely as a Leroy chronometer. Phileas Fogg was, in fact, precision in human form; even the way he held his hands and feet revealed it, for in humans, as in animals, the limbs themselves express the passions.

He was so precise that he never needed to hurry, was invariably ready, and wasted neither a step nor a movement. He never walked a step farther than necessary and always took the shortest route to wherever he was going; he made no needless gestures, and no one ever saw him excited or upset. No one in the world moved more deliberately, yet he always arrived exactly on time.

He lived by himself, outside, one might say, every social connection; and since he knew that friction must be allowed for in this world, and that friction slows things down, he never rubbed up against anyone.

Passepartout, for his part, was a Parisian through and through. Ever since leaving his own country for England to work as a valet, he had searched unsuccessfully for a master who suited him. He was nothing like those impudent fools in Molière who stare boldly and carry their noses in the air. He was an honest fellow with a pleasant face, slightly protruding lips, a gentle, helpful manner, and the kind of good round head one likes to find on a friend’s shoulders. His eyes were blue and his complexion ruddy; he was solidly built, almost stout, with a muscular body whose strength the exercises of his younger years had fully developed. His brown hair was rather untidy. Ancient sculptors, we are told, knew eighteen ways of arranging Minerva’s locks; Passepartout knew only one way of arranging his own: three strokes with a wide-toothed comb, and his grooming was done.

It would have been rash to predict how Passepartout’s lively temperament would fit in with Mr. Fogg’s. Whether the new servant could become as completely methodical as his master demanded was impossible to say; only experience could answer that question. In his early years Passepartout had led something of a wandering life, and now he longed for peace. So far, however, he had not found it, although he had served in ten English households already. He had been unable to settle in any of them. To his dismay, his masters always proved unpredictable and irregular in their habits, forever racing around the country or hunting for adventure. His last employer, young Lord Longferry, a Member of Parliament, spent his nights in the Haymarket taverns and was all too often carried home in the morning on policemen’s shoulders. Wishing to respect the gentleman he served, Passepartout ventured a gentle protest against this behaviour. It was badly received, so he left. When he heard that Mr. Phileas Fogg needed a servant, that his life followed an unbroken routine, and that he neither travelled nor spent nights away from home, he felt certain he had found the place he wanted. He applied and, as we have seen, was taken on.

At half past eleven, then, Passepartout found himself alone in the Saville Row house. He immediately began to inspect it, making a thorough tour from cellar to attic. This clean, orderly, solemn residence delighted him; it seemed like a snail’s shell, both lit and heated by gas, which served perfectly well for both purposes. On reaching the second floor, Passepartout at once recognised the room intended for him and found it entirely satisfactory. Electric bells and speaking-tubes connected it with the floors below, and an electric clock stood on the mantelpiece, exactly like the one in Mr. Fogg’s bedroom. Both ticked off the same second at precisely the same instant. “Very good; that will suit me,” Passepartout told himself.

Then he noticed a card hanging above the clock. A closer look showed it to be a timetable of the household’s daily routine. It listed every duty of the servant from eight in the morning, the precise moment when Phileas Fogg got up, until half past eleven, when he left for the Reform Club. Every detail of service appeared: tea and toast at twenty-three minutes past eight, shaving water at thirty-seven minutes past nine, and dressing at twenty minutes to ten. Everything to be done between half past eleven in the morning and midnight, when this methodical gentleman went to bed, had been anticipated and arranged.

Mr. Fogg had a generously stocked wardrobe, all in excellent taste. Every pair of trousers, every coat and waistcoat, carried a number showing the time of year and the season when it should take its turn being laid out for wear; his shoes followed the same system. In short, the Saville Row house, which under the celebrated but dissolute Sheridan must have been a shrine to disorder and restlessness, now embodied the ideal of cosiness, comfort, and method. There was no study and there were no books: Mr. Fogg would have had no use for them, since the Reform provided two libraries, one of general literature and another of law and politics. His bedroom contained a medium-sized safe built to withstand both fire and burglars. But nowhere did Passepartout find firearms or hunting weapons; everything indicated habits of the utmost peace and tranquillity.

After examining the house from top to bottom, he rubbed his hands, broke into a broad smile, and said happily, “This is exactly what I was looking for! Ah, Mr. Fogg and I will get along together! Such a home-loving, orderly gentleman! An absolute machine; well, serving a machine doesn’t bother me.”

chapters.title: Chapter 3. In which a Conversation Takes Place which Seems Likely to Cost Phileas Fogg Dear
paragraphs: After closing his front door at half past eleven, Phileas Fogg put his right foot ahead of his left five hundred and seventy-five times, and his left ahead of his right five hundred and seventy-six times, and arrived at the Reform Club. This imposing building in Pall Mall could not have cost less than three millions. He went straight to the dining room, whose nine windows looked onto an attractive garden where the trees were already turning autumn gold, and sat at his usual table, already laid for him. His breakfast comprised a side dish, grilled fish with Reading sauce, a scarlet slice of roast beef accompanied by mushrooms, a rhubarb and gooseberry tart, and a small piece of Cheshire cheese. With all this he drank several cups of the tea for which the Reform was famous. At thirteen minutes to one he got up and made his way to the great hall, a magnificent room hung with paintings in elaborate frames. A footman brought him an uncut _Times_; he cut its pages with the practised skill of someone thoroughly familiar with this delicate task. Reading it occupied Phileas Fogg until a quarter to four, after which he turned to the _Standard_, which kept him busy until dinner. Dinner followed the same pattern as breakfast. At twenty minutes to six Mr. Fogg returned to the reading room and settled down with the _Pall Mall_. Half an hour later several Reform members entered and gathered by the fireplace, where a coal fire burned steadily. These were his regular whist partners: the engineer Andrew Stuart; the bankers John Sullivan and Samuel Fallentin; the brewer Thomas Flanagan; and Gauthier Ralph, a Director of the Bank of England. All were wealthy and held in high esteem, even in a club whose membership included the princes of English commerce and finance.
“Well, Ralph,” Thomas Flanagan asked, “what news is there of that robbery?”
“Oh, the Bank will have to bear the loss,” Stuart answered.

“On the contrary,” Ralph interrupted, “I still hope we shall catch the thief. Expert detectives have gone to every major port in America and on the Continent. He’ll have to be a clever fellow to escape them.”
“But do you have a description of the thief?” Stuart asked.
“To begin with, he is no thief at all,” Ralph replied firmly.
“What! A man runs off with fifty-five thousand pounds, and he isn’t a thief?”
“No.”
“Then perhaps he is a manufacturer.”
“According to the _Daily Telegraph_, he is a gentleman.”

Phileas Fogg made this observation, emerging from behind his newspapers. He bowed to his friends and joined their discussion. The incident they were discussing, the talk of the town, had taken place three days earlier at the Bank of England. A bundle of banknotes worth fifty-five thousand pounds had disappeared from the chief cashier’s desk while that official was recording a payment of three shillings and sixpence. Naturally, he could not look everywhere at once. It should be mentioned that the Bank of England places a touching trust in the public’s honesty. Neither guards nor bars protect its wealth; gold, silver, and banknotes lie openly exposed, at the mercy of whoever happens to walk in. One sharp observer of English life relates that, while visiting a room in the Bank, curiosity led him to examine a gold ingot weighing seven or eight pounds. He picked it up, studied it, and handed it to his neighbour, who passed it to the next man. Travelling from hand to hand, the ingot eventually reached the end of a dark passage, and did not come back to its place for half an hour. Throughout this time the cashier never even looked up. On the present occasion, however, matters had gone less smoothly. When the heavy clock in the “drawing office” struck five and the bundle of notes could not be found, the amount was entered in the profit and loss account. As soon as the theft came to light, specially chosen detectives hurried to Liverpool, Glasgow, Havre, Suez, Brindisi, New York, and other ports, encouraged by the offer of two thousand pounds plus five per cent of whatever money they recovered. Other detectives received orders to watch closely everyone arriving in London or leaving it by train, and a judicial inquiry began immediately.

There were sound reasons for believing the _Daily Telegraph_’s claim that the thief belonged to no professional gang. On the day of the theft, a well-dressed gentleman with polished manners and an air of prosperity had been seen walking back and forth in the paying room where the crime occurred. A description was readily obtained and sent to the detectives. Some optimists, Ralph among them, remained hopeful that he would be caught. Newspapers and clubs could talk of little else; everywhere people debated the likelihood of a successful pursuit. The Reform Club was particularly stirred up, since several members were Bank officials.

Ralph refused to admit that the detectives were likely to fail; he believed the promised reward would greatly encourage their energy and determination. Stuart was far from convinced, and they continued their argument as they sat down at the whist table. Stuart partnered Flanagan, while Fallentin played with Phileas Fogg. Conversation stopped during play, only to start up again in the intervals between rubbers.
“I still say,” Stuart declared, “that the odds favour the thief. He must be a very sharp fellow.”
“But where can he escape to?” Ralph asked. “He will be safe in no country.”
“Nonsense!”
“Well then, where could he go?”
“Oh, that I can’t tell you. The world is large enough.”
“It used to be,” Phileas Fogg said quietly. “Your cut, sir,” he added, offering Thomas Flanagan the cards.
The argument subsided during the rubber; when it ended, Stuart returned to it.
“What do you mean, ‘used to be’? Has the world become smaller?”

“Of course,” Ralph replied. “Mr. Fogg is right. The world has shrunk, since a man can travel round it ten times faster now than he could a hundred years ago. That also makes the hunt for this thief more likely to succeed.”
“And makes it easier for the thief to escape, too.”
“Please play your card, Mr. Stuart,” said Phileas Fogg.

Stuart, still sceptical, remained unconvinced. As soon as the hand ended, he said eagerly, “That is a curious way of proving the world has shrunk, Ralph. So, because a man can travel round it in three months—”
“In eighty days,” Phileas Fogg broke in.

“Exactly so, gentlemen,” John Sullivan added. “Just eighty days, now that the Great Indian Peninsula Railway has opened the stretch between Rothal and Allahabad. This is the _Daily Telegraph_’s calculation:—

London to Suez, travelling _viâ_ Mont Cenis and Brindisi by train and steamboat: 7 days. Suez to Bombay, travelling by steamer: 13 days. Bombay to Calcutta, travelling by train: 3 days. Calcutta to Hong Kong, travelling by steamer: 13 days. Hong Kong to Yokohama (Japan), travelling by steamer: 6 days. Yokohama to San Francisco, travelling by steamer: 22 days. San Francisco to New York, travelling by train: 7 days. New York to London, travelling by steamer and train: 9 days. The complete journey totals 80 days.”
“Yes, eighty days!” Stuart exclaimed, misdealing in his excitement. “But that allows nothing for bad weather, headwinds, shipwrecks, railway accidents, and all the rest.”
“Everything is allowed for,” Phileas Fogg replied, playing on throughout the argument.
“But suppose the Hindoos or Indians tear up the tracks,” Stuart answered. “Suppose they stop the trains, plunder the luggage vans, and scalp the travellers!”
“Everything is allowed for,” Fogg answered calmly, then laid down his cards and added, “Two trumps.”
It was Stuart’s turn to deal. He collected the cards and continued, “In theory you are right, Mr. Fogg, but in practice—”
“In practice as well, Mr. Stuart.”
“I should like to see you manage it in eighty days.”
“That is up to you. Shall we set off?”
“Heaven save me! But I would bet four thousand pounds that no one could make that journey under those conditions.”
“On the contrary, it can certainly be done,” Mr. Fogg replied.
“Then go and do it!”
“Travel round the world within eighty days?”
“Yes.”
“Nothing would please me more.”
“When?”
“Immediately. But I must warn you that you will pay for the journey.”
“Absurd!” Stuart cried, growing irritated by his friend’s persistence. “Come now, let us get back to our game.”
“Then you must deal again,” Phileas Fogg said. “The cards were misdealt.”
With a trembling hand Stuart picked up the pack, then abruptly set it down again.
“Very well, Mr. Fogg,” he said. “Agreed: I shall stake four thousand pounds on it.”
“Do calm down, my dear Stuart,” Fallentin said. “He is only joking.”
“If I say I will bet,” Stuart replied, “I mean exactly that.”
“Very good,” said Mr. Fogg. Turning to the others, he went on, “There are twenty thousand pounds to my credit at Baring’s, and I am perfectly willing to stake them.”
“Twenty thousand pounds!” Sullivan cried. “Twenty thousand pounds that a single unexpected delay would cost you!”
“There is no such thing as the unforeseen,” Phileas Fogg replied quietly.
“But eighty days, Mr. Fogg, is only an estimate of the shortest possible time needed to complete the journey.”
“A minimum used properly is enough for anything.”
“But to stay within it, you will have to leap from train to steamer, and from steamer back to train, with mathematical precision.”
“My leaps will be mathematically precise.”
“You cannot be serious.”

“A true Englishman does not joke about anything as serious as a wager,” Phileas Fogg replied solemnly. “Against anyone willing to take the bet, I stake twenty thousand pounds that I shall go round the world in eighty days or fewer: nineteen hundred and twenty hours, or one hundred and fifteen thousand two hundred minutes. Is the wager accepted?”
“We accept it,” Messrs. Stuart, Fallentin, Sullivan, Flanagan, and Ralph answered after conferring together.
“Excellent,” said Mr. Fogg. “The Dover train departs at a quarter to nine. I shall be on it.”
“Tonight, you mean?” Stuart asked.

“Tonight,” Phileas Fogg replied. He took a pocket almanac out and checked it, then added, “Today being Wednesday, the 2nd of October, I must return to London, to this very room in the Reform Club, by a quarter to nine in the evening on Saturday, the 21st of December. Otherwise, gentlemen, the twenty thousand pounds standing in my name at Baring’s will be yours, both in fact and by right. Here is my cheque for the sum.”

A written record of the bet was immediately prepared and signed by all six men, while Phileas Fogg remained stoically calm. He was certainly not betting for profit. He had staked twenty thousand pounds, half his fortune, only because he realised the other half might be needed to accomplish this difficult—one might even say impossible—undertaking. His opponents, by contrast, seemed deeply unsettled, less by the size of their stakes than by their misgivings about accepting a wager whose terms were so hard on their friend.
As the clock struck seven, the others proposed breaking off the game to give Mr. Fogg time to prepare for his departure.
“I am already quite prepared,” he answered in his usual calm voice. “Diamonds are trumps; please play, gentlemen.”

chapters.title: Chapter 4. In which Phileas Fogg Astounds Passepartout, His Servant
paragraphs: At twenty-five minutes past seven, Phileas Fogg left the Reform Club, having won twenty guineas at whist and said goodbye to his friends.

Passepartout had carefully studied the timetable of his duties and was astonished to see his master break his routine by appearing at such an unusual hour. According to the schedule, he should not have returned to Saville Row until precisely midnight.
Going into his bedroom, Mr. Fogg called, “Passepartout!”
Passepartout gave no answer. Surely the call could not be for him; this was the wrong hour.
“Passepartout!” Mr. Fogg called again, his voice no louder than before.
At this, Passepartout appeared.
“I have called twice,” his master remarked.
“But it isn’t midnight yet,” the servant answered, holding up his watch.
“I am aware of that; you are not to blame. In ten minutes we leave for Dover and Calais.”
A bewildered grin spread across Passepartout’s round face. He plainly had not understood what his master meant.
“Monsieur intends to go away from home?”
“Yes,” Phileas Fogg answered. “We shall travel round the world.”
Passepartout stared, eyebrows raised and hands lifted in the air. His astonishment was so overwhelming that he seemed on the point of collapsing.
“All round the world!” he whispered.
“Within eighty days,” Mr. Fogg replied. “Which means we have no time to waste.”
“And the trunks?” Passepartout gasped, shaking his head from side to side without realising it.

“No trunks. A carpet-bag will do, with two shirts and three pairs of stockings for each of us. We can buy clothing along the way. Bring my mackintosh and travelling cloak downstairs, and some sturdy shoes, although we shall not walk much. Hurry!”
Passepartout attempted an answer but found himself speechless. He left, climbed to his room, dropped into a chair, and muttered, “Well, this is a fine thing! And all I wanted was a quiet life!”

He began preparing for departure almost without thinking. Around the world in eighty days! Had his master lost his senses? No. Was he making a joke, then? They were going to Dover: very well! Then to Calais: so much the better! After all, Passepartout had been away from France for five years and would be glad to set foot in his own country again. Perhaps they would reach Paris, and what a pleasure it would be to see Paris once more. Surely a gentleman who spent his steps so sparingly would go no farther. No doubt of it—but that did not alter the fact that this man, until now so devoted to staying home, was actually going away!
By eight o’clock Passepartout had packed the little carpet-bag with clothing for himself and his master. Still troubled, he carefully closed his bedroom door and went downstairs to Mr. Fogg.

Mr. Fogg was entirely prepared. Tucked under his arm was a red-bound Bradshaw’s Continental Railway Steam Transit and General Guide, containing the arrival and departure times of trains and steamers. Taking the carpet-bag, he opened it and slipped inside a substantial roll of Bank of England notes, acceptable wherever his travels might take him.
“Have you remembered everything?” he asked.
“Everything, monsieur.”
“The mackintosh and my cloak?”
“They are both here.”
“Good!” He handed Passepartout the carpet-bag. “Carry this, and look after it carefully: it contains twenty thousand pounds.”
Passepartout almost let the bag fall, as though those twenty thousand pounds were gold coins whose weight was pulling him down.

Master and servant went downstairs and double-locked the front door. At the end of Saville Row they hired a cab, which drove swiftly to Charing Cross. It pulled up outside the station at twenty minutes past eight. Passepartout jumped down from the box and followed his master. Mr. Fogg had paid the driver and was about to enter the station when a poor woman carrying a child approached and sorrowfully begged for help. Her bare feet were coated with mud; a ragged feather dangled from her miserable bonnet, and a torn shawl covered her shoulders.
Mr. Fogg drew out the twenty guineas he had just won at whist and gave them to her. “Take these, my good woman. I am glad we met,” he said, and walked on.
Passepartout felt tears starting in his eyes; his master’s kindness had touched his easily moved heart.
After quickly buying two first-class tickets to Paris, Mr. Fogg was walking across the station towards his train when he spotted his five friends from the Reform.
“Well, gentlemen,” he said, “as you see, I am leaving. When I return, an examination of my passport will let you judge whether I have completed the journey we agreed upon.”
“Oh, there will be no need for that, Mr. Fogg,” Ralph replied courteously. “As a gentleman of honour, your word will be quite sufficient.”
“You remember the deadline for your return to London?” Stuart asked.
“Eighty days from now: Saturday, the 21st of December, 1872, at a quarter to nine in the evening. Goodbye, gentlemen.”
At twenty minutes to nine, Phileas Fogg and his servant took their seats in a first-class carriage. Five minutes later the whistle shrieked, and the train eased slowly out of the station.

It was a dark night, with a fine rain falling steadily. Settled comfortably in his corner, Phileas Fogg said nothing. Passepartout, still dazed by the whole affair, held automatically onto the carpet-bag and the immense treasure inside it.
As the train sped through Sydenham, Passepartout abruptly gave a cry of dismay.
“What has happened?” Mr. Fogg asked.
“Oh dear! In the rush—I—I forgot—”
“What?”
“I left the gas burning in my room!”
“Very well, young man,” Mr. Fogg answered calmly. “It will go on burning, and you will pay for it.”

chapters.title: Chapter 5. In which a New Species of Funds, Unknown to the Moneyed Men, Appears on ’change
paragraphs: Phileas Fogg had rightly guessed that his departure would cause considerable excitement in London’s West End. News of the wager circulated through the Reform Club, giving its members a thrilling subject to discuss. Soon it travelled from the club into newspapers all over England. This much-vaunted “tour of the world” was debated, challenged, and argued over as passionately as though it were another Alabama claim. A few sided with Phileas Fogg, but the vast majority shook their heads and opposed him. Given the available means of transport, they declared, travelling round the world in so little time was absurd and impossible, except in theory and on paper. The _Times, Standard, Morning Post_, and _Daily News_, along with twenty other highly respectable newspapers, dismissed his undertaking as madness. Only the _Daily Telegraph_ offered him cautious support. Most people considered him insane and blamed his friends at the Reform for accepting a bet that so clearly revealed the disturbed state of the man proposing it.

The question prompted articles as passionate as they were reasoned, for geography is an English favourite. Readers of every class eagerly consumed the columns devoted to Phileas Fogg’s venture. At first a few daring souls, chiefly women, championed him. His cause gained further popularity when the _Illustrated London News_ printed his portrait, copied from a photograph at the Reform Club. A handful of _Daily Telegraph_ readers even ventured to say, “After all, why shouldn’t he? Stranger things have happened.”

Finally, on the 7th of October, the Royal Geographical Society’s bulletin published a lengthy article examining the matter from every angle and demonstrating the complete foolishness of the undertaking.

Everything, it argued, opposed the travellers: every obstacle that either man or nature could put in their way. Success required a miraculous coordination of arrivals and departures, and that was impossible. In Europe, where distances were comparatively short, he might perhaps trust trains to arrive on schedule. But could he be entirely confident of crossing India in three days or the United States in seven? Mechanical breakdowns, derailments, collisions, bad weather, lines blocked by snow—did not every one of these count against Phileas Fogg? On winter voyages by steamer, would he not be at the mercy of winds and fog? Were even the finest ocean steamers not often two or three days late? A single delay would be enough to destroy the whole sequence of connections. If Phileas Fogg missed a steamer even once, even by an hour, he would have to wait for the next sailing, and his attempt would be irretrievably ruined.
The article caused a great stir. Reprinted in every newspaper, it dealt a serious blow to the spirits of those supporting the reckless traveller.

Everyone knows that England is the home of betting men, a class above mere gamblers; wagering is part of the national temperament. The public as well as Reform members staked large sums on or against Phileas Fogg, whose name appeared in betting books like that of a racehorse. Bonds were created and traded on the Exchange. “Phileas Fogg bonds” sold at their face value or above it, and business was brisk. Five days after the Geographical Society’s article appeared, however, demand began to ebb: “Phileas Fogg” fell. The bonds were offered in bundles, first of five, then ten, until eventually no one would accept fewer than twenty, fifty, a hundred!

Only Lord Albemarle, an elderly gentleman paralysed and confined to his chair, still stood by Phileas Fogg. This nobleman would have given his fortune for the chance to travel round the world himself, even if it took ten years. He staked five thousand pounds on Phileas Fogg. When people pointed out both the folly and the pointlessness of the adventure, he merely answered, “If it can be done, the first man to do it should be an Englishman.”

Fogg’s supporters grew fewer and fewer. Everyone was turning against him; the odds reached a hundred and fifty, then two hundred to one. A week after his departure, something happened that left him without a backer at any price.
One evening at nine o’clock, as the police commissioner sat in his office, he was handed this telegram:
_From Suez to London._
TO ROWAN, COMMISSIONER OF POLICE, SCOTLAND YARD: Bank robber located: Phileas Fogg. Forward warrant for his arrest to Bombay immediately.
FIX, _Detective_.

The telegram changed everything at once. The polished gentleman vanished, replaced by a bank robber. His photograph, hanging among the other members’ portraits in the Reform Club, was scrutinised closely: feature for feature, it matched the description supplied to the police. People remembered Phileas Fogg’s secretive habits, his solitary life, his abrupt departure. It now seemed obvious that his proposed trip round the world was a wager only in name; his sole purpose was to escape the detectives and shake them off his trail.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. In which Fix, the Detective, Betrays a Very Natural Impatience
paragraphs: This was how the telegram concerning Phileas Fogg came to be sent:

The Peninsular and Oriental Company’s steamer “Mongolia” was expected at Suez at eleven in the morning on Wednesday, the 9th of October. An iron vessel of two thousand eight hundred tons burden and five hundred horsepower, she regularly sailed between Brindisi and Bombay _viâ_ the Suez Canal. She ranked among the company’s fastest ships, invariably exceeding ten knots an hour on the Brindisi–Suez passage and nine and a half on the passage from Suez to Bombay.

Two men were walking along the wharves among the locals and visitors staying in what had once been a scattered village and was now, thanks to M. Lesseps’s enterprise, a rapidly expanding town. One was the British consul at Suez. Despite the English Government’s prophecies and Stephenson’s gloomy predictions, he regularly watched English ships from his office window as they passed each day along the great canal. It had cut at least in half the old, circuitous voyage from England to India around the Cape of Good Hope. His companion was a short, slightly built man with an alert, intelligent face; bright eyes peered from beneath eyebrows that twitched constantly. Just now he was visibly impatient, pacing nervously and unable to remain still for a moment. This was Fix, one of the detectives sent from England to hunt the bank robber. His assignment was to examine closely every passenger reaching Suez and pursue anyone who looked suspicious or resembled the criminal’s description, received two days earlier from police headquarters in London. The prospect of the handsome reward awaiting success clearly spurred him on, and he waited for the “Mongolia” with a feverish impatience that was easy to understand.
“So, consul,” he asked for the twentieth time, “you say this ship is never late?”

“Never, Mr. Fix,” answered the consul. “She was reported at Port Said yesterday, and the remaining distance is nothing to a vessel like her. As I have told you, the ‘Mongolia’ has beaten the company’s scheduled times and won its prize for exceptional speed.”
“Is she sailing here straight from Brindisi?”

“Straight from Brindisi, where she picks up the Indian mail. She sailed from there at five on Saturday afternoon. Be patient, Mr. Fix; she will arrive on time. Though I must say, I cannot see how your description will enable you to identify this man, even supposing he is aboard the ‘Mongolia.’”

“With these fellows, consul, you sense their presence more than recognise them. You need a nose for them, a sort of sixth sense combining sight, hearing, and smell. I have arrested more than one such gentleman in my career. If my thief is on that ship, I guarantee he will not get away from me.”
“I trust you are right, Mr. Fix. It was a very considerable theft.”

“A magnificent theft, consul: fifty-five thousand pounds! Such good fortune doesn’t often come our way. Burglars nowadays are becoming downright contemptible! A fellow gets himself hanged for a few shillings!”

“Mr. Fix,” the consul said, “I admire your way of putting it, and I wish you success, but I fear it will be anything but easy. Surely you see that the description you hold looks remarkably like that of an honest man?”

“Consul,” the detective declared with absolute certainty, “great thieves always look respectable. Men with villainous faces have only one option: they must remain honest, or they would be arrested on sight. The art lies in exposing the villain behind an honest face. No easy business, I grant you, but a true art.”
Mr. Fix plainly had more than a trace of a good opinion of himself.

Gradually the quay grew livelier. Sailors from different countries, merchants, ship-brokers, porters, and fellahs hurried back and forth as though the steamer’s arrival were imminent. The day was clear and a little cold. In the pale sunlight the town’s minarets rose over the houses. A pier stretched some two thousand yards out into the anchorage. On the Red Sea one could make out fishing-smacks and coastal boats, a few still preserving the fantastic shapes of ancient galleys.
Moving through the busy throng, Fix gave each passer-by the swift, searching glance that was his habit.
The time was now half past ten.
“Still no steamer!” he cried as the harbour clock sounded.
“She must be close by now,” his companion answered.
“How much time will she spend at Suez?”
“Four hours, enough to load her coal. Aden, at the far end of the Red Sea, is thirteen hundred and ten miles from Suez, so she needs to take on a fresh supply.”
“Then does she sail straight from Suez to Bombay?”
“She calls at no other port.”

“Excellent!” said Fix. “If the thief is aboard, he will surely disembark at Suez and take another route to the Dutch or French colonies in Asia. He must realise he would not be safe for an hour in India, since it is English territory.”
“Unless he is unusually clever,” the consul objected. “As you know, an English criminal is always better hidden in London than anywhere else.”

The remark gave the detective something to think about, and the consul left him to return to his office. Alone now, Fix grew more impatient than ever: he had a feeling the robber was on the “Mongolia.” If the man had left London for the New World, the natural choice would be the route _viâ_ India, less closely watched, and harder to watch, than the Atlantic passage. A series of piercing whistles soon interrupted these reflections and announced the “Mongolia.” Porters and fellahs rushed along the quay while a dozen boats put out to meet her. Before long her enormous hull appeared between the banks, and as she anchored in the roadstead the clock struck eleven. An unusually large number of passengers were aboard. A few remained on deck admiring the picturesque view of the town, but most climbed into the boats and came ashore at the quay.

Fix stationed himself where he could carefully study the face and figure of everyone arriving. Presently a passenger forced his way energetically through the crowd of pestering porters, approached him, and politely asked for directions to the English consulate. He showed Fix a passport he wanted _visaed_. Instinctively the detective took it and glanced quickly at the bearer’s description. He almost betrayed his surprise with an involuntary movement: the details matched exactly the description of the bank robber sent to him by Scotland Yard.
“Does this passport belong to you?” he asked.
“No, it belongs to my master.”
“And where is your master—”
“He remained aboard the ship.”
“He will have to visit the consul himself, though, to prove that he is the passport’s owner.”
“Oh, must he really do that?”
“It is absolutely essential.”
“Where will I find the consulate?”
“Over there, at the corner of the square,” Fix replied, indicating a house two hundred paces away.
“I shall fetch my master, then, though he won’t be very pleased to have to interrupt what he is doing.”
With a bow to Fix, the passenger went back to the steamer.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Which Once More Demonstrates the Uselessness of Passports as Aids to Detectives
paragraphs: The detective hurried along the quay and made straight for the consul’s office, where he was immediately shown in to see the official.
“Consul,” he began without introduction, “I have very good grounds for thinking my man is travelling on the ‘Mongolia.’” He then described the incident with the passport.

“Well, Mr. Fix,” the consul answered, “I should be glad to have a look at the scoundrel. But perhaps he will not come—assuming he is the man you take him for. A thief hardly wants to leave a record of his escape, and in any case he need not have his passport countersigned.”
“If he is as clever as I believe, consul, he will certainly come here.”
“To get a _visa_ on his passport?”
“Exactly. Passports do nothing but inconvenience honest people and help scoundrels escape. I assure you, coming here would suit him perfectly. But I hope you will refuse to _visa_ his passport.”
“Why should I? If it is a genuine passport, I cannot lawfully refuse.”
“Even so, I must detain him here until London can send me a warrant for his arrest.”
“Ah, that is your affair. But I cannot—”

Before the consul could finish, someone knocked at the door and two strangers came in. One was the servant Fix had spoken to on the quay. The other, his master, offered his passport and asked the consul to be kind enough to _visa_ it. The consul took the document and read it closely. From a corner, Fix watched the newcomer—devoured him with his eyes would be nearer the truth.
“Your name is Mr. Phileas Fogg?” the consul asked after examining the passport.
“It is.”
“And this is the man who serves you?”
“Yes: a Frenchman whose name is Passepartout.”
“Have you come from London?”
“Yes.”
“And your destination is—”
“To Bombay.”
“Very well, sir. You realise a _visa_ serves no purpose here, and you do not need a passport?”
“I do, sir,” Phileas Fogg answered. “But your _visa_ will provide the evidence I want that I have passed through Suez.”
“As you wish, sir.”
The consul signed and dated the passport, then stamped it with his official seal. Mr. Fogg paid the usual charge, bowed without warmth, and left, with his servant behind him.
“Well?” the detective asked him.
“Well, everything about his appearance and behaviour suggests an entirely honest man,” the consul replied.
“Perhaps. But that is beside the point. Would you agree, consul, that this imperturbable gentleman matches, feature for feature, the description of the robber sent to me?”
“Yes, I admit it. But descriptions, as you know—”

“I shall get to the bottom of it,” Fix broke in. “The servant seems less secretive than his employer. And he is French: he will not be able to keep from talking. Excuse me for a little while, consul.”
Fix set out to look for Passepartout.

After leaving the consulate, meanwhile, Mr. Fogg went down to the quay, gave Passepartout some instructions, and took a boat back to the “Mongolia.” In his cabin he opened his notebook, which held these entries:
“Departure from London: Wednesday, October 2nd, 8.45 p.m.
“Arrival in Paris: Thursday, October 3rd, 7.20 a.m.
“Departure from Paris: Thursday, 8.40 a.m.
“Arrival in Turin, via Mont Cenis: Friday, October 4th, 6.35 a.m.
“Departure from Turin: Friday, 7.20 a.m.
“Arrival in Brindisi: Saturday, October 5th, 4 p.m.
“Departure aboard the ‘Mongolia’: Saturday, 5 p.m.
“Arrival in Suez: Wednesday, October 9th, 11 a.m.
“Time spent travelling in total: 158½ hours, or six and a half days.”

The dates appeared in an itinerary arranged in columns, recording the month, date, and day of both the scheduled and actual arrivals at each main stopping place: Paris, Brindisi, Suez, Bombay, Calcutta, Singapore, Hong Kong, Yokohama, San Francisco, New York, and London. It covered the period from the 2nd of October to the 21st of December, with space beside every destination to enter time gained or lost. This systematic account therefore held every necessary detail, allowing Mr. Fogg to know at any moment whether he was ahead of schedule or behind it. On this Friday, October 9th, he recorded reaching Suez and noted that so far he had neither gained time nor lost it. He then calmly sat down to breakfast in his cabin, without once considering a visit to the town. He belonged to that class of Englishmen who prefer to view foreign countries through their servants’ eyes.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. In which Passepartout Talks Rather More, Perhaps, than is Prudent
paragraphs: Fix soon caught up with Passepartout, who was strolling about the quay and taking everything in, as though he, at least, felt no obligation to avoid seeing the sights.
“Well, my friend,” the detective said as he approached, “did you get the passport _visaed_?”
“Ah, monsieur, it’s you?” Passepartout replied. “Yes, thank you, the passport is taken care of.”
“And now you are having a look round?”
“Yes, though we move so quickly that travelling feels like a dream. This really is Suez, then?”
“Yes.”
“Here in Egypt?”
“Of course. This is Egypt.”
“And also in Africa?”
“In Africa.”

“Africa!” Passepartout repeated. “Imagine it, monsieur: I never thought we would get beyond Paris. And my entire view of Paris came between twenty past seven and twenty to nine in the morning, through a carriage window on the way from the Northern station to the Lyons station, in pouring rain! How sorry I am not to have visited Père la Chaise again, or the circus in the Champs Elysées!”
“So you must be in a terrible hurry?”
“Not I, but my master certainly is. That reminds me: I need to buy shoes and shirts. We left with no trunks, just a carpet-bag.”
“I can take you to a very good shop that will have everything you need.”
“That is most kind of you, monsieur.”
They set off side by side, with Passepartout talking freely all the way.
“Whatever else happens,” he said, “don’t let me miss the steamer.”
“There is plenty of time left; it is only noon.”
Passepartout brought out his large watch. “Noon!” he cried. “But it is only eight minutes to ten.”
“That watch of yours is slow.”
“My watch? Monsieur, this is a family heirloom, handed down from my great-grandfather! It doesn’t gain or lose five minutes in a whole year. A perfect chronometer, I assure you.”
“Now I understand,” Fix said. “You still have it set to London time, two hours behind Suez. You should reset it at noon in every country you visit.”
“Reset my watch? Never!”
“Then it will no longer keep time with the sun.”
“That is the sun’s misfortune, monsieur. In that case it is the sun that is wrong!”
The good fellow defiantly slipped his watch back into its pocket. After a few silent minutes, Fix asked, “So you left London in something of a hurry?”
“I should think we did! Last Friday, at eight in the evening, Monsieur Fogg returned from his club. Three-quarters of an hour later we were on our way.”
“But where does your master intend to go?”
“Straight on, all the time. He plans to circle the world.”
“The whole world?” Fix exclaimed.
“Yes, in eighty days! He claims it is for a bet, but between ourselves I don’t believe a word. That would make no sense. There must be something else behind it.”
“Ah! So Mr. Fogg is something of a character?”
“He most certainly is.”
“Does he have money?”

“Undoubtedly. He has an enormous amount with him, all in brand-new banknotes, and he is not reluctant to spend it on the journey. He has promised the ‘Mongolia’ engineer a substantial reward if we reach Bombay well ahead of schedule.”
“Have you been in your master’s service for a long time?”
“Not at all. I began working for him on the very day we left London.”

One can imagine how these answers affected a detective already brimming with suspicion and excitement. The hurried departure from London so soon after the theft, the huge sum in Mr. Fogg’s possession, his urgency to reach distant lands, the excuse of an eccentric and reckless wager: everything reinforced Fix’s theory. He went on questioning poor Passepartout and discovered that the servant knew almost nothing about his master. Mr. Fogg lived alone in London and was reputed to be rich, though the source of his wealth was unknown. His business and his habits were equally mysterious and impossible to penetrate. Fix now felt certain that Phileas Fogg would not end his voyage at Suez but really intended to continue to Bombay.
“Is Bombay a long way from here?” Passepartout asked.
“Quite a distance: ten days’ travel by sea.”
“And which country would Bombay be in?”
“India.”
“In Asia?”
“Certainly.”
“The devil! I was about to tell you that something is worrying me: my gas-burner!”
“Your what?”

“The gas-burner in my room. I forgot to put it out, and at this very moment it is burning at my expense. I have worked it out, monsieur: every twenty-four hours costs me two shillings, precisely sixpence more than my wages. So you can see that the longer we travel—”

Did Fix attend to Passepartout’s anxiety over his gas? Probably not. He was thinking out a plan instead of listening. By now they had reached the shop. Fix left his companion to buy what he needed, reminded him not to miss the ship, and hurried to the consulate. Complete certainty had restored the detective’s composure.
“Consul,” he said, “all doubt is gone. I have found my man. He is pretending to be an eccentric who intends to circle the world in eighty days.”
“Then he is a clever fellow,” the consul replied, “and means to get back to London after shaking off the police of both countries.”
“We shall have to see about that,” Fix answered.
“But could you have made a mistake?”
“I have made no mistake.”
“Why would a thief be so eager to obtain a _visa_ proving that he came through Suez?”
“Why indeed? I cannot say. But hear what I have learned.”
He briefly recounted the most significant details of what Passepartout had told him during their walk.
“So everything seems to point against him,” the consul said. “What do you intend to do now?”

“Telegraph London to send an arrest warrant to Bombay without delay; board the ‘Mongolia’; follow my scoundrel to India; and there, on English soil, politely arrest him, holding my warrant in one hand and placing the other on his shoulder.”

Having delivered this plan in a cool, casual tone, the detective said goodbye to the consul and went to the telegraph office. From there he sent the message to the London police that we have already seen. A quarter of an hour later, carrying a small bag, Fix boarded the “Mongolia.” Before many more moments had passed, the fine steamer was heading at full speed into the Red Sea.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. In which the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean Prove Propitious to the Designs of Phileas Fogg
paragraphs: Suez and Aden are exactly thirteen hundred and ten miles apart, a distance the company’s timetable allows its steamers one hundred and thirty-eight hours to cover. Thanks to the engineer’s energetic efforts, the “Mongolia” was moving so fast that she looked likely to arrive well before that limit. Most of those who had boarded at Brindisi were travelling to India: some to Bombay, others through Bombay to Calcutta, now the shortest route since a railway crossed the Indian peninsula. They included civil officials and military officers of various ranks. The officers served either with the regular British forces or in command of Sepoy troops, and since the central government had taken over the East India Company’s powers, their pay had been generous: £280 for sub-lieutenants, £2,400 for brigadiers, and £4,000 for divisional generals. Between the military passengers, several wealthy young English tourists, and the purser’s efforts to make everyone welcome, life aboard the “Mongolia” passed pleasantly and quickly. The cabin tables offered the finest food at breakfast, lunch, dinner, and supper at eight. The ladies conscientiously changed their outfits twice daily; when the sea was calm, music, dancing, and games made the hours fly.

But like most long, narrow gulfs, the Red Sea is changeable and frequently rough. Whenever the wind blew from the African or Asian shore, the “Mongolia” and her long hull rolled alarmingly. The ladies quickly vanished below, the pianos fell silent, and the singing and dancing stopped at once. The sturdy ship nevertheless drove straight towards the straits of Bab-el-Mandeb, undeterred by wind or waves. And what was Phileas Fogg doing meanwhile? One might imagine him anxiously monitoring each change in the wind, each disorderly surge of the sea—in short, every circumstance that might slow the “Mongolia” and interfere with his journey. If any such possibilities occupied him, however, not a sign of it appeared on his face or in his behaviour.

He remained the same unruffled Reform Club member, surprised by nothing and as constant as the ship’s chronometers. Rarely curious enough even to go on deck, he passed the Red Sea’s memorable sights with complete indifference. He made no effort to identify the historic towns and villages whose picturesque outlines stood against the sky along its shores. Nor did he show any fear of the dangers of the Arabic Gulf, spoken of with such horror by ancient historians and never entered by ancient sailors without lavish sacrifices to win the gods’ favour. How, then, did this eccentric gentleman spend his time on the “Mongolia”? He ate four substantial meals every day, heedless of even the ship’s most persistent pitching and rolling, and played whist without tiring, having found companions as devoted to the game as himself. A tax collector travelling to his post at Goa, the Rev. Decimus Smith returning to his Bombay parish, and an English brigadier-general on his way back to his brigade at Benares completed the party. With Mr. Fogg they played for hours in absorbed silence.

Passepartout, too, suffered no seasickness and faithfully ate his meals in the forward cabin. He rather liked the voyage: his food and accommodation were good, the passing sights interested him greatly, and he comforted himself with the mistaken belief that his master’s whim would run its course at Bombay. On the day after leaving Suez, he was delighted to find on deck the helpful gentleman with whom he had walked and talked along the quays.
“Unless I am mistaken,” he said, approaching with his friendliest smile, “you are the gentleman who kindly offered to show me round Suez?”
“Ah! Yes, I remember you perfectly. You serve that unusual Englishman—”
“Exactly so, Monsieur—”
“Fix.”
“Monsieur Fix,” Passepartout continued, “what a pleasure to find you aboard. Where are you travelling to?”
“To Bombay, just as you are.”
“Excellent! Have you travelled this route before?”
“Several times, yes. I work as an agent for the Peninsular Company.”
“So you are familiar with India?”
“Yes, indeed,” Fix replied, choosing his words carefully.
“Is India an interesting sort of place?”
“Extremely interesting. Mosques and minarets, temples and fakirs, pagodas, tigers, snakes, elephants! I hope you have plenty of time to look at everything.”

“I hope so too, Monsieur Fix. Surely a sensible man should not spend his life leaping from steamer to train and back from train to steamer, claiming he will circle the world in eighty days! No, you can depend on it: these acrobatics will come to an end at Bombay.”
“And is Mr. Fogg keeping well?” Fix asked with a perfectly casual air.
“Very well, and so am I. The sea air gives me the appetite of a starving ogre.”
“Yet I never happen to see your master up on deck.”
“No, never. He has no curiosity whatever.”
“Has it occurred to you, Mr. Passepartout, that this supposed eighty-day journey might cover some secret business—a diplomatic mission, perhaps?”
“Goodness, Monsieur Fix, I assure you I have no idea, and I would not spend half a crown to find out.”

After that encounter, Passepartout and Fix often talked together, the detective taking particular care to win the good fellow’s trust. He frequently treated him to a glass of whiskey or pale ale in the ship’s bar. Passepartout always accepted with cheerful courtesy and privately judged Fix to be the finest of companions.

Meanwhile the “Mongolia” continued at a brisk pace. On the 13th they sighted Mocha, encircled by ruined walls on which date-trees grew; behind it, extensive coffee plantations could be seen on the mountains. Passepartout was delighted by this famous town. Its round walls and dismantled fort reminded him of a gigantic coffee cup and saucer. The following night they sailed through the Strait of Bab-el-Mandeb, whose Arabic name means “The Bridge of Tears.” Next day they stopped for coal at Steamer Point, northwest of Aden harbour. Supplying steamers with fuel so far from the mines is a serious expense: the Peninsular Company spends some eight hundred thousand pounds a year on it. In these distant waters a ton of coal costs three or four pounds sterling.

With sixteen hundred and fifty miles still to sail before Bombay, the “Mongolia” had to spend four hours taking on coal at Steamer Point. This stop had already been allowed for and therefore did not disturb Phileas Fogg’s schedule. Moreover, instead of arriving at Aden on the morning of the 15th as expected, the ship had reached it on the evening of the 14th, gaining fifteen hours.

Mr. Fogg went ashore at Aden with his servant to obtain another _visa_ for his passport; unnoticed, Fix followed them. Once the _visa_ was secured, Mr. Fogg returned to the ship and his usual routine. Passepartout, as always, wandered through the town, among the Somalis, Banyans, Parsees, Jews, Arabs, and Europeans who made up Aden’s twenty-five thousand inhabitants. He marvelled at the defences that made it the Gibraltar of the Indian Ocean, and at the enormous cisterns where English engineers were still working two thousand years after Solomon’s engineers.

“Very remarkable, _very_ remarkable,” Passepartout told himself on his return to the ship. “I can see that travelling is certainly useful if one wants to see something new.” At six in the evening the “Mongolia” slowly left the anchorage and soon regained the Indian Ocean. She had one hundred and sixty-eight hours to reach Bombay. Conditions were favourable: a northwest wind filled every sail and helped the engine along. There was little rolling. The ladies reappeared on deck in fresh outfits, and singing and dancing began again. The voyage was going splendidly, and Passepartout was delighted that chance had given him so agreeable a companion as the charming Fix. Towards noon on Sunday, October 20th, the Indian coast came into view. Two hours later a pilot boarded. Hills outlined the distant horizon, and soon they could clearly distinguish the rows of palms adorning Bombay. The steamer entered the anchorage formed by the islands in the bay and drew alongside the Bombay quays at half past four.

Phileas Fogg was just completing the thirty-third rubber played during the voyage. He and his partner had boldly taken all thirteen tricks, bringing this fine campaign to a brilliantly victorious close.

The “Mongolia” had reached Bombay on the 20th instead of her scheduled date, the 22nd. Phileas Fogg had thus gained two days since leaving London. Without the least excitement, he recorded the fact in the gains column of his itinerary.

chapters.title: Chapter 10. In which Passepartout is only too Glad to Get Off with the Loss of His Shoes
paragraphs: Everyone knows the vast, inverted triangle called India, broad in the north and tapering to its southern point. It covers fourteen hundred thousand square miles, with a population of one hundred and eighty million unevenly distributed across it. Over most of this enormous country the British Crown exercises effective and despotic power. Its governor-general is based in Calcutta, with governors in Madras, Bombay, and Bengal, and a lieutenant-governor in Agra.

Strictly speaking, however, British India covers only seven hundred thousand square miles and has between one hundred and one hundred and ten million inhabitants. Much of India remains outside British rule, and certain fierce rajahs in the interior are entirely independent. The celebrated East India Company held supreme power from 1756, when the English first secured a foothold where Madras now stands, until the great Sepoy uprising. Province by province it expanded, buying territories from native chiefs whom it seldom actually paid, and appointing the governor-general and the civil and military officials below him. But the East India Company has now disappeared, and the Crown directly controls the British possessions in India. The country’s appearance, its customs, and the distinctions between its peoples change from day to day.

Travelling in India once meant the old, cumbersome choices of walking, riding a horse, being carried in a palanquin, or jolting in an unwieldy coach. Now swift steamboats sail the Indus and the Ganges, while a great railway with numerous connecting branches crosses the peninsula from Bombay to Calcutta in three days. Its course across India is far from straight. Bombay and Calcutta are only a thousand to eleven hundred miles apart in a direct line, but the railway’s winding route adds more than a third to that distance.

The Great Indian Peninsula Railway broadly follows this course: from Bombay it runs through Salcette, reaches the mainland opposite Tannah, crosses the Western Ghauts, and heads northeast to Burhampoor. It skirts the almost independent territory of Bundelcund, climbs towards Allahabad, then turns east to meet the Ganges at Benares. After drawing a little away from the river, it continues southeast through Burdivan and the French town of Chandernagor, finally ending at Calcutta.
At half past four in the afternoon, the “Mongolia” passengers came ashore. The Calcutta train was to depart at eight precisely.

Mr. Fogg said goodbye to his whist partners and disembarked. He gave his servant several errands, stressed that he must reach the station promptly at eight, and set off for the passport office, his measured footsteps marking seconds like an astronomical clock. As for Bombay’s wonders—its celebrated city hall and magnificent library, its forts, docks, bazaars, mosques, synagogues, Armenian churches, and the grand Malabar Hill pagoda with its two many-sided towers—he had not the slightest wish to see them. He would not even trouble to inspect Elephanta’s masterpieces, the mysterious underground chambers hidden southeast of the docks, or those splendid relics of Buddhist architecture, the Kanherian grottoes on Salcette island.

When his business at the passport office was finished, Phileas Fogg went calmly to the station and ordered dinner. Among the dishes, the landlord particularly urged him to try some “native rabbit” giblets, a speciality of which he was proud.

Mr. Fogg tasted the dish and found it distinctly unappetising, despite the spicy sauce. He rang for the landlord. When the man appeared, Fogg fixed his clear gaze on him and asked, “Is this rabbit, sir?”
“Yes, my lord,” the scoundrel replied without hesitation. “A rabbit from the jungle.”
“And did this particular rabbit mew when it was killed?”
“Mew, my lord! A rabbit, mewing! I give you my word—”
“Please spare me your assurances, landlord, and remember that cats were once regarded as sacred in India. Those were good days.”
“Good for the cats, my lord?”
“And perhaps for travellers too!”

Mr. Fogg then calmly resumed his meal. Fix had disembarked a little later than he did and gone straight to Bombay police headquarters. Introducing himself as a London detective, he explained why he had come and set out the case against the suspected thief, then anxiously asked whether a warrant had arrived from London. None had reached the office; indeed, there had not yet been enough time for it to arrive. Bitterly disappointed, Fix tried to persuade the head of the Bombay police to issue an arrest order. The director refused: this was a London matter, and only the London authorities could legally supply the warrant. Fix did not argue further and reluctantly accepted that he must wait for the vital document. Meanwhile he resolved never to let the mysterious rogue out of his sight while he remained in Bombay. Like Passepartout, he had no doubt that Phileas Fogg would stay there, at least long enough for the warrant to reach them.

Passepartout, however, understood immediately from the orders his master gave on leaving the “Mongolia” that Bombay would be abandoned just as Suez and Paris had been. The journey would continue at least to Calcutta, and possibly farther. He began to wonder whether Mr. Fogg’s wager might be entirely serious, and whether fate really intended to drive him round the world in eighty days, however much he longed for a quiet life!

After buying the required supply of shirts and shoes, he strolled through streets crowded with people of many nations: Europeans, Persians in pointed caps, Banyas in round turbans, Sindes in square bonnets, Parsees in black mitres, and Armenians in long robes. A Parsee festival happened to be under way. These descendants of Zoroaster’s sect—the most industrious, civilised, intelligent, and austere of the East Indians, including Bombay’s richest native merchants—were celebrating a kind of religious carnival. Amid its processions and spectacles, Indian dancing-girls in rose-coloured gauze, gathered with gold and silver, danced lightly and with perfect modesty to viols and clattering tambourines. Naturally, Passepartout watched these unusual ceremonies with eyes wide and mouth hanging open, looking like the most inexperienced simpleton one could imagine.

Unfortunately for both himself and his master, curiosity carried him farther away than he meant to go. At last, after watching the Parsee carnival wind into the distance, he turned towards the station. Then he caught sight of the magnificent pagoda on Malabar Hill and felt an irresistible urge to go inside. He had no idea that Christians were forbidden to enter certain Indian temples, or that even worshippers must leave their shoes outside before entering. It should be mentioned here that British policy wisely imposes severe penalties on those who disregard the practices of native religions.

Thinking he was doing no harm, Passepartout entered as any innocent visitor might. He was soon absorbed in admiring the splendid Brahmin decoration all around him when, without warning, he found himself flat on the sacred paving stones. Looking up, he saw three furious priests. They attacked him at once, tore off his shoes, and beat him while shouting fiercely. The nimble Frenchman quickly sprang to his feet, brought down two of his long-robed opponents with punches and vigorous kicks, and fled the pagoda as fast as he could. Once in the street, he soon lost the third priest by disappearing into the crowd.
At five minutes to eight, Passepartout burst breathlessly into the station, without hat or shoes and with the package of shirts and shoes lost in the struggle.

Fix stood on the platform. He had followed Mr. Fogg there and now saw that he really meant to leave Bombay. The detective had decided to pursue the suspected thief to Calcutta and farther if necessary. Hidden in a shadowy corner, he escaped Passepartout’s notice but overheard the servant’s brief account of his adventure to Mr. Fogg.

“I trust there will be no repetition of this,” Phileas Fogg said coldly as he boarded the train. Thoroughly downcast, poor Passepartout followed him in silence. Fix was about to step into another carriage when a sudden thought made him change his plans.
“No, I shall remain here,” he muttered. “A crime has been committed on Indian territory. Now I have him.”
At that moment the engine shrieked, and the train moved away into the darkness of the night.

chapters.title: Chapter 11. In which Phileas Fogg Secures a Curious Means of Conveyance at a Fabulous Price
paragraphs: The train had left on time. Among the passengers were a number of officers, government officials, and opium and indigo merchants whose business called them to the eastern coast. Passepartout rode in the same carriage as his master, and a third passenger sat in the seat opposite them. This was Sir Francis Cromarty, one of Mr. Fogg’s whist partners on the “Mongolia,” now on his way to rejoin his corps at Benares. Sir Francis was a tall, fair man of fifty who had distinguished himself greatly in the last Sepoy revolt. He made India his home, paying only brief visits to England at rare intervals, and was nearly as familiar as a native with the customs, history, and character of India and its people. But Phileas Fogg, who was not traveling but only tracing a circumference, took no pains to inquire into such matters. He was a solid body, moving along an orbit around the terrestrial globe according to the laws of rational mechanics. At that very moment he was calculating in his head the number of hours that had passed since his departure from London, and, had it been in his nature to make a useless display, he would have rubbed his hands in satisfaction. Sir Francis Cromarty had observed the oddity of his traveling companion—though his only chance to study him had come while dealing the cards and between two rubbers—and he asked himself whether a human heart really beat beneath this cold exterior, and whether Phileas Fogg had any sense of the beauties of nature. The brigadier-general was free to admit privately that, of all the eccentric people he had ever met, none compared to this product of the exact sciences.

Phileas Fogg had not hidden from Sir Francis his plan to go round the world, nor the circumstances under which he had set out. The general saw in the wager only a useless eccentricity and a lack of sound common sense. In the way this strange gentleman was carrying on, he would leave the world without having done any good to himself or anyone else.

An hour after leaving Bombay the train had passed the viaducts and the Island of Salcette and had reached the open country. At Callyan they came to the junction of the branch line that descends toward south-eastern India by Kandallah and Pounah. Passing Pauwell, they entered the defiles of the mountains, with their basalt bases and summits crowned with thick, green forests. Phileas Fogg and Sir Francis Cromarty exchanged a few words from time to time, and now Sir Francis, picking up the conversation again, remarked, “Some years ago, Mr. Fogg, you would have run into a delay at this point that would probably have cost you your wager.”
“How so, Sir Francis?”
“Because the railway stopped at the foot of these mountains, and the passengers had to cross them in palanquins or on ponies to reach Kandallah on the other side.”
“Such a delay would not have disrupted my plans in the least,” said Mr. Fogg. “I have always foreseen the likelihood of certain obstacles.”

“But, Mr. Fogg,” Sir Francis continued, “you run the risk of having some trouble over this worthy fellow’s adventure at the pagoda.” Passepartout, his feet comfortably wrapped in his travelling blanket, was sound asleep and never dreamed that anyone was talking about him. “The Government is very severe on that kind of offense. It is especially careful that the religious customs of the Indians be respected, and if your servant had been caught—”

“Very well, Sir Francis,” Mr. Fogg replied. “If he had been caught, he would have been convicted and punished, and then he would have quietly gone back to Europe. I don’t see how this affair could have delayed his master.”

The conversation lapsed again. During the night the train left the mountains behind and passed Nassik, and the next day rolled on across the flat, well-cultivated country of the Khandeish, with its scattered villages, above which rose the minarets of the pagodas. This fertile region is watered by numerous small rivers and clear streams, most of them tributaries of the Godavery.

Passepartout, when he woke and looked out, could not believe he was actually crossing India in a railway train. The locomotive, driven by an English engineer and fed with English coal, sent its smoke out over plantations of cotton, coffee, nutmeg, clove, and pepper, while the steam curled in spirals around clusters of palm trees, among which appeared picturesque bungalows, viharis (a kind of abandoned monastery), and marvelous temples enriched with the inexhaustible ornament of Indian architecture. Then they came upon vast tracts stretching to the horizon, with jungles inhabited by snakes and tigers that fled at the noise of the train, followed by forests pierced by the railway and still haunted by elephants which gazed at the passing train with pensive eyes. Beyond Milligaum, the travelers crossed the deadly country so often stained with blood by the worshippers of the goddess Kali. Not far off rose Ellora with its graceful pagodas, and the famous Aurungabad, capital of the ferocious Aureng-Zeb, now the chief town of one of the detached provinces of the kingdom of the Nizam. It was thereabouts that Feringhea, the Thuggee chief, king of the stranglers, had once held sway. These ruffians, bound by a secret oath, strangled victims of every age in honor of the goddess Death, never shedding a drop of blood. There was a time when this part of the country could hardly be crossed without corpses turning up in every direction. The English Government has managed to reduce these murders greatly, though the Thuggees still exist and continue to practice their horrible rites.

At half-past twelve the train stopped at Burhampoor, where Passepartout was able to buy a pair of Indian slippers, decorated with false pearls, in which, with obvious vanity, he proceeded to encase his feet. The travelers ate a hurried breakfast and set off for Assurghur, after following for a short distance the banks of the small river Tapty, which empties into the Gulf of Cambray near Surat.

Passepartout was now sunk in absorbing reverie. Up until their arrival at Bombay he had hoped that the journey would end there; but now that they were clearly tearing across India at full speed, the mood of his daydreams had suddenly changed. His old vagabond nature came back to him; the fantastic ideas of his youth once again took hold of him. He began to regard his master’s project as serious in earnest, to believe in the reality of the bet, and therefore in the tour round the world and the necessity of completing it within the appointed time. He was already worrying about possible delays and accidents that might happen on the way. He felt himself personally invested in the wager and trembled at the thought that he might have been the cause of losing it through his unforgivable folly of the night before. Far less cool-headed than Mr. Fogg, he was far more restless, counting and recounting the days that had passed, cursing whenever the train stopped, accusing it of sluggishness, and silently blaming Mr. Fogg for not having bribed the engineer. The worthy fellow had no idea that, while such methods might speed up a steamer, they could not work on a railway.

Toward evening the train entered the defiles of the Sutpour Mountains, which separate the Khandeish from Bundelcund. The next day Sir Francis Cromarty asked Passepartout what time it was, and the latter, after consulting his watch, answered that it was three in the morning. This famous timepiece, always set to the Greenwich meridian—which was now some seventy-seven degrees to the westward—was at least four hours slow. Sir Francis corrected Passepartout’s time, whereupon Passepartout made the same remark he had made to Fix.
