When the general insisted that the watch should be adjusted at each new meridian, since he was constantly traveling east, that is, into the face of the sun, and therefore the days were shorter by four minutes for every degree crossed, Passepartout stubbornly refused to alter his watch, which he kept on London time. It was a harmless delusion that could do no one any harm.

At eight o’clock the train stopped in the middle of a clearing some fifteen miles beyond Rothal, where there were several bungalows and workmen’s cabins. The conductor, walking along the carriages, called out, “Passengers will get out here!”
Phileas Fogg looked at Sir Francis Cromarty for an explanation, but the general could not say what had brought them to a halt in the middle of this forest of date palms and acacias.
Passepartout, no less surprised, rushed out and quickly came back, crying, “Monsieur, no more railway!”
“What do you mean?” asked Sir Francis.
“I mean that the train isn’t going on.”
The general at once stepped out, while Phileas Fogg calmly followed him, and together they walked over to the conductor.
“Where are we?” asked Sir Francis.
“At the hamlet of Kholby.”
“Do we stop here?”
“Certainly. The railway isn’t finished.”
“What! Not finished?”
“No. There are still a matter of fifty miles to be laid between here and Allahabad, where the line begins again.”
“But the papers announced the opening of the railway throughout.”
“What would you have, officer? The papers were wrong.”
“Yet you sell tickets from Bombay to Calcutta,” Sir Francis retorted, growing heated.
“No doubt,” the conductor replied; “but the passengers know they must arrange their own transportation from Kholby to Allahabad.”
Sir Francis was furious. Passepartout would gladly have knocked the conductor down and did not dare look at his master.
“Sir Francis,” Mr. Fogg said quietly, “we will, if you please, look around for some means of conveyance to Allahabad.”
“Mr. Fogg, this is a delay very much to your disadvantage.”
“No, Sir Francis; it was foreseen.”
“What! You knew that the line—”

“Not at all; but I knew that some obstacle or other would sooner or later come up on my route. Nothing, therefore, is lost. I have two days, which I have already gained, to sacrifice. A steamer leaves Calcutta for Hong Kong at noon on the 25th. Today is the 22nd, and we shall reach Calcutta in time.”
There was nothing to say in reply to so confident an answer.

It was all too true that the railway ended at this point. The papers were like certain watches that have a way of running too fast, and they had been premature in announcing the completion of the line. Most of the travelers were aware of this break, and on leaving the train they began hiring whatever vehicles the village could provide: four-wheeled palki-gharis, wagons drawn by zebus, carriages that looked like pagodas on the move, palanquins, ponies, and what not.
Mr. Fogg and Sir Francis Cromarty, after searching the village from end to end, came back without having found anything.
“I shall go on foot,” said Phileas Fogg.

Passepartout, who had just rejoined his master, made a sour grimace as he thought of his magnificent but all-too-flimsy Indian shoes. Happily he too had been looking around, and after a moment’s hesitation he said, “Monsieur, I think I have found a means of conveyance.”
“What?”
“An elephant! An elephant belonging to an Indian who lives only a hundred steps from here.”
“Let’s go and see the elephant,” replied Mr. Fogg.

They soon reached a small hut, near which, enclosed within some high palings, stood the animal in question. An Indian came out of the hut and, at their request, led them inside the enclosure. The elephant, which its owner had raised not as a beast of burden but for warlike purposes, was half-tamed. The Indian had already begun, by frequently irritating him and feeding him every three months on sugar and butter, to give him a ferocity foreign to his nature—a method often used by those who train Indian elephants for battle. Fortunately for Mr. Fogg, however, the animal’s training in that direction had not gone far, and the elephant still kept his natural gentleness. Kiouni—this was the name of the beast—could no doubt travel quickly for a long time, and, in the absence of any other means of conveyance, Mr. Fogg resolved to hire him. But elephants are far from cheap in India, where they are growing scarce. The males, which alone are fit for circus shows, are much sought after, especially since only a few of them are domesticated. So when Mr. Fogg proposed to hire Kiouni, the Indian flatly refused. Mr. Fogg persisted, offering the extravagant sum of ten pounds an hour for the loan of the animal to Allahabad. Refused. Twenty pounds? Refused as well. Forty pounds? Still refused. Passepartout jumped at each new offer; but the Indian would not be tempted. And yet the offer was a tempting one, for, supposing the elephant took fifteen hours to reach Allahabad, his owner would receive no less than six hundred pounds sterling.

Phileas Fogg, without getting in the least flustered, then proposed to buy the animal outright, and at first offered a thousand pounds for him. The Indian, perhaps thinking he was about to drive a great bargain, still refused.

Sir Francis Cromarty took Mr. Fogg aside and begged him to reflect before going any further. The gentleman replied that he was not in the habit of acting rashly, that a bet of twenty thousand pounds was at stake, that the elephant was absolutely necessary to him, and that he would secure him even if he had to pay twenty times his value. Returning to the Indian, whose small, sharp eyes, glistening with greed, showed that with him it was only a question of how high a price he could get, Mr. Fogg offered first twelve hundred, then fifteen hundred, eighteen hundred, two thousand pounds. Passepartout, usually so red-faced, was fairly white with suspense.
At two thousand pounds the Indian gave in.
“What a price, good heavens!” cried Passepartout, “for an elephant.”

It only remained now to find a guide, which was comparatively easy. A young Parsee with an intelligent face offered his services, which Mr. Fogg accepted, promising so generous a reward as to substantially sharpen his zeal. The elephant was led out and equipped. The Parsee, an accomplished elephant driver, covered his back with a sort of saddle-cloth and attached to each of his flanks one of those curiously uncomfortable howdahs. Phileas Fogg paid the Indian with some banknotes that he drew from the famous carpet-bag, a proceeding that seemed to wring poor Passepartout’s vitals out of him. Then he offered to carry Sir Francis to Allahabad, an invitation the brigadier gratefully accepted, since one traveler more would hardly tire the gigantic beast. Provisions were purchased at Kholby, and while Sir Francis and Mr. Fogg took the howdahs on either side, Passepartout got astride the saddle-cloth between them. The Parsee perched himself on the elephant’s neck, and at nine o’clock they set out from the village, the animal striding off through the dense forest of palms by the shortest route.

chapters.title: Chapter 12. In which Phileas Fogg and His Companions Venture Across the Indian Forests, and What Ensued
paragraphs: To save time, the guide left the railway line, which was still under construction, on his left. The line twisted unpredictably around the Vindhia Mountains and never ran straight for long. The Parsee knew every road and path in the district, and he said that cutting directly through the forest would save them twenty miles.

Phileas Fogg and Sir Francis Cromarty sat buried up to their necks in the special howdahs that had been fitted for them, and the elephant’s fast trot, urged along by the skilful Parsee, shook them terribly. They bore the discomfort with true British composure, hardly speaking, and hardly able even to see one another. Passepartout was perched on the animal’s back and took the full force of every jolt as the creature strode along. Following his master’s advice, he took great care to keep his tongue clear of his teeth, or he would have bitten it clean off. The good fellow was thrown from the elephant’s neck to its rump and back again, and he leaped about like a clown on a springboard. Even so, he laughed through all the bouncing, and every so often he pulled a lump of sugar from his pocket and slipped it into Kiouni’s trunk, which accepted it without breaking its steady trot in the slightest.

After two hours the guide halted the elephant and gave him an hour’s rest. Kiouni drank his fill at a spring nearby, then began tearing into the branches and bushes around him. Neither Sir Francis nor Mr. Fogg minded the delay, and both climbed down with relief. “Why, he’s made of iron!” cried the general, looking at Kiouni with admiration.
“Forged iron,” answered Passepartout, who was busy getting a quick breakfast ready.

At noon the Parsee gave the signal to move on. Before long the landscape turned wild. Groves of date and dwarf palms replaced the thick forests, and then came huge dry plains, thinly dotted with scrub and strewn with great blocks of syenite. Travellers rarely visit this part of Bundelcund. Its people are fanatical, steeped in the most dreadful practices of the Hindoo faith. The English have never managed to gain full control of the territory, which lies under the sway of rajahs who are nearly impossible to reach in their unassailable mountain strongholds. Several times the travellers saw bands of fierce-looking natives who made angry, threatening gestures when they noticed the elephant striding across country. The Parsee steered clear of them as far as he could. They saw few animals along the way, and even the monkeys scampered off the path, twisting and grimacing in a way that sent Passepartout into fits of laughter.

Yet in the middle of all this good humour, one thought nagged at the faithful servant. What was Mr. Fogg going to do with the elephant once they reached Allahabad? Take him along? Impossible! Shipping him would cost a fortune. Sell him, then, or turn him loose? Surely the excellent animal deserved some consideration. And if Mr. Fogg decided to give Kiouni to him, Passepartout, he would be in a real fix. These worries kept eating at him for a long while.

They had crossed the main ridge of the Vindhias by eight in the evening, and they stopped again on the northern slope, in a ruined bungalow. They had covered nearly twenty-five miles that day, and the station at Allahabad was just as far away.

The night was cold. The Parsee built a fire in the bungalow from a few dry branches, and its warmth was very welcome. The provisions bought at Kholby made a good enough supper, and the travellers ate greedily. The conversation began with a few scattered remarks and soon gave way to loud, steady snoring. The guide kept watch over Kiouni, who slept on his feet, propped against the trunk of a big tree. Nothing disturbed the sleepers during the night, though now and then a panther growled or monkeys chattered and broke the silence. The more dangerous animals gave no cry and made no move against the people in the bungalow. Sir Francis slept deeply, like an honest soldier worn out by exhaustion. Passepartout’s sleep was full of restless dreams about the bouncing of the day before. Mr. Fogg slept as peacefully as if he were at home in his quiet house in Saville Row.

They set off again at six in the morning, and the guide hoped to reach Allahabad by evening. If so, Mr. Fogg would lose only part of the forty-eight hours he had gained since the start of the tour. Kiouni picked up his fast pace again and soon came down the lower slopes of the Vindhias. Around noon they passed the village of Kallenger, on the Cani, one of the tributaries of the Ganges. The guide avoided inhabited places, since he thought it safer to stay in the open country along the first slopes of the great river’s basin. Allahabad was now only twelve miles to the north-east. They stopped beneath a clump of banana trees and made the most of the fruit, which was as nourishing as bread and as rich as cream, and they enjoyed it thoroughly.

At two o’clock the guide led them into a dense forest that stretched for several miles, since he preferred to travel under the cover of trees. So far they had met with nothing unpleasant, and the trip seemed about to end successfully, when the elephant grew uneasy and stopped short.
It was four o’clock by then.
“What is it?” asked Sir Francis, leaning out to look.
“I don’t know, officer,” answered the Parsee, who was straining to hear a muffled din coming through the thick branches.

The noise grew clearer. It now sounded like human voices in the distance, mixed with brass instruments. Passepartout was all eyes and ears. Mr. Fogg waited patiently and said nothing. The Parsee jumped down, tied the elephant to a tree and pushed into the thicket. He soon came back and said:
“A procession of Brahmins is coming this way. We must keep them from seeing us, if we can.”

The guide untied the elephant and led him into a thicket, asking the travellers as he did so not to move. He stood ready to jump onto the animal’s back at an instant’s notice if they had to flee, though he plainly expected the faithful procession to go by without noticing them, hidden as they were in the thick leaves.

The harsh clash of voices and instruments came closer, and now droning chants joined the beat of tambourines and cymbals. The head of the procession came into view under the trees, a hundred paces off, and the strange figures taking part in the religious rite could be made out easily through the branches. The priests came first, wearing mitres on their heads and long robes of lace. Men, women and children crowded around them, singing a kind of mournful psalm that tambourines and cymbals broke up at regular intervals. Behind them they pulled a cart on large wheels, whose spokes were shaped like serpents twisted around each other. Four richly decked zebus drew the cart, and on it stood a hideous four-armed statue. Its body was painted a dull red, and it had haunted eyes, wild hair, a lolling tongue and lips stained with betel. It stood upright on the body of a fallen, headless giant.
Sir Francis recognised the statue and whispered, “The goddess Kali, the goddess of love and death.”
“Of death, maybe,” Passepartout muttered back, “but of love? That ugly old hag? Never!”
The Parsee made a gesture for them to keep silent.

A band of old fakirs leaped and shrieked wildly around the statue. They were striped with ochre and covered in cuts from which blood trickled drop by drop. These stupid fanatics are the same sort who, at the great Indian festivals, still hurl themselves under the wheels of Juggernaut. Behind them came some Brahmins in all the splendour of Eastern dress, leading a woman who stumbled at every step. She was young, and as fair-skinned as a European. Her head, neck, shoulders, ears, arms, hands and toes were weighed down with jewels and gems, with bracelets, earrings and rings. A gold-bordered tunic under a thin muslin robe showed the outline of her body.

The guards who followed the young woman made a harsh contrast with her. They wore bare sabres at their belts and carried long inlaid pistols, and they bore a corpse on a palanquin. It was the body of an old man, richly dressed as a rajah. He wore, just as in life, a turban embroidered with pearls, a robe of silk and gold cloth, a cashmere scarf sewn with diamonds, and the magnificent weapons of a Hindoo prince. Next came the musicians, and last of all a rearguard of leaping fakirs whose shouts sometimes drowned out the instruments. They brought up the end of the procession.
Sir Francis watched the procession with a sorrowful face. Then he turned to the guide and said, “A suttee.”

The Parsee nodded and put a finger to his lips. The procession wound slowly away beneath the trees, and soon its last ranks vanished into the depths of the forest. The singing gradually faded. Now and then a cry sounded far off, until finally everything was quiet again.
Phileas Fogg had heard what Sir Francis said, and as soon as the procession was gone he asked, “What is a suttee?”
“A suttee,” answered the general, “is a human sacrifice, but a voluntary one. The woman you just saw will be burned tomorrow at daybreak.”
“Oh, the scoundrels!” cried Passepartout, who could not hold back his outrage.
“And the corpse?” asked Mr. Fogg.
“That is the prince, her husband,” said the guide, “an independent rajah of Bundelcund.”
“Is it possible,” Phileas Fogg went on, his voice showing not the slightest emotion, “that such barbaric customs still exist in India, and that the English have not been able to stamp them out?”

“These sacrifices don’t happen in most of India,” answered Sir Francis, “but we have no power over these wild regions, least of all here in Bundelcund. The whole district north of the Vindhias is the scene of constant murder and plunder.”
“The poor wretch!” exclaimed Passepartout. “To be burned alive!”

“Yes,” answered Sir Francis, “burned alive. And if she weren’t, you can’t imagine how her relatives would treat her. They would shave her head, keep her on a meagre ration of rice and treat her with contempt. She would be regarded as unclean and would die in some corner like a mangy dog. The prospect of such a terrible existence drives these poor creatures to the sacrifice far more than love or religious fanaticism does. Sometimes, though, the sacrifice really is voluntary, and the government has to step in actively to prevent it. Several years ago, when I was living at Bombay, a young widow asked the governor’s permission to be burned along with her husband’s body. As you can imagine, he refused. The woman left the town, took refuge with an independent rajah and carried out her self-chosen fate there.”
While Sir Francis spoke, the guide shook his head several times, and now he said, “The sacrifice that will take place tomorrow at dawn is not a voluntary one.”
“How do you know?”
“Everyone in Bundelcund knows about this affair.”
“But the poor creature didn’t seem to be putting up any resistance,” Sir Francis observed.
“That is because they drugged her with hemp and opium smoke.”
“But where are they taking her?”
“To the pagoda of Pillaji, two miles from here. She will spend the night there.”
“And the sacrifice will take place—”
“Tomorrow, at the very first light of dawn.”

The guide now led the elephant out of the thicket and leaped onto his neck. Just as he was about to start Kiouni forward with his special whistle, Mr. Fogg stopped him and said to Sir Francis Cromarty, “Suppose we save this woman.”
“Save the woman, Mr. Fogg!”
“I still have twelve hours to spare. I can use them for that.”
“Why, you are a man of heart!”
“Sometimes,” answered Phileas Fogg quietly. “When I have the time.”

chapters.title: Chapter 13. In which Passepartout Receives a New Proof that Fortune Favors the Brave
paragraphs: The plan was a bold one, full of difficulty, perhaps impossible. Mr. Fogg was about to risk his life, or at least his liberty, and with it the success of his tour. But he did not hesitate, and he found in Sir Francis Cromarty an enthusiastic ally.
As for Passepartout, he was ready for anything that might be proposed. His master’s idea charmed him; he sensed a heart, a soul, beneath that icy exterior. He was beginning to love Phileas Fogg.
There remained the guide: what course would he take? Would he not side with the Indians? Failing his help, they needed at least to be sure of his neutrality.
Sir Francis put the question to him frankly.
“Officers,” replied the guide, “I am a Parsee, and this woman is a Parsee. Command me as you will.”
“Excellent!” said Mr. Fogg.
“However,” the guide went on, “it is certain that we shall risk not only our lives, but horrible tortures, if we are caught.”
“That is foreseen,” replied Mr. Fogg. “I think we must wait till night before acting.”
“I think so,” said the guide.

The worthy Indian then gave some account of the victim. She was, he said, a celebrated beauty of the Parsee race and the daughter of a wealthy Bombay merchant. She had received a thoroughly English education in that city, and from her manners and intelligence would be taken for a European. Her name was Aouda. Left an orphan, she had been married against her will to the old rajah of Bundelcund; and, knowing the fate that awaited her, she had escaped, been recaptured, and condemned by the rajah’s relatives—who had an interest in her death—to the sacrifice from which it seemed she could not escape.

The Parsee’s narrative only strengthened Mr. Fogg and his companions in their generous plan. It was decided that the guide should steer the elephant toward the pagoda of Pillaji, which he accordingly approached as quickly as possible. Half an hour later they halted in a copse some five hundred feet from the pagoda, where they were well concealed; but they could hear the groans and cries of the fakirs distinctly.

They then discussed how to get at the victim. The guide was familiar with the pagoda of Pillaji, in which, he declared, the young woman was imprisoned. Could they enter one of its doors while the whole party of Indians lay in a drunken sleep, or was it safer to try to make a hole in the walls? That could only be decided on the spot and at the moment; but it was certain that the abduction must be made that very night, not when the victim was led to her funeral pyre at break of day. Then no human intervention could save her.

As soon as night fell, around six o’clock, they decided to make a reconnaissance around the pagoda. The cries of the fakirs were just ceasing; the Indians were in the act of sinking into the drunkenness produced by liquid opium mingled with hemp, and it might be possible to slip between them to the temple itself.

The Parsee, leading the others, crept noiselessly through the wood, and in ten minutes they found themselves on the banks of a small stream, from which, by the light of the rosin torches, they could make out a pyre of wood, on top of which lay the embalmed body of the rajah, which was to be burned with his wife. The pagoda, whose minarets loomed above the trees in the deepening dusk, stood a hundred steps away.
“Come!” whispered the guide.
He slipped through the brush more cautiously than ever, followed by his companions; the silence around them was broken only by the low murmuring of the wind among the branches.

Soon the Parsee stopped on the edge of the glade, which was lit up by the torches. The ground was covered by groups of Indians, motionless in their drunken sleep; it looked like a battlefield strewn with the dead. Men, women, and children lay together.

In the background, among the trees, the pagoda of Pillaji loomed distinctly. Much to the guide’s disappointment, the rajah’s guards, lit by torches, were watching at the doors and marching to and fro with bare sabres; and the priests, no doubt, were watching within as well.

The Parsee, now satisfied that it was impossible to force an entrance to the temple, advanced no farther but led his companions back. Phileas Fogg and Sir Francis Cromarty also saw that nothing could be attempted on that side. They stopped, and held a whispered consultation.
“It is only eight now,” said the brigadier, “and these guards may go to sleep too.”
“It is not impossible,” replied the Parsee.
They lay down at the foot of a tree and waited.

The time seemed long; the guide kept leaving them to look out from the edge of the wood, but the guards watched steadily by the glare of the torches, and a dim light crept through the windows of the pagoda.

They waited till midnight; but no change came over the guards, and it became clear that they could not be counted on to give in to sleep. The other plan must be carried out: an opening in the walls of the pagoda must be made. The question remained whether the priests were keeping watch beside their victim as steadily as the soldiers were at the door.

After a final consultation, the guide announced he was ready for the attempt and moved forward, the others following. They took a roundabout way so as to reach the pagoda at the rear. They came up to the walls about half-past twelve without having met anyone; here there was no guard, nor were there windows or doors.
The night was dark. The waning moon barely cleared the horizon and was covered by heavy clouds; the height of the trees deepened the darkness.

It was not enough to reach the walls; an opening had to be made in them, and for this purpose the party had only their pocket-knives. Happily the temple walls were built of brick and wood, which could be cut through with little difficulty; once one brick had been pried out, the rest would give way easily.

They set noiselessly to work, and the Parsee on one side and Passepartout on the other began to loosen the bricks so as to make an opening two feet wide. They were getting on quickly when suddenly a cry was heard inside the temple, followed almost at once by other cries answering from outside. Passepartout and the guide stopped. Had they been heard? Was the alarm being raised? Common prudence urged them to fall back, and they did so, followed by Phileas Fogg and Sir Francis. They hid themselves in the wood again and waited until the disturbance, whatever it was, ceased, holding themselves ready to resume their attempt without delay. But, awkwardly enough, the guards now appeared at the rear of the temple and stationed themselves there, ready to prevent any surprise.

It would be difficult to describe the disappointment of the party, thus interrupted in their work. They could no longer reach the victim; how, then, could they save her? Sir Francis shook his fists, Passepartout was beside himself, and the guide gnashed his teeth with rage. The unruffled Fogg waited without betraying any emotion.
“There is nothing for us to do but go away,” whispered Sir Francis.
“Nothing but go away,” echoed the guide.
“Stop,” said Fogg. “I am not due at Allahabad until tomorrow before noon.”
“But what can you hope to do?” asked Sir Francis. “In a few hours it will be daylight, and—”
“The chance that now seems lost may turn up at the last moment.”

Sir Francis would have liked to read Phileas Fogg’s eyes. What was this cool Englishman thinking? Was he planning to make a rush for the young woman at the very moment of the sacrifice and boldly snatch her from her executioners?

That would be utter folly, and it was hard to believe Fogg was such a fool. Sir Francis agreed, however, to remain to the end of this terrible drama. The guide led them to the rear of the glade, where they were able to watch the sleeping groups.
Meanwhile Passepartout, who had perched himself on the lower branches of a tree, was turning over an idea that had first struck him like a flash and was now firmly lodged in his brain.

He had begun by saying to himself, “What folly!” and then repeated, “Why not, after all? It’s a chance—perhaps the only one; and with such sots!” Thinking this, he slipped, with the suppleness of a serpent, down to the lowest branches, whose tips bent almost to the ground.

The hours passed, and the lighter tints in the sky now announced the approach of day, though it was not yet light. This was the moment. The slumbering crowd stirred to life, the tambourines sounded, songs and cries went up; the hour of the sacrifice had come. The doors of the pagoda swung open, and a bright light escaped from inside, in the midst of which Mr. Fogg and Sir Francis caught sight of the victim. Having shaken off the stupor of intoxication, she seemed to be struggling to escape from her executioner. Sir Francis’s heart pounded; and, convulsively seizing Mr. Fogg’s hand, he found an open knife in it. Just at that moment the crowd began to move. The young woman had again fallen into a stupor brought on by the fumes of hemp, and was carried among the fakirs, who escorted her with their wild religious cries.

Phileas Fogg and his companions, mingling with the rear ranks of the crowd, followed; and in two minutes they reached the banks of the stream and stopped fifty paces from the pyre, on which the rajah’s corpse still lay. In the half-light they saw the victim, quite senseless, stretched out beside her husband’s body. Then a torch was brought, and the wood, heavily soaked with oil, instantly caught fire.

At this moment Sir Francis and the guide seized Phileas Fogg, who, in an instant of mad generosity, was about to rush onto the pyre. But he had quickly pushed them aside when the whole scene suddenly changed. A cry of terror went up. The whole crowd threw themselves to the ground, terror-stricken.

The old rajah was not dead, then, since he rose all at once, like a spectre, took up his wife in his arms, and stepped down from the pyre in the midst of the clouds of smoke, which only heightened his ghostly appearance.
Fakirs and soldiers and priests, seized with sudden terror, lay there with their faces to the ground, not daring to lift their eyes and look upon such a prodigy.

The unconscious victim was carried along by the vigorous arms that supported her, and which she did not seem to burden in the least. Mr. Fogg and Sir Francis stood upright, the Parsee bowed his head, and Passepartout, no doubt, was scarcely less stupefied.
The resurrected rajah approached Sir Francis and Mr. Fogg, and, in an abrupt tone, said, “Let us be off!”

It was Passepartout himself, who had slipped onto the pyre in the midst of the smoke and, taking advantage of the darkness that still hung over them, had delivered the young woman from death! It was Passepartout who, playing his part with a fortunate boldness, had passed through the crowd in the midst of the general terror.

A moment later all four of the party had vanished into the woods, and the elephant was bearing them away at a rapid pace. But the cries and noise, and a ball that whizzed through Phileas Fogg’s hat, told them the trick had been discovered.

The old rajah’s body did, indeed, now appear on the burning pyre; and the priests, recovering from their terror, realized that an abduction had taken place. They rushed into the forest, followed by the soldiers, who fired a volley after the fugitives; but the latter quickly increased the distance between them, and before long found themselves out of reach of bullets and arrows.

chapters.title: Chapter 14. In which Phileas Fogg Descends the Whole Length of the Beautiful Valley of the Ganges Without Ever Thinking of Seeing It
paragraphs: The reckless rescue had succeeded, and Passepartout spent the next hour laughing delightedly over it. Sir Francis warmly clasped the good fellow’s hand, while his master said, “Well done!”—high praise indeed from him. Passepartout answered that Mr. Fogg deserved all the credit. He himself had simply had a “queer” idea. He laughed at the thought that for a few moments he, Passepartout, former gymnast and fire-brigade sergeant, had been a charming woman’s husband: an ancient, embalmed rajah! The young Indian woman, meanwhile, had known nothing of these events. Wrapped in a travelling blanket, she now rested in one of the howdahs.

Under the Parsee’s expert direction, the elephant moved quickly through the forest, still dark, and within an hour of leaving the pagoda had crossed a broad plain. They stopped at seven. The young woman remained utterly exhausted and unresponsive. The guide gave her a little brandy and water, but could not dispel the heavy drowsiness that clouded her senses. Sir Francis knew the effects of intoxication from hemp fumes and reassured the others about her condition. Her future worried him more. He told Phileas Fogg that if Aouda stayed in India, she would inevitably be recaptured by the men who meant to kill her. Their fellow fanatics were spread throughout the country; despite the English police, they could seize their victim in Madras, Bombay, or Calcutta. Only by leaving India for good could she be safe.
Phileas Fogg answered that he would consider what should be done.

They arrived at Allahabad station around ten. Here the railway resumed after the gap, and the train could carry them to Calcutta in under twenty-four hours. Phileas Fogg would therefore have time to board the Hong Kong steamer, which sailed from Calcutta at noon the following day, October 25th.

They settled the young woman in a station waiting room. Passepartout was sent to buy personal necessities for her, together with a dress, a shawl, and some furs, his master placing no limit on the expense. He set out at once into Allahabad—the City of God—one of India’s holiest cities. It stands at the meeting of the sacred Ganges and Jumna, whose waters draw pilgrims from throughout the peninsula. According to the Ramayana legends, the Ganges has its source in heaven and descends to earth through Brahma’s intervention.

While shopping, Passepartout made sure to take a good look at the city. Its once-imposing defensive fort had become a state prison, and its trade had dwindled. He searched in vain for a bazaar like the one he used to visit in Regent Street. Eventually he found a bad-tempered elderly Jew dealing in second-hand goods, from whom he bought a dress of Scotch fabric, a large cloak, and a fine otter-skin pelisse. He paid seventy-five pounds without hesitation and returned triumphantly to the station.
The effects of the treatment Aouda had received from the priests of Pillaji gradually wore off. As she returned to herself, her lovely eyes regained their gentle Indian expression.
In celebrating the beauty of the queen of Ahmehnagara, the poet-king Ucaf Uddaul writes:

“Her shining hair, parted in two, frames the harmonious lines of her pale, delicate cheeks, radiant with freshness and colour. Her ebony eyebrows have the shape and grace of the bow of Kama, god of love. Beneath long, silky lashes, the black pupils of her large, clear eyes hold the purest reflections and a heavenly light, like the sacred lakes of Himalaya. Her teeth, fine and even and white, shine between smiling lips like drops of dew within the half-hidden heart of a passion-flower. Her finely shaped ears, her vermilion hands, and her tiny feet, curved and tender as a lotus-bud, gleam with the brilliance of Ceylon’s loveliest pearls and Golconda’s most dazzling diamonds. Her slender, supple waist, which one hand could encircle, reveals the rounded lines of her figure and the beauty of her bosom, where youth in full bloom displays its abundant treasures. Beneath the silk folds of her tunic, she seems moulded from pure silver by the divine hand of Vicvarcarma, the immortal sculptor.”

Without applying this poetic rapture to Aouda, it is enough to say that she was a charming woman in every European sense of the expression. She spoke exceptionally pure English. The guide had not overstated matters when he said that education had transformed the young Parsee woman.

As the train prepared to leave Allahabad, Mr. Fogg paid the guide exactly the agreed fee for his work, without adding a farthing. Passepartout was astonished, remembering how much his master owed the man’s devotion. At Pillaji he had risked his life, and if the Indians caught him afterwards he would scarcely escape their revenge. There was also Kiouni to deal with. What was to become of an elephant bought at such a price? Phileas Fogg had already settled that question.
“Parsee,” he told the guide, “you have given us both service and devotion. I have paid you for the service, but not the devotion. Would you care to keep the elephant? He belongs to you.”
The guide’s eyes shone with emotion.
“Your honour is making me a wealthy man!” he cried.
“Keep him, guide,” Mr. Fogg replied. “Even then, I shall remain in your debt.”
“Good!” cried Passepartout. “Accept him, my friend. Kiouni is a courageous, faithful animal.” He went over and fed the elephant several lumps of sugar. “Here you are, Kiouni; here, and here.”

The elephant grunted contentedly, curled his trunk round Passepartout’s waist, and raised him to the height of his own head. Entirely unafraid, Passepartout stroked him, and the animal lowered him gently back to the ground.

Soon Phileas Fogg, Sir Francis Cromarty, and Passepartout were speeding towards Benares in a railway carriage with Aouda, who had been given the best seat. They covered the eighty miles in two hours. During the journey she fully regained consciousness. Imagine her amazement at finding herself on a train, wearing European clothes and surrounded by complete strangers! Her companions first gave her a little liquor to restore her strength, and Sir Francis then explained everything that had happened. He particularly praised the courage with which Phileas Fogg had readily risked his own life to save her, and told how Passepartout’s audacious idea had brought the rescue to its happy conclusion. Mr. Fogg remained silent. Passepartout, embarrassed, kept saying that “there was nothing worth mentioning.”

Aouda’s thanks to her rescuers were deeply moving, expressed more in tears than speech; her beautiful eyes conveyed gratitude more clearly than her lips could. Then her thoughts returned to the sacrifice and the dangers still threatening her, and she shuddered in terror.

Understanding what troubled Aouda, Phileas Fogg sought to reassure her by offering to take her with him to Hong Kong. There she could stay safely until the affair had died down. She accepted eagerly and gratefully. It appeared that she had a Parsee relative among the leading merchants of Hong Kong, a wholly English city though it stands on an island off the Chinese coast.

At half past twelve they stopped at Benares. Brahmin legends place the city on the site of ancient Casi, which, like Mahomet’s tomb, once hung suspended between earth and heaven. Modern Benares, called the Athens of India by Orientalists, rests much less poetically on solid ground. As the train entered, Passepartout caught sight of brick houses and clay huts that gave the place a desolate appearance.

Sir Francis Cromarty was leaving them at Benares, since the troops he was rejoining were camped a few miles north of the city. He wished Phileas Fogg every success and hoped he would return one day on a visit less unusual but more rewarding. Mr. Fogg gave his hand a slight squeeze. Aouda, mindful of what she owed Sir Francis, said goodbye more warmly, and the gallant general gave Passepartout a hearty handshake.

Beyond Benares the railway followed the Ganges valley for a time. Through the carriage windows the travellers glimpsed Behar’s varied scenery: green-clad mountains; fields of barley, wheat, and corn; jungles inhabited by green alligators; tidy villages; and forests still thick with leaves. Elephants bathed in the sacred river. Despite the late season and the cold air, groups of Indians solemnly performed their ritual washing. These devout Brahmins were Buddhism’s fiercest enemies. They worshipped Vishnu, the sun god; Shiva, the divine embodiment of natural forces; and Brahma, supreme ruler of priests and lawmakers. What would these gods make of today’s anglicised India, with steamers racing and whistling along the Ganges, alarming the gulls on its waters, the turtles crowding its banks, and the faithful living beside it?

The landscape flashed past, except when steam briefly hid it altogether. The travellers could barely distinguish Chupenie’s fort, twenty miles southwest of Benares, once the stronghold of Behar’s rajahs; Ghazipur and its celebrated rose-water works; Lord Cornwallis’s tomb on the left bank of the Ganges; the fortified town of Buxar; or Patna, a great centre of manufacture and trade and the site of India’s chief opium market. Nor could they properly see Monghir, more than merely European, as English as Manchester or Birmingham, with iron foundries, factories making edged tools, and tall chimneys sending black smoke into the sky.

Night settled over the countryside. The train raced on at full speed among the roars of tigers, bears, and wolves fleeing the locomotive. Bengal’s marvels vanished into the darkness: Golconda, ruined Gour, the former capital Murshedabad, Burdwan, Hugly, and the French town of Chandernagor, where Passepartout would have been proud to see his country’s flag flying.
They reached Calcutta at seven in the morning. The Hong Kong packet sailed at noon, leaving Phileas Fogg five hours to spare.

His journal scheduled his arrival in Calcutta for the 25th of October, and he had arrived on exactly that date. He was therefore neither ahead nor behind. As we have seen, the two days won between London and Bombay had been spent crossing India. Yet one should not imagine that Phileas Fogg regretted losing them.

chapters.title: Chapter 15. In which the Bag of Banknotes Disgorges Some Thousands of Pounds More
paragraphs: The train pulled into the station. Passepartout jumped out first, and Mr. Fogg followed, helping his lovely companion down. Phileas Fogg meant to go straight to the Hong Kong steamer so that Aouda could be made comfortable for the voyage. He did not want to leave her side while they were still in dangerous territory.
Just as he was leaving the station, a policeman stepped up and said, “Mr. Phileas Fogg?”
“That is me.”
“And is this man your servant?” the policeman added, pointing at Passepartout.
“Yes.”
“Please, both of you, come along with me.”

Mr. Fogg showed no surprise at all. The policeman represented the law, and to an Englishman the law is sacred. Passepartout tried to argue the point, but the policeman rapped him with his stick, and Mr. Fogg signalled him to obey.
“May this young lady come with us?” he asked.
“She may,” the policeman answered.

The policeman took Mr. Fogg, Aouda and Passepartout to a palkigahri, a kind of four-wheeled carriage pulled by two horses. They climbed in and were driven off. For the twenty minutes the ride lasted, nobody said a word. They crossed the “black town” first, with its narrow streets, its wretched, filthy huts and its squalid crowds. After that came the “European town,” a welcome change, with its bright brick houses shaded by coconut trees, its forest of masts, and its elegantly dressed riders and handsome carriages going back and forth, even at that early hour.

The carriage halted in front of a modest house that did not look much like a private home. The policeman asked his prisoners (for that is what they really were) to get out. He led them into a room with barred windows and said, “You will appear before Judge Obadiah at half past eight.”
Then he left and shut the door behind him.
“Why, we are prisoners!” exclaimed Passepartout, dropping into a chair.
Aouda, struggling to hide her distress, said to Mr. Fogg, “Sir, you must leave me to my fate! You are being treated like this because of me, because you saved me!”

Phileas Fogg simply said that this was impossible. It was highly unlikely that anyone would arrest him for stopping a suttee. The people complaining would never dare to bring such a charge. There had to be some mistake. Besides, he would not abandon Aouda in any case, but would escort her to Hong Kong.
“But the steamer leaves at noon!” Passepartout said anxiously.
“We shall be on board by noon,” his master answered calmly.
He said it so firmly that Passepartout could not help muttering to himself, “Parbleu, that’s certain! We’ll be on board before noon.” But he was far from reassured.

At half past eight the door opened and the policeman came in. He asked them to follow him and led them into the next hall. It was clearly a courtroom, and a crowd of Europeans and natives already filled the back of it.

Mr. Fogg and his two companions sat on a bench facing the desks of the magistrate and his clerk. A moment later Judge Obadiah came in, a fat, round man, with the clerk behind him. He took a wig down from a nail and hastily pulled it onto his head.
“First case,” he said. Then he put a hand to his head and exclaimed, “Heh! This isn’t my wig!”
“No, your worship,” the clerk answered. “It’s mine.”
“My dear Mr. Oysterpuff, how is a judge supposed to pass a wise sentence in a clerk’s wig?”
The wigs were swapped.
Passepartout was growing anxious, because the hands of the big clock above the judge seemed to be racing around the dial.
“First case,” Judge Obadiah said again.
“Phileas Fogg?” called Oysterpuff.
“I am here,” said Mr. Fogg.
“Passepartout?”
“Present,” answered Passepartout.
“Good,” said the judge. “Prisoners, we have been looking for you for two days on the trains from Bombay.”
“But what are we accused of?” Passepartout asked impatiently.
“You are about to be told.”
“I am an English subject, sir,” said Mr. Fogg, “and I have the right—”
“Have you been mistreated?”
“Not at all.”
“Very well. Bring in the complainants.”
At the judge’s order a door was thrown open, and three Indian priests came in.
“So that’s it,” Passepartout muttered. “These are the villains who wanted to burn our young lady.”

The priests took their places in front of the judge. The clerk then read out in a loud voice a charge of sacrilege against Phileas Fogg and his servant, who were accused of desecrating a place that the Brahmin religion holds sacred.
“You hear the charge?” the judge asked.
“Yes, sir,” answered Mr. Fogg, checking his watch, “and I admit it.”
“You admit it?”
“I admit it, and I want to hear these priests admit, in their turn, what they were about to do at the pagoda of Pillaji.”
The priests exchanged glances. They did not seem to follow what he had said.
“Yes,” cried Passepartout hotly. “At the pagoda of Pillaji, where they were about to burn their victim.”
The judge stared in astonishment, and the priests were dumbfounded.
“What victim?” said Judge Obadiah. “Burn whom? In Bombay itself?”
“Bombay?” cried Passepartout.
“Of course. We are not talking about the pagoda of Pillaji, but about the pagoda of Malabar Hill, at Bombay.”
“And as proof,” the clerk added, “here are the very shoes the desecrator left behind.”
With that he set a pair of shoes on his desk.
“My shoes!” cried Passepartout, who was so surprised that this reckless outcry slipped out before he could stop it.
You can imagine how confused master and servant were. They had completely forgotten the Bombay affair, and now it was the reason they were being held in Calcutta.

Fix the detective had seen what an advantage Passepartout’s escapade gave him. He had put off his own departure for twelve hours and gone to see the priests of Malabar Hill. He knew that the English authorities punished this sort of offence very harshly, so he promised the priests a handsome sum in damages and sent them on to Calcutta by the next train. Because of the delay caused by the rescue of the young widow, Fix and the priests reached the Indian capital ahead of Mr. Fogg and his servant. A telegram had already warned the magistrates to arrest the pair if they turned up. You can imagine Fix’s disappointment when he found that Phileas Fogg had not appeared in Calcutta. He decided that the robber must have stopped somewhere along the route and gone into hiding in the southern provinces. For twenty-four hours Fix watched the station in feverish anxiety. At last he was rewarded by the sight of Mr. Fogg and Passepartout arriving with a young woman, whose presence he could not begin to explain. He rushed off to find a policeman, and that was how the party came to be arrested and brought before Judge Obadiah.

If Passepartout had been a little less preoccupied, he would have noticed the detective tucked away in a corner of the courtroom, following the proceedings with an interest that is easy to understand. For the warrant had failed to reach him at Calcutta, just as it had at Bombay and Suez.
Unfortunately Judge Obadiah had heard Passepartout’s rash outburst, and the poor fellow would have given anything to take it back.
“The facts are admitted?” asked the judge.
“Admitted,” Mr. Fogg answered coldly.

“Since,” the judge went on, “English law protects the religions of the Indian people equally and strictly, and since the man Passepartout has admitted violating the sacred pagoda of Malabar Hill, at Bombay, on the 20th of October, I sentence the said Passepartout to fifteen days in prison and a fine of three hundred pounds.”
“Three hundred pounds!” cried Passepartout, shocked at the size of the sum.
“Silence!” shouted the constable.

“And since,” the judge continued, “it has not been proved that the master did not conspire with the servant in this act, and since the master must in any case be held responsible for the acts of his paid servant, I sentence Phileas Fogg to a week in prison and a fine of one hundred and fifty pounds.”

Fix quietly rubbed his hands in satisfaction. If Phileas Fogg could be held in Calcutta for a week, that was more than enough time for the warrant to arrive. Passepartout was stunned. This sentence would ruin his master. A twenty-thousand-pound wager lost, because he, like a prize fool, had gone into that dreadful pagoda!

Phileas Fogg was as composed as if the verdict had nothing to do with him, and he did not so much as raise an eyebrow while it was read out. Just as the clerk was calling the next case, he stood up and said, “I offer bail.”
“That is your right,” said the judge.
Fix’s blood ran cold, but he recovered himself when he heard the judge announce that bail would be one thousand pounds for each prisoner.
“I will pay it immediately,” said Mr. Fogg. He took a roll of banknotes from the carpet-bag that Passepartout was holding and laid them on the clerk’s desk.
“This sum will be returned to you when you are released from prison,” said the judge. “In the meantime you are free on bail.”
“Come!” said Phileas Fogg to his servant.
“But at least let them give me back my shoes!” cried Passepartout angrily.
“Ah, these are pretty expensive shoes!” he muttered as they were handed over. “More than a thousand pounds apiece, and they pinch my feet besides.”

Mr. Fogg offered Aouda his arm and left, with the crestfallen Passepartout trailing behind. Fix still hoped that the robber would not abandon the two thousand pounds after all, but would choose to serve out his week in jail, and he set out after Mr. Fogg. That gentleman hailed a carriage, and soon the party was set down on one of the quays.

The “Rangoon” lay half a mile off in the harbour, with the flag signalling departure flying from her masthead. Eleven o’clock was striking, so Mr. Fogg was an hour ahead of time. Fix watched them get out of the carriage and row off to the steamer in a boat, and he stamped his feet in frustration.

“So the rascal is getting away after all!” he exclaimed. “Two thousand pounds thrown away! He spends like a thief! I’ll follow him to the ends of the earth if I have to, but at this rate the stolen money will soon be gone.”

The detective was not far wrong. Since leaving London, between travel costs, bribes, the purchase of the elephant, bail and fines, Mr. Fogg had already spent over five thousand pounds along the way. And the share of the recovered money that was promised to the detectives was shrinking fast.

chapters.title: Chapter 16. In which Fix Does Not Seem to Understand in the Least What is Said to Him
paragraphs: The “Rangoon,” one of the Peninsular and Oriental Company’s vessels serving Chinese and Japanese waters, was an iron screw steamer of about seventeen hundred and seventy tons, powered by four-hundred-horsepower engines. Although she could match the “Mongolia” for speed, her fittings were inferior, and Aouda’s accommodation was less comfortable than Phileas Fogg would have liked. Still, the journey from Calcutta to Hong Kong covered only some three thousand five hundred miles and took ten to twelve days. The young woman, moreover, was easy to please.

In the first days aboard, Aouda came to know her protector better and repeatedly expressed her profound gratitude for his help. The unruffled gentleman appeared to receive her thanks coldly: neither his manner nor his voice revealed the faintest feeling. Yet he seemed constantly alert to anything that might improve her comfort. Every day he visited at regular hours, less to speak himself than to sit and listen to her. His courtesy was faultless, but it had the precision of an automaton whose movements had been programmed for that purpose. Aouda did not quite understand him, although Passepartout had explained something of his master’s eccentricity and made her smile with the story of the wager driving him round the world. She owed Phileas Fogg her life, after all, and gratitude always cast him in a noble light.

Aouda confirmed the moving account of her past given by the Parsee guide. She did indeed belong to the highest of India’s native races. Many Parsee merchants had grown immensely wealthy in the cotton trade; one of them, Sir Jametsee Jeejeebhoy, had been made a baronet by the English government. Aouda was related to this eminent man, and the person she hoped to join in Hong Kong was his cousin Jeejeeh. She could not know whether he would offer her protection, but Mr. Fogg tried to put her worries to rest, assuring her that everything would be arranged mathematically—that was the very word he used. Aouda fixed her great eyes on him, eyes “clear as the sacred lakes of the Himalaya.” But Fogg, unyielding and as reserved as ever, showed no inclination to plunge into that lake.

For the first few days the voyage went smoothly, with fine weather and favourable winds. Soon they sighted Great Andaman, the largest of the Bay of Bengal islands, its picturesque Saddle Peak rising two thousand four hundred feet above the water. The steamer sailed close to shore, but none of the savage Papuans appeared. They occupy humanity’s lowest rank, though they are not cannibals, as some have claimed.

As the ship passed the islands, the views were magnificent. Immense forests of palms, arecs, bamboo, teak, giant mimosa, and towering ferns filled the foreground, with graceful mountain silhouettes against the sky behind them. Along the coast, thousands of valuable swallows swarmed, their nests providing a luxury delicacy for the tables of the Celestial Empire. The varied scenery of the Andamans soon fell behind, however, and the “Rangoon” sped towards the Straits of Malacca, the gateway to the China seas.

Meanwhile, what was happening to detective Fix, unhappily dragged from one country to the next? He had boarded the “Rangoon” in Calcutta without Passepartout noticing, after leaving instructions to forward the arrest warrant to Hong Kong if it arrived. He hoped to stay out of sight until the voyage ended. Passepartout believed him still in Bombay; explaining his presence on this ship without arousing suspicion would have been difficult. Necessity nevertheless drove him to renew his acquaintance with the worthy servant, as we shall see.

Hong Kong now held all the detective’s hopes and wishes. The stop at Singapore would be too short for him to take any effective action. He must arrest the thief in Hong Kong, or probably lose him for ever. It was the last English territory on their route; beyond it, China, Japan, and America offered Fogg almost certain sanctuary. If the warrant finally reached Hong Kong, Fix could arrest him and hand him over to the local police, ending the difficulty. Beyond Hong Kong, however, an ordinary warrant would be useless. Extradition papers would be needed, bringing delays and complications that the rogue could exploit to escape justice.

During long hours alone in his cabin, Fix weighed these possibilities, telling himself again and again, “Either the warrant will be waiting in Hong Kong, and I can arrest my man, or it will not. In that case I absolutely must prevent him leaving. Bombay was a failure, and Calcutta was a failure. If Hong Kong is another, my reputation is finished. Whatever it costs, I _must_ succeed! But if holding him there becomes my only option, how am I to do it?”

Fix decided that as a last resort he would take Passepartout into his confidence and reveal what sort of man his master really was. He was certain that the servant was no accomplice. Once he knew the truth, and feared being implicated himself, Passepartout would surely help the detective. But this was a risky approach, to be used only when everything else had failed. One word from servant to master could ruin the whole pursuit. Fix was therefore in a painful predicament. Then a fresh thought struck him: Aouda’s presence aboard the “Rangoon,” travelling with Phileas Fogg, gave him something new to consider.

Who was she? What circumstances had brought her into Fogg’s company? They had plainly met between Bombay and Calcutta, but where? Was it a chance encounter, or had Fogg gone into the interior specifically to find this attractive young woman? Fix was thoroughly puzzled. Perhaps, he thought, this was a scandalous elopement. The notion took such hold of him that he decided to exploit the supposed intrigue. Married or unmarried, the woman might enable him to create difficulties in Hong Kong that Mr. Fogg could not buy his way out of, however much he paid.
But dare he wait for Hong Kong? Fogg had an infuriating habit of leaping straight from one ship to another. Before anything could be done, he might be well on his way to Yokohama.

Fix concluded that he must alert the English authorities and send advance notice of the “Rangoon.” That would be simple: the ship called at Singapore, which had a telegraph connection with Hong Kong. Before taking any firmer action, though, he finally decided to question Passepartout. Getting him to talk would present no difficulty, and with no time to waste, Fix prepared to reveal his presence.
It was the 30th of October. The “Rangoon” was expected to reach Singapore the following day.

Leaving his cabin, Fix went up on deck. Passepartout was walking back and forth near the bow. The detective hurried over, putting on an air of utter astonishment. “You, here aboard the ‘Rangoon’?” he cried.

“Monsieur Fix, you’re on this ship?” Passepartout answered in genuine surprise, recognising his friend from the “Mongolia.” “I left you in Bombay, and now here you are travelling to Hong Kong! Are you circling the world as well?”
“No, no,” said Fix. “Hong Kong is where I shall stop, for a few days at least.”
“Hmm!” Passepartout seemed puzzled for a moment. “Then how have I managed not to see you since we sailed from Calcutta?”
“Oh, a little seasickness kept me in my berth. The Gulf of Bengal suits me less well than the Indian Ocean. And how is Mr. Fogg doing?”
“As healthy and punctual as ever, not a single day late! But there is something you don’t know, Monsieur Fix: we have a young lady travelling with us.”
“A young lady?” the detective echoed, acting as though he did not understand.

Passepartout then told him Aouda’s story, the incident at the Bombay pagoda, the elephant bought for two thousand pounds, the rescue, the arrest and sentence in the Calcutta court, and his own and Mr. Fogg’s release on bail. Although Fix knew all about those last events, he pretended that every part of the account was equally new to him. Passepartout was delighted to have so attentive an audience.
“Does your master intend to take the young woman all the way to Europe?”
“Certainly not. We are only taking her to the protection of a relative, a wealthy merchant who lives in Hong Kong.”
“No opening there,” Fix thought, hiding his disappointment. “Would you care for a glass of gin, Mr. Passepartout?”
“With pleasure, Monsieur Fix. We must at least share a friendly drink aboard the ‘Rangoon.’”

chapters.title: Chapter 17. Showing What Happened on the Voyage from Singapore to Hong Kong
paragraphs: After this conversation the detective and Passepartout often met on deck. Fix kept his distance, though, and made no further attempt to draw out his companion about Mr. Fogg. He caught a glimpse of that mysterious gentleman once or twice, but Mr. Fogg mostly stayed in the cabin, where he kept Aouda company or, following his unshakeable habit, played a hand of whist.

Passepartout began to wonder in earnest what odd chance kept Fix on the very route his master was following. It was truly worth pondering. This undeniably pleasant and obliging man had first turned up at Suez, then appeared on the “Mongolia,” then left the ship at Bombay, which he gave out as his destination, and now had shown up unexpectedly on the “Rangoon.” Why was he following Mr. Fogg step by step? What was Fix after? Passepartout was ready to bet his Indian shoes, which he kept with religious care, that Fix would also leave Hong Kong when they did, and probably on the same steamer.

Passepartout could have racked his brains for a hundred years without hitting on what the detective was really up to. It would never have occurred to him that Phileas Fogg was being hunted around the globe as a thief. But human nature drives us to solve every mystery, and Passepartout suddenly hit on an explanation for Fix’s movements that was in fact quite reasonable. Fix, he decided, could only be an agent sent by Mr. Fogg’s friends at the Reform Club to follow him and make sure he really went around the world as agreed.

“It’s obvious!” the good servant told himself again, proud of his own cleverness. “He’s a spy, sent to keep an eye on us! And that is not quite fair, either, to spy on Mr. Fogg, who is such an honourable man! Ah, gentlemen of the Reform, this will cost you dearly!”

Passepartout was delighted with his discovery, but he decided to say nothing to his master, since Mr. Fogg would be rightly offended by this distrust from his opponents. He did resolve to tease Fix whenever he got the chance, with mysterious hints that would not give away what he really suspected.

On the afternoon of Wednesday, 30th October, the “Rangoon” entered the Strait of Malacca, which divides the Malay peninsula from Sumatra. Rugged, mountainous little islands hid the beauties of that noble island from the passengers’ view. At four the next morning the “Rangoon” dropped anchor at Singapore to take on coal, half a day ahead of her scheduled arrival. Phileas Fogg noted this gain in his journal. Then, with Aouda, who had said she would like a walk ashore, he left the ship.
Fix suspected every move Mr. Fogg made, so he followed them carefully, taking care not to be seen. Passepartout, laughing to himself at Fix’s manoeuvres, went about his usual errands.

The island of Singapore does not look imposing, since it has no mountains, but its appearance is not without charm. It is like a park crisscrossed by pleasant roads and avenues. A handsome carriage, drawn by a pair of sleek New Holland horses, took Phileas Fogg and Aouda in among rows of palms with glossy leaves, and clove trees whose cloves form the heart of a half-open flower. Pepper plants took the place of the thorny hedges of European fields. Sago bushes and big ferns with magnificent fronds varied the look of this tropical climate, while nutmeg trees in full leaf filled the air with a penetrating fragrance. Agile, grinning troops of monkeys skipped about in the trees, and there was no shortage of tigers in the jungles.

After two hours’ drive through the countryside, Aouda and Mr. Fogg went back to the town. It is a huge cluster of heavy, irregular-looking houses, ringed by charming gardens full of tropical fruits and plants. At ten o’clock they went back on board, closely followed by the detective, who had kept them in sight the whole time.

Passepartout had been buying several dozen mangoes. This fruit is as big as a good-sized apple, dark brown outside and bright red inside, and its white flesh melts in the mouth and gives lovers of fine food a delicious sensation. He was waiting for them on deck and was only too happy to offer some to Aouda, who thanked him very graciously.

At eleven o’clock the “Rangoon” steamed out of Singapore harbour, and within a few hours the high mountains of Malacca had dropped out of sight, together with their forests, which are home to the most beautifully furred tigers in the world. Singapore lies some thirteen hundred miles from the island of Hong Kong, a small English colony off the Chinese coast. Phileas Fogg hoped to make the trip in six days, to be in time for the steamer leaving on the 6th of November for Yokohama, the chief Japanese port.
The “Rangoon” carried a large number of passengers, and many of them left at Singapore, among them a number of Indians, Ceylonese, Chinese, Malays and Portuguese, mostly travelling second class.

The weather, which had been fine until then, turned with the last quarter of the moon. The sea ran high, and at times the wind rose almost to a gale, but luckily it blew from the south-west and so helped the steamer along. The captain raised the sails whenever he could, and with steam and sail working together the ship made rapid progress along the coasts of Anam and Cochin China. Because the “Rangoon” was badly built, though, extra precautions were needed in poor weather. The time lost this way nearly drove Passepartout out of his mind, yet it seemed not to bother his master in the least. Passepartout blamed the captain, the engineer and the crew, and sent everyone connected with the ship to the land where the pepper grows. Perhaps the thought of the gas burning mercilessly at his expense in Saville Row had something to do with his fiery impatience.
“So you are in a great hurry,” Fix said to him one day, “to reach Hong Kong?”
“A very great hurry!”
“I suppose Mr. Fogg is anxious to catch the steamer for Yokohama?”
“Terribly anxious.”
“So you believe in this journey around the world?”
“Completely. Don’t you, Mr. Fix?”
“I? I don’t believe a word of it.”
“You’re a sly dog!” said Passepartout, giving him a wink.

This remark disturbed Fix, though he could not say why. Had the Frenchman guessed his real purpose? He did not know what to think. But how could Passepartout have found out that he was a detective? Still, the way the man spoke clearly meant more than his words said.
The next day Passepartout went even further, since he simply could not hold his tongue.
“Mr. Fix,” he said in a teasing tone, “will we be so unlucky as to lose you when we get to Hong Kong?”
“Why,” Fix answered, a little embarrassed, “I don’t know. Perhaps—”

“Ah, if only you would come on with us! An agent of the Peninsular Company can’t stop partway, you know! You were only going to Bombay, and here you are in China. America is not far off, and from America to Europe is just a step.”
Fix gazed hard at his companion, whose face was perfectly calm, and laughed along with him. But Passepartout kept on teasing and asked whether he made much money in his present line of work.
“Yes and no,” said Fix. “There’s good luck and bad luck in this business. But you must understand that I don’t travel at my own expense.”
“Oh, I’m quite sure of that!” cried Passepartout, laughing heartily.

Fix was thoroughly puzzled. He went down to his cabin and gave himself up to thought. He was clearly under suspicion. Somehow the Frenchman had found out that he was a detective. But had he told his master? What part was he playing in all this? Was he an accomplice or not? Was the game up, then? Fix spent several hours turning all this over in his mind. At times he thought all was lost, then he persuaded himself that Fogg did not know he was there, and then he could not decide what course was best.

Even so, he kept a cool head, and in the end he resolved to be frank with Passepartout. If he found he could not arrest Fogg at Hong Kong, and if Fogg got ready to leave that last foothold of English territory, then he, Fix, would tell Passepartout everything. Either the servant was his master’s accomplice, in which case the master knew about his activities and he would fail, or the servant knew nothing of the robbery, and in that case it would be in his interest to abandon the robber.

That was how matters stood between Fix and Passepartout. Meanwhile Phileas Fogg moved about above them in perfect, unconscious majesty. He was travelling methodically in his orbit around the world, paying no attention to the lesser stars that circled around him. Yet close by there was what astronomers would call a disturbing star, one that might have stirred up some agitation in this gentleman’s heart. But no! To Passepartout’s great surprise, Aouda’s charms had no effect. And if there were any disturbances, they would have been harder to calculate than those of Uranus that led to the discovery of Neptune.

It grew more astonishing to Passepartout every day. He could read in Aouda’s eyes how deep her gratitude to his master ran. Phileas Fogg, brave and gallant though he was, must be quite heartless, he thought. As for any feeling this journey might have awakened in him, there was plainly no trace of it, while poor Passepartout lived in a constant daydream.

One day he was leaning on the railing of the engine room, watching the machinery, when a sudden lurch of the steamer lifted the propeller out of the water. Steam came hissing out of the valves, and this made Passepartout indignant.
“The valves aren’t getting enough pressure!” he exclaimed. “We’re not moving. Oh, these English! If this were an American ship, we might blow up, but at least we would go faster!”

chapters.title: Chapter 18. In which Phileas Fogg, Passepartout, and Fix Go each about His Business
paragraphs: Bad weather marked the final days of the voyage. The wind stubbornly held in the northwest, blowing hard and slowing the steamer. The “Rangoon” rolled heavily, and her passengers grew weary of the enormous, endless waves thrown across their path. On the 3rd of November the weather developed into something of a tempest. Furious squalls tossed the ship about, and the waves rose high. Every sail was reefed, but even the bare rigging caught too much wind, shaking and whistling in the gale. The ship could make only slow progress. Her captain reckoned she would reach Hong Kong twenty hours late, or later still if the storm continued.

Phileas Fogg watched the raging sea with his usual composure, though it seemed determined to delay him personally. His expression never altered, even for an instant. A twenty-hour delay would make him miss the Yokohama steamer and would almost certainly cost him his wager. Yet this man of iron nerve showed neither irritation nor impatience. One might have thought the storm had been anticipated and entered in his schedule. Aouda marvelled that he remained as calm as on the day they first met.

Fix saw the situation quite differently. The storm delighted him; only if wind and waves had driven the “Rangoon” back would his pleasure have been complete. Every delay increased his hopes by making it more likely that Fogg would have to spend several days in Hong Kong. Now heaven itself was on his side, sending squalls and gusts to help him. He was seasick, but that small inconvenience counted for nothing. While his body writhed in misery, his spirit leapt with triumphant hope.

Passepartout’s fury at the weather was beyond words. Until now everything had gone so well! Land and sea appeared to serve his master; trains and steamers obeyed him, and wind and steam worked together to hurry him along. Had their luck finally turned? Passepartout was as agitated as though the twenty thousand pounds were his own. The storm maddened him, the gale drove him wild, and he longed to whip the stubborn sea into submission. Poor fellow! Fix took care to hide his satisfaction. Had it shown, Passepartout might scarcely have stopped himself from striking him.

Unable to sit quietly below, Passepartout stayed on deck throughout the storm. He fancied he could speed the ship along by helping the crew. Questions poured from him upon the captain, officers, and sailors, who could not help laughing at his impatience. He wanted to know exactly when the storm would end. They referred him to the barometer, which showed no intention of rising. Passepartout shook it, without any visible result: neither shaking nor curses could persuade it to change its mind.

On the 4th, however, the sea began to settle and the storm weakened. The wind swung south and once again favoured them. Passepartout’s mood brightened with the weather. Some sails were set, and the “Rangoon” returned to full speed. But the lost time could not be recovered. Land was not sighted until five on the morning of the 6th, although they had been due on the 5th. Phileas Fogg was twenty-four hours late; naturally, they would miss the Yokohama ship.

At six a pilot boarded and went to the bridge to steer the “Rangoon” through the channels into Hong Kong. Passepartout desperately wanted to ask whether the Yokohama steamer had sailed, but dared not: he wished to keep his last spark of hope alive until the final moment. He had confided his fears to Fix. That crafty scoundrel! Fix tried to console him by saying that Mr. Fogg could take the next ship and still arrive in time, which merely sent Passepartout into a rage.
Mr. Fogg had more courage than his servant. He went directly to the pilot and calmly asked whether he knew when the next steamer would sail from Hong Kong to Yokohama.
“At high tide tomorrow morning,” the pilot told him.
“Ah!” Mr. Fogg replied, showing no trace of surprise.
Hearing this exchange, Passepartout would gladly have thrown his arms round the pilot; Fix would just as gladly have wrung his neck.
“And what is this steamer called?” Mr. Fogg asked.
“The ‘Carnatic.’”
“Was she not scheduled to leave yesterday?”
“She was, sir, but one boiler needed repairs. They therefore postponed her sailing until tomorrow.”
“Thank you,” Mr. Fogg replied, descending to the saloon with mathematical precision.
Passepartout seized the pilot’s hand and shook it vigorously in his joy. “Pilot, you are the finest fellow alive!” he exclaimed.

To this day the pilot probably cannot explain why his answers earned such an enthusiastic reception. He returned to the bridge and steered among the mass of junks, tankas, and fishing boats crowding Hong Kong harbour.
At one o’clock the “Rangoon” drew alongside the quay, and her passengers began to disembark.

Chance had favoured Phileas Fogg in a remarkable way. Without the boiler repairs that held the “Carnatic” in port, she would have sailed on the 6th of November, leaving passengers for Japan to wait a week for another ship. Mr. Fogg was indeed twenty-four hours late, but that delay need not seriously threaten the rest of his journey.

The steamer crossing the Pacific from Yokohama to San Francisco connected directly with the Hong Kong boat and could not leave until that boat arrived. If Mr. Fogg reached Yokohama a day behind schedule, he could surely make it up without difficulty during the twenty-two-day Pacific crossing. Thus, thirty-five days after leaving London, he stood about twenty-four hours behind his plan.
The “Carnatic” was advertised to depart at five the next morning. Mr. Fogg had sixteen hours to complete his Hong Kong business: settling Aouda safely with her wealthy relative.

Once ashore, he escorted her to a palanquin and they went to the Club Hotel. He obtained a room for the young woman, made certain she had everything she needed, then left to find her cousin Jeejeeh. Passepartout was instructed to stay at the hotel until his return, so that Aouda would not be left entirely alone.

Mr. Fogg went to the Exchange, certain that everyone there would know a Parsee merchant so rich and prominent. A broker he questioned told him that Jeejeeh had left China two years earlier. Having retired with an enormous fortune, he now lived in Europe, probably in Holland, the broker thought, since most of his business had been with Dutch merchants. Phileas Fogg returned to the hotel and asked to speak briefly with Aouda. Without further preliminaries, he told her that Jeejeeh no longer lived in Hong Kong and was most likely in Holland.
For a moment Aouda was silent. She drew a hand across her forehead and considered what she had heard. Then, in her gentle, sweet voice, she asked, “What should I do, Mr. Fogg?”
“The answer is quite simple,” the gentleman replied. “Continue to Europe.”
“But I could not impose—”
“You are not imposing, and you do not interfere with my plans in the slightest. Passepartout!”
“Monsieur.”
“Visit the ‘Carnatic’ and reserve three cabins for us.”
Delighted that the young woman, who always treated him so kindly, would remain with them on the journey, Passepartout set off briskly to carry out his master’s instructions.

chapters.title: Chapter 19. In which Passepartout Takes a too Great Interest in His Master, and What Comes of It
paragraphs: Hong Kong is an island ceded to England under the Treaty of Nankin after the war of 1842. English skill in colonisation has established an important city and an excellent harbour there. It lies at the mouth of the Canton River, about sixty miles from the Portuguese settlement of Macao on the opposite coast. In the contest for Chinese commerce, Hong Kong has overtaken Macao, and most Chinese goods in transit now pass through its warehouses. Its docks, hospitals, wharves, Gothic cathedral, government house, and macadamised streets make it look like a town in Kent or Surrey transported by some strange magic to the other side of the world.

Hands in his pockets, Passepartout wandered towards Victoria port, studying the curious palanquins and other vehicles, and the groups of Chinese, Japanese, and Europeans moving through the streets. Hong Kong reminded him of Bombay, Calcutta, and Singapore: here too, English dominance was visible everywhere. Victoria port held a jumble of ships from every nation—English, French, American, and Dutch warships and merchantmen, Japanese and Chinese junks, sempas, tankas, and flower-boats resembling floating flowerbeds. Among the crowds he noticed several local men who looked extremely old and wore yellow. When he stopped at a barber’s for a shave, he learned that they were all at least eighty. At that age a man is allowed to wear yellow, the Imperial colour. Without quite knowing why, Passepartout found this highly amusing.
At the quay from which they would board the “Carnatic,” Passepartout was unsurprised to find Fix pacing back and forth. The detective looked deeply troubled and disappointed.

“A bad business,” Passepartout murmured, “for those gentlemen at the Reform Club!” He greeted Fix with a cheerful smile, as though unaware of his distress. The detective certainly had cause to curse his continuing bad luck. The warrant had not arrived! It was undoubtedly on its way, but could not possibly reach Hong Kong for several more days. Since this was the final English territory on Mr. Fogg’s itinerary, the thief would escape unless Fix found a way to hold him there.
“Well, Monsieur Fix,” Passepartout asked, “have you made up your mind to accompany us all the way to America?”
“Yes,” Fix answered between clenched teeth.
“Splendid!” Passepartout laughed heartily. “I knew you wouldn’t be able to bring yourself to leave us. Come along and book your passage.”

At the shipping office they reserved cabins for four people. Handing over the tickets, the clerk explained that the “Carnatic” repairs were finished. Instead of departing the following morning as advertised, she would sail that very evening.
“My master will like that even better,” Passepartout said. “I shall go and tell him at once.”

Fix decided it was time for a bold step: he would reveal everything to Passepartout. It appeared to be his only chance of holding Phileas Fogg in Hong Kong for several more days. He invited the servant into a tavern he noticed on the quay. Inside was a large, attractively decorated room, with a broad camp-bed covered in cushions at one end.
