Several people lay there fast asleep. Around thirty customers sat at small tables scattered through the room, drinking English beer, porter, gin, and brandy while smoking long red-clay pipes. These contained little balls of opium mixed with essence of rose. Every so often a smoker, overcome by the drug, slid beneath his table; waiters then lifted him by head and feet and carried him to the bed. Twenty of these stupefied drunkards already lay upon it.

Fix and Passepartout realised they had entered a smoking-house frequented by those miserable, corpse-like, senseless creatures to whom English merchants sell one million four hundred thousand pounds’ worth of the wretched drug opium each year—thousands surrendered to one of humanity’s most contemptible vices! The Chinese government had tried in vain to combat it with harsh laws. At first confined to the rich, the habit gradually spread to the poorer classes, and its devastation could no longer be checked. Throughout the Celestial Empire, men and women smoke opium everywhere and at every hour. Once accustomed to it, victims cannot do without it except at the cost of terrible bodily convulsions and agony. A heavy smoker may consume eight pipes daily, but he dies within five years. It was in one of these dens that Fix and Passepartout found themselves while seeking a friendly drink. Passepartout had no money, but accepted willingly, hoping to repay the hospitality another time.

They called for two bottles of port. The Frenchman drank his share with enthusiasm, while Fix watched him closely. Their conversation turned to the journey, and Passepartout was particularly cheerful about Fix’s decision to continue travelling with them. Once the bottles were empty, though, he stood up to inform his master that the “Carnatic” would sail at a different hour.
Fix seized his arm. “Wait just a moment,” he said.
“What is it, Mr. Fix?”
“There is something serious I need to discuss with you.”
“Something serious!” Passepartout exclaimed, swallowing the last wine in his glass. “Well, tomorrow will do for that. I have no time now.”
“Wait! It is your master I want to talk about.”
At these words Passepartout studied his companion carefully. There was an odd expression on Fix’s face. He sat down again.
“What exactly do you want to tell me?”
Resting a hand on Passepartout’s arm, Fix lowered his voice. “You have worked out who I am?”
“Parbleu!” Passepartout answered with a smile.
“Then I shall explain the whole business—”
“When I already know all about it, my friend! Ah! That is a good one. Still, go ahead, go ahead. First let me say that those gentlemen have wasted their money on you.”
“Wasted it!” Fix replied. “You sound very certain. Plainly you don’t realise how much money is involved.”
“Certainly I do,” Passepartout answered. “Twenty thousand pounds.”
“Fifty-five thousand!” Fix replied, squeezing his companion’s hand.
“What!” the Frenchman cried. “Monsieur Fogg has dared to stake—fifty-five thousand pounds! All the more reason not to waste another instant,” he went on, rising hurriedly.
Fix forced him back into his chair. “Fifty-five thousand pounds,” he repeated. “And success means two thousand pounds for me. Help me, and five hundred of it is yours.”
“Help you?” Passepartout exclaimed, his eyes opening wide in amazement.
“Yes. Help me hold Mr. Fogg here for another two or three days.”
“What are you saying? Those gentlemen aren’t content with following my master and questioning his honour: now they want to hinder his progress! I am ashamed for them!”
“What exactly are you talking about?”
“I am saying it is disgraceful cheating. They might just as well ambush Mr. Fogg and pocket his money!”
“That is precisely what we intend to do.”

“So it is a conspiracy,” Passepartout cried. The drink was going to his head and making him increasingly excited, for he kept drinking without noticing. “An actual conspiracy! And they call themselves gentlemen. Bah!”
Fix was beginning to feel bewildered.
“Members of the Reform Club!” Passepartout went on. “You should understand, Monsieur Fix, that my master is an honourable man, and if he bets, he means to win honestly!”
“Who, exactly, do you believe I am?” Fix asked, studying him closely.

“Parbleu! Someone employed by the Reform Club members to interfere with my master’s journey. I discovered your little secret some time ago, but I have taken very good care not to mention it to Mr. Fogg.”
“So he has heard nothing of it?”
“Nothing at all,” Passepartout replied, draining another glass.

The detective rubbed his forehead and hesitated. What should he do now? Passepartout’s misunderstanding seemed genuine, yet it complicated his plan. Clearly the servant was not his master’s accomplice, as Fix had been inclined to believe.
“Well,” the detective told himself, “if he is not involved in the crime, he will assist me.”
There was no time to waste. Fogg had to be kept in Hong Kong, so Fix decided to reveal the entire truth.
“Listen,” he said abruptly. “You are wrong about me. I am not employed by members of the Reform Club—”
“Bah!” Passepartout answered, plainly making fun of him.
“I am a detective with the police, sent by headquarters in London.”
“You are a detective?”
“I can prove it. Here are my official credentials.”
When Fix produced the document, whose authenticity was beyond question, Passepartout stared in astonishment, unable to say a word.
“Mr. Fogg’s bet,” Fix continued, “is simply a cover story. You and the Reform gentlemen have been taken in. He had a reason for making you his unwitting accomplice.”
“But what reason?”

“Listen carefully. On September 28th, fifty-five thousand pounds were stolen from the Bank of England. Fortunately, a description of the thief was obtained. Here it is: it matches Mr. Phileas Fogg in every particular.”
“Utter nonsense!” Passepartout shouted, bringing his fist down on the table. “No man is more honourable than my master!”

“How could you know? You know almost nothing about him. You began serving him on the day he left, and he departed on a ridiculous pretext, taking no trunks but a large sum in banknotes. Yet you dare insist that he is honest!”
“Yes, yes,” the unhappy fellow kept repeating automatically.
“Do you want to find yourself under arrest as his accomplice?”

Overwhelmed by the accusation, Passepartout buried his head in his hands, unable to meet the detective’s eyes. Phileas Fogg, Aouda’s rescuer, so brave and generous—a thief! And yet so much seemed to point against him! Passepartout struggled to drive away the suspicions forcing themselves into his mind. He could not bear to believe his master guilty.
“At any rate, what do you want me to do?” he finally managed to ask.
“Here is the position,” Fix answered. “I have followed Mr. Fogg this far, but the arrest warrant I requested from London has not yet reached me. You must help me detain him in Hong Kong—”
“Me! But I—”
“I shall give you a share of the Bank of England’s two-thousand-pound reward.”
“Never!” Passepartout answered. He tried to stand, but mental and physical exhaustion sent him sinking back again.

“Mr. Fix,” he stammered, “even if your story were true—even if my master really were the thief you are pursuing, which I deny—I have served him, and I still serve him. I have witnessed his goodness and generosity. I shall never betray him, not for all the gold in the world. Where I come from, we don’t eat that sort of bread!”
“You are refusing?”
“I am refusing.”
“Then forget I spoke of it,” Fix said, “and let us have another drink.”
“Yes, another drink!”

The liquor was taking an ever stronger hold on Passepartout. Fix, convinced that he must keep the servant apart from his master at any cost, meant to finish the job. Several opium-filled pipes lay on the table. He slipped one into Passepartout’s hand. The servant took it, placed it between his lips, lit it, and inhaled several times. Under the drug’s influence his head grew heavy and dropped onto the table.
“At last!” Fix said, looking at the unconscious Passepartout. “No one will tell Mr. Fogg when the ‘Carnatic’ is leaving; and even if he hears, he will have to sail without this damned Frenchman!”
Fix then settled the bill and went out of the tavern.

chapters.title: Chapter 20. In which Fix Comes Face to Face with Phileas Fogg
paragraphs: While these events were unfolding at the opium den, Mr. Fogg, unaware of the danger he was in of missing the steamer, was quietly escorting Aouda through the streets of the English quarter, making the necessary purchases for the long voyage ahead. It was all very well for an Englishman like Mr. Fogg to circle the globe with nothing but a carpet-bag; a lady could not be expected to travel comfortably under such conditions. He carried out the task with his characteristic composure, and to every protest from his beautiful companion—who was bewildered by his patience and generosity—he invariably replied:
“It is in the interest of my journey—part of my programme.”

Their purchases made, they returned to the hotel, where they dined at a lavishly served table-d’hôte. Afterward Aouda, shaking hands with her protector in the English fashion, retired to her room to rest. Mr. Fogg spent the rest of the evening absorbed in the Times and the Illustrated London News.

If he had been capable of being surprised by anything, it would have been the failure of his servant to return by bedtime. But, knowing that the steamer would not leave for Yokohama until the next morning, he did not trouble himself about it. When Passepartout failed to answer his master’s bell the following morning, Mr. Fogg betrayed not the slightest annoyance. He simply picked up his carpet-bag, called for Aouda, and sent for a palanquin.

It was now eight o’clock; at half-past nine, when the tide would be high, the “Carnatic” was due to leave the harbor. Mr. Fogg and Aouda climbed into the palanquin, their luggage following behind on a wheelbarrow, and half an hour later they stepped onto the quay from which they were to embark. There Mr. Fogg learned that the “Carnatic” had sailed the previous evening. He had expected to find both the steamer and his servant waiting, and was forced to give up both; yet no sign of disappointment appeared on his face, and he merely remarked to Aouda, “It is an accident, madam; nothing more.”
At that moment a man who had been watching him closely approached. It was Fix, who bowed and addressed Mr. Fogg: “Weren’t you, like me, sir, a passenger on the ‘Rangoon’ that arrived yesterday?”
“I was, sir,” replied Mr. Fogg coldly. “But I have not the honor—”
“Forgive me; I thought I would find your servant here.”
“Do you know where he is, sir?” Aouda asked anxiously.
“What!” Fix exclaimed, feigning surprise. “Isn’t he with you?”
“No,” said Aouda. “He has not appeared since yesterday. Could he have boarded the ‘Carnatic’ without us?”
“Without you, madam?” answered the detective. “Excuse me, but did you intend to sail on the ‘Carnatic’?”
“Yes, sir.”

“So did I, madam, and I am terribly disappointed. The ‘Carnatic’, her repairs completed, left Hong Kong twelve hours ahead of schedule without giving any notice; and now we must wait a week for another steamer.”

As he said “a week,” Fix felt his heart leap with joy. Fogg held up in Hong Kong for a week! There would be time for the warrant to arrive, and fortune was at last smiling on the representative of the law. His horror can be imagined when he heard Mr. Fogg say, in his unruffled voice, “But there are other vessels besides the ‘Carnatic,’ it seems to me, in the harbor of Hong Kong.”

And, offering his arm to Aouda, he set off toward the docks in search of some craft about to depart. Fix, dumbfounded, followed; it was as if he were tied to Mr. Fogg by an invisible thread. Chance, however, seemed truly to have abandoned the man it had served so well until now. For three hours Phileas Fogg roamed about the docks, determined, if necessary, to charter a vessel to carry him to Yokohama; but he could only find ships that were loading or unloading and therefore could not set sail. Fix began to hope again.
But Mr. Fogg, far from being discouraged, kept up his search, resolved not to stop even if he had to go as far as Macao, when he was approached on one of the wharves by a sailor.
“Is your honor looking for a boat?”
“Do you have a boat ready to sail?”
“Yes, your honor; a pilot-boat—No. 43—the best in the harbor.”
“Is she fast?”
“Eight to nine knots an hour. Would you like to look at her?”
“Yes.”
“Your honor will be pleased with her. Is it for a sea outing?”
“No; for a voyage.”
“A voyage?”
“Yes. Will you agree to take me to Yokohama?”
The sailor leaned on the railing, opened his eyes wide, and said, “Is your honor joking?”
“No. I have missed the ‘Carnatic,’ and I must reach Yokohama by the 14th at the latest to catch the boat for San Francisco.”
“I am sorry,” said the sailor, “but it’s impossible.”
“I offer you a hundred pounds a day, and an additional reward of two hundred pounds if I reach Yokohama on time.”
“Are you serious?”
“Entirely.”
The pilot walked a short distance away and gazed out to sea, obviously torn between the urge to earn a large sum and the fear of venturing so far. Fix was in agonizing suspense.
Mr. Fogg turned to Aouda and asked, “You would not be afraid, would you, madam?”
“Not with you, Mr. Fogg,” she answered.
The pilot now returned, turning his hat over in his hands.
“Well, pilot?” said Mr. Fogg.

“Well, your honor,” he replied, “I couldn’t risk myself, my men, or my little boat of barely twenty tons on so long a voyage at this time of year. Besides, we couldn’t reach Yokohama in time, for it’s sixteen hundred and sixty miles from Hong Kong.”
“Only sixteen hundred,” said Mr. Fogg.
“It’s the same thing.”
Fix breathed more easily.
“But,” added the pilot, “it might be arranged another way.”
Fix stopped breathing altogether.
“How?” asked Mr. Fogg.

“By going to Nagasaki, at the southern tip of Japan, or even to Shanghai, which is only eight hundred miles from here. By heading for Shanghai we wouldn’t have to sail wide of the Chinese coast, which would be a great advantage, since the currents run northward and would help us.”
“Pilot,” said Mr. Fogg, “I must catch the American steamer at Yokohama, not at Shanghai or Nagasaki.”
“Why not?” returned the pilot. “The San Francisco steamer does not start from Yokohama. It calls at Yokohama and Nagasaki, but it sails from Shanghai.”
“You are sure of that?”
“Absolutely.”
“And when does the boat leave Shanghai?”

“On the 11th, at seven in the evening. We have, then, four days ahead of us—that is, ninety-six hours; and in that time, with good luck and a south-west wind, and a calm sea, we could make those eight hundred miles to Shanghai.”
“And you could leave—”
“In an hour; as soon as provisions could be got on board and the sails set.”
“It’s a bargain. Are you the master of the boat?”
“Yes; John Bunsby, master of the ‘Tankadere.’”
“Would you like some earnest-money?”
“If it would not inconvenience your honor—”
“Here are two hundred pounds on account.” Then, turning to Fix, Phileas Fogg added, “sir, if you would like to take advantage—”
“Thank you, sir; I was about to ask the favor.”
“Very well. In half an hour we shall go on board.”
“But poor Passepartout?” Aouda pressed, deeply troubled by the servant’s disappearance.
“I shall do all I can to find him,” Phileas Fogg replied.

While Fix, in a feverish, anxious state, headed for the pilot-boat, the others made their way to the police-station at Hong Kong. There Phileas Fogg gave Passepartout’s description and left a sum of money to be spent searching for him. After the same formalities had been carried out at the French consulate, and after the palanquin had stopped at the hotel to collect the luggage that had been sent back there, they returned to the wharf.
It was now three o’clock; and pilot-boat No. 43, with its crew on board and its provisions stowed away, was ready to depart.

The “Tankadere” was a neat little craft of twenty tons, as gracefully built as a racing yacht. Her gleaming copper sheathing, her galvanized iron-work, her deck white as ivory, all bore witness to the pride John Bunsby took in keeping her presentable. Her two masts leaned a little backward; she carried a brigantine, foresail, storm-jib, and standing-jib, and was well rigged for running before the wind; and she seemed capable of brisk speed, which, in fact, she had already proved by winning several prizes in pilot-boat races. The crew of the “Tankadere” was made up of John Bunsby, the master, and four tough sailors familiar with the Chinese seas. John Bunsby himself, a man of about forty-five, vigorous, sun-burned, with a lively expression in his eye and an energetic, self-reliant countenance, would have inspired confidence in the most timid passenger.

Phileas Fogg and Aouda went on board, where they found Fix already installed. Below deck was a square cabin whose walls bulged out into cot-shaped recesses above a circular divan; in the center stood a table fitted with a swinging lamp. The accommodation was cramped, but tidy.
“I am sorry to have nothing better to offer you,” said Mr. Fogg to Fix, who bowed without replying.
The detective felt something close to humiliation at benefiting from Mr. Fogg’s kindness.
“It’s certain,” he thought, “that scoundrel as he is, he is a polite one!”

The sails and the English flag were hoisted at ten past three. Mr. Fogg and Aouda, seated on deck, cast a last glance at the quay, hoping to catch sight of Passepartout. Fix was not without his fears that chance might bring the unfortunate servant—whom he had treated so badly—in this direction; in which case an explanation the reverse of satisfactory to the detective would have followed. But the Frenchman did not appear, and was no doubt still lying under the stupefying effects of the opium.
John Bunsby, the master, at last gave the order to depart, and the “Tankadere,” catching the wind in her brigantine, foresail, and standing-jib, bounded briskly forward over the waves.

chapters.title: Chapter 21. In which the Master of the “tankadere” Runs Great Risk of Losing a Reward of Two Hundred Pounds
paragraphs: This eight-hundred-mile voyage was a perilous undertaking on a craft of twenty tons, and at this season of the year. The Chinese seas are usually rough, prone to terrible gales, especially during the equinoxes; and it was now early November.

It would clearly have been to the master’s advantage to carry his passengers all the way to Yokohama, since he was paid a fixed sum per day; but to attempt such a voyage would have been reckless, and it was imprudent even to try for Shanghai. Still, John Bunsby believed in the “Tankadere,” which rode the waves like a seagull; and perhaps he was not mistaken.
Late in the day they passed through the capricious channels of Hong Kong, and the “Tankadere,” driven by favourable winds, behaved admirably.
“I do not need, pilot,” said Phileas Fogg, once they had reached the open sea, “to tell you to use every ounce of speed.”
“Trust me, your honour. We are carrying every sail the wind will allow. The topmasts would add nothing, and are only used when entering port.”
“It’s your trade, not mine, pilot, and I leave it to you.”

Phileas Fogg, standing upright with legs braced wide apart like a sailor, gazed without staggering at the swelling waters. The young woman, seated aft, was deeply moved as she looked out over the ocean, now darkening with twilight, on which she had ventured in so frail a vessel. Above her head rustled the white sails, which looked like great white wings. Carried forward by the wind, the boat seemed to be flying through the air.
Night came on. The moon was entering her first quarter, and her thin light would soon die out in the mist on the horizon. Clouds were rising from the east, and had already overcast part of the sky.

The pilot had hung out his lights, a necessary precaution in these seas crowded with vessels bound landward; for collisions are common occurrences, and at the speed she was going, the slightest shock would shatter the gallant little craft.

Fix, seated in the bow, gave himself up to his thoughts. He kept apart from his fellow-passengers, knowing Mr. Fogg’s preference for silence; besides, he was not eager to talk to the man whose favours he had accepted. He was also thinking about what came next. It seemed certain that Fogg would not stop at Yokohama, but would board the next boat for San Francisco; and the vast expanse of America would guarantee him impunity and safety. Fogg’s plan struck Fix as the simplest in the world. Instead of sailing directly from England to the United States, like a common criminal, he had crossed three-quarters of the globe, so as to reach the American continent more surely; and there, after shaking off the police, he would quietly enjoy himself on the fortune stolen from the bank. But once in the United States, what would he, Fix, do? Should he abandon the chase? No, a hundred times no! Until he had secured the extradition warrant, he would not let his man out of sight for an hour. It was his duty, and he would see it through. At least there was one thing to be thankful for: Passepartout was not with his master; and it was crucial, after the confidences Fix had let slip to him, that the servant should never get a chance to speak with his master.

Phileas Fogg was also thinking about Passepartout, who had so strangely disappeared. Looking at the matter from every angle, it did not seem impossible to him that, by some mistake, the man might have boarded the “Carnatic” at the last minute; and this was Aouda’s opinion too, who deeply regretted the loss of the good fellow to whom she owed so much. They might still find him at Yokohama; for if the “Carnatic” had carried him there, it would be easy to check whether he had been on board.

A brisk breeze rose around ten o’clock; but, though it might have been prudent to reef the sails, the pilot, after carefully examining the sky, left the rigging as it was. The “Tankadere” handled the sails admirably, as she drew a great deal of water, and everything was prepared for high speed in case of a gale.
Mr. Fogg and Aouda went below to the cabin at midnight, where Fix had already preceded them, lying down on one of the cots. The pilot and crew remained on deck all night.

At sunrise the next day, which was the 8th of November, the boat had covered more than a hundred miles. The log showed an average speed of between eight and nine miles an hour. The “Tankadere” still carried all sail, and was achieving her greatest possible speed. If the wind held, the odds were in her favour. During the day she kept close to the coast, where the currents were favourable; the coastline, irregular in profile and visible at times through the gaps in the haze, was at most five miles distant. The sea was less rough, since the wind was coming off the land — a lucky circumstance for the boat, which, given her small tonnage, would have suffered in a heavy swell.
The breeze fell off a little around noon, and shifted to the south-west. The pilot put up his topmasts, but took them down again within two hours, as the wind freshened once more.

Mr. Fogg and Aouda, happily unaffected by the rough sea, ate with good appetite, and Fix was invited to share their meal, which he accepted with secret chagrin. To travel at this man’s expense and live off his provisions was distasteful to him. Still, he had to eat, and so he ate.

When the meal was over, he drew Mr. Fogg aside and said, “Sir” — this “sir” scorched his lips, and he had to hold himself back from grabbing this “gentleman” by the collar — “sir, you have been very kind to give me a passage on this boat. But although my means will not let me spend as freely as you do, I must insist on paying my share —”
“Let us not speak of it, sir,” replied Mr. Fogg.
“But if I insist —”
“No, sir,” repeated Mr. Fogg in a tone that left no room for reply. “This is part of my general expenses.”
Fix, as he bowed, felt half choked, and went forward where he settled himself and did not open his mouth for the rest of the day.

Meanwhile they were making great progress, and John Bunsby was full of hope. Several times he assured Mr. Fogg that they would reach Shanghai in time; to which that gentleman replied that he was counting on it. The crew set to work in earnest, spurred on by the reward to be won. Not a sheet was left untightened, not a sail was not vigorously hoisted; not a single lurch could be blamed on the man at the helm. They worked as hard as if they were racing in a Royal yacht regatta.

By evening the log showed they had covered two hundred and twenty miles from Hong Kong, and Mr. Fogg could hope to reach Yokohama without recording any delay in his journal; in which case the many mishaps that had befallen him since he left London would not seriously affect his journey.

The “Tankadere” entered the Straits of Fo-Kien, which separate the island of Formosa from the Chinese coast, in the small hours of the night, and crossed the Tropic of Cancer. The sea was very rough in the straits, full of eddies formed by the counter-currents, and the choppy waves broke her course, while it became very difficult to stand on deck.

At daybreak the wind began to blow hard again, and the sky seemed to promise a gale. The barometer signalled a swift change, the mercury rising and falling capriciously; the sea, too, in the south-east, was rolling long surges that pointed to a tempest. The sun had set the evening before in a red mist, amid the phosphorescent flickers of the ocean.
John Bunsby studied the threatening sky for a long time, muttering between his teeth. At last he said in a low voice to Mr. Fogg, “Shall I speak plainly to your honour?”
“Of course.”
“Well, we are going to have a squall.”
“Is the wind from the north or the south?” Mr. Fogg asked quietly.
“From the south. Look! A typhoon is rising.”
“Glad it’s a typhoon from the south, since it will carry us forward.”

“Oh, if you take it that way,” said John Bunsby, “I’ve nothing more to say.” John Bunsby’s hunch was right. At a less advanced season of the year the typhoon, according to a famous meteorologist, would have passed by like a glowing cascade of electric flame; but in the winter equinox, there was every reason to fear it would burst on them with great violence.

The pilot took his precautions in advance. He reefed every sail, the topmasts were taken down; all hands went forward to the bows. A single triangular sail of heavy canvas was hoisted as a storm-jib, to catch the wind from behind. Then they waited.

John Bunsby had asked his passengers to go below; but being shut up in so narrow a space, with so little air, and the boat tossing in the gale, was far from pleasant. Neither Mr. Fogg, Fix, nor Aouda would agree to leave the deck.

The storm of rain and wind came down on them around eight o’clock. With only its scrap of sail, the “Tankadere” was lifted like a feather by a wind whose violence can scarcely be described. To compare her speed to four times that of a locomotive at full steam would be an understatement.

The boat ran northward like this all day long, carried by monstrous waves, fortunately always keeping a speed equal to theirs. Twenty times she seemed about to be swallowed by these mountains of water rising behind her; but the pilot’s skilful handling saved her. The passengers were often drenched in spray, but they bore it stoically. Fix cursed under his breath, no doubt; but Aouda, her eyes fixed on her protector, whose coolness astonished her, proved herself worthy of him, and weathered the storm bravely. As for Phileas Fogg, it seemed as if the typhoon were a scheduled part of his programme.

Up to this point the “Tankadere” had held her northward course; but towards evening the wind, shifting three points, blew down from the north-west. The boat, now lying in the trough of the waves, shook and rolled terribly; the sea struck her with fearful violence. At night the tempest grew worse. John Bunsby watched the dark coming on and the storm rising with grim foreboding. He thought a while, then asked his crew whether it was not time to slacken speed. After a consultation he went up to Mr. Fogg and said, “I think, your honour, we should do well to make for one of the ports along the coast.”
“I think so too.”
“Ah!” said the pilot. “But which one?”
“I know of only one,” answered Mr. Fogg calmly.
“And that is —”
“Shanghai.”
At first the pilot did not seem to grasp it; he could scarcely take in such determination and tenacity. Then he cried, “Well — yes! Your honour is right. To Shanghai!”
So the “Tankadere” kept steadily on her northward course.

The night was truly terrible; it would be a miracle if the craft did not founder. Twice it might have been all over with her if the crew had not been constantly on watch. Aouda was exhausted, but did not utter a word of complaint. More than once Mr. Fogg rushed over to shield her from the violence of the waves.

Day returned. The tempest still raged with undiminished fury; but the wind had now shifted back to the south-east. It was a favourable change, and the “Tankadere” again surged forward over this mountainous sea, though the waves crossed one another and sent shocks and counter-shocks through her that would have broken a less solidly built craft. From time to time the coast was visible through the broken mist, but no other vessel was in sight. The “Tankadere” was alone on the sea.

There were some signs of a calm at noon, and these became clearer as the sun sank towards the horizon. The tempest had been as brief as it was terrific. The passengers, thoroughly exhausted, could now eat a little and get some rest.

The night was comparatively quiet. Some of the sails were hoisted again, and the boat made good speed. The next morning at dawn they sighted the coast, and John Bunsby was able to say that they were not a hundred miles from Shanghai. A hundred miles, with only one day to cover them! That very evening Mr. Fogg was due in Shanghai, if he did not want to miss the steamer to Yokohama. Had there been no storm — which had cost them several hours — they would already be within thirty miles of their destination.

The wind grew decidedly calmer, and happily the sea fell with it. Every sail was now hoisted, and by noon the “Tankadere” was within forty-five miles of Shanghai. Six hours remained to cover that distance. Everyone on board feared it could not be done, and every man — Phileas Fogg excepted, no doubt — felt his heart pound with impatience. The boat would have to keep up an average of nine miles an hour, and the wind was slackening every moment! It was a fickle breeze, coming off the coast, and after it passed the sea grew smooth. Still, the “Tankadere” was so light, and her fine sails caught the inconstant breezes so well, that, with the help of the currents, John Bunsby found himself at six o’clock no more than ten miles from the mouth of the Shanghai River. Shanghai itself lies at least twelve miles up the river. At seven they were still three miles from Shanghai. The pilot swore an angry oath; the two-hundred-pound reward was clearly slipping out of his grasp. He looked at Mr. Fogg. Mr. Fogg was perfectly calm; and yet at this moment his whole fortune was on the line.
At that very moment, too, a long black funnel, crowned with wreaths of smoke, appeared on the rim of the waters. It was the American steamer, leaving for Yokohama on schedule.
“Confound her!” cried John Bunsby, shoving back the rudder with a desperate jerk.
“Signal her!” said Phileas Fogg quietly.

A small brass cannon stood on the forward deck of the “Tankadere,” used for signalling in the fogs. It was loaded to the muzzle; but just as the pilot was about to touch a red-hot coal to the touchhole, Mr. Fogg said, “Hoist your flag!”
The flag was run up at half-mast, this being the signal of distress, in the hope that the American steamer, seeing it, would alter her course a little, so as to come to the pilot-boat’s aid.
“Fire!” said Mr. Fogg. And the boom of the little cannon rang out through the air.

chapters.title: Chapter 22. In which Passepartout Finds Out That, Even at the Antipodes, it is Convenient to Have Some Money in One’s Pocket
paragraphs: The “Carnatic,” setting sail from Hong Kong at half-past six on the 7th of November, headed at full steam towards Japan. She carried a large cargo and a cabin crowded with passengers. Two staterooms aft, however, stood empty — the ones engaged by Phileas Fogg.
The next day a passenger with a half-stupefied look, an unsteady walk, and hair in disarray was seen to emerge from the second cabin and stagger to a seat on deck.

It was Passepartout; and what had happened to him was this. Shortly after Fix left the opium den, two waiters had lifted the unconscious Passepartout and carried him to the bed reserved for the smokers. Three hours later, haunted even in his dreams by one fixed idea, the poor fellow woke and struggled against the stupefying grip of the narcotic. The thought of an unfulfilled duty shook off his torpor, and he hurried out of this den of drunkenness. Staggering and propping himself up against the walls, falling and crawling back to his feet, driven on irresistibly by a kind of instinct, he kept crying out, “The ‘Carnatic!’ the ‘Carnatic!’”

The steamer lay puffing alongside the quay, on the point of departure. Passepartout had only a few steps to take; and, throwing himself onto the gangplank, he crossed it and collapsed unconscious on the deck just as the “Carnatic” was casting off. Several sailors, evidently used to this kind of scene, carried the poor Frenchman down to the second cabin, and Passepartout did not wake until they were a hundred and fifty miles out from China. So he found himself the next morning on the deck of the “Carnatic,” eagerly breathing in the invigorating sea air. The fresh breeze sobered him. He began to gather his wits — a difficult task — but at last he remembered the events of the previous evening: Fix’s confession, the opium house.
“Clearly,” he said to himself, “I was abominably drunk! What will Mr. Fogg say? At least I haven’t missed the steamer, which is the main thing.”

Then, thinking of Fix: “As for that scoundrel, I hope we’ve seen the last of him, and that he didn’t dare, as he threatened, to follow us on board the ‘Carnatic.’ A detective on the trail of Mr. Fogg, accused of robbing the Bank of England! Nonsense! Mr. Fogg is no more a robber than I am a murderer.”

Should he tell his master about Fix’s real mission? Would it be right to reveal the part the detective was playing? Or would it be better to wait until Mr. Fogg reached London again, and then let him know that an agent of the metropolitan police had been chasing him around the world, and have a good laugh over it? No doubt about it; or at least, it was worth thinking through. The first thing to do was to find Mr. Fogg and apologise for his strange behaviour.

Passepartout got up and made his way, as best he could against the rolling of the steamer, to the after-deck. He saw no one resembling either his master or Aouda. “All right!” he muttered. “Aouda isn’t up yet, and Mr. Fogg has probably found some whist partners.”

He went down to the saloon. Mr. Fogg was not there. Passepartout only had to ask the purser for the number of his master’s stateroom. The purser replied that he knew of no passenger by the name of Fogg.
“I beg your pardon,” said Passepartout, pressing on. “He is a tall gentleman, quiet, not very talkative, and has with him a young lady —”
“There is no young lady on board,” the purser interrupted. “Here is the passenger list; see for yourself.”
Passepartout scanned the list, but his master’s name was not on it. All at once an idea struck him.
“Wait! Am I on the ‘Carnatic’?”
“Yes.”
“Bound for Yokohama?”
“Certainly.”
For an instant Passepartout had feared he was on the wrong boat; but although he really was on the “Carnatic,” his master was not.

He dropped onto a seat as if struck by lightning. Now he saw it all. He remembered that the time of sailing had been changed, that he was supposed to have told his master, and that he had failed to do so. It was his fault, then, that Mr. Fogg and Aouda had missed the steamer. Yes — but it was even more the fault of the traitor who, in order to separate him from his master and detain Mr. Fogg at Hong Kong, had tricked him into getting drunk! He saw the detective’s scheme clearly now; and at this moment Mr. Fogg was surely ruined, his wager lost, and perhaps Passepartout himself arrested and jailed! At this thought Passepartout tore at his hair. Ah, if Fix ever fell within his reach, what a reckoning there would be!

After his first wave of dejection, Passepartout grew calmer and began to take stock of his situation. It was certainly not an enviable one. He found himself on the way to Japan — and what should he do once he got there? His pocket was empty; he had not a single shilling, not so much as a penny. Luckily his passage had been paid for in advance; and he had five or six days in which to decide on his next move. He fell on his meals with an appetite, eating for Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and himself. He helped himself as generously as if Japan were a desert where nothing edible was to be found.

At dawn on the 13th the “Carnatic” entered the port of Yokohama. This is a major port of call in the Pacific, where all the mail-steamers, and those carrying travellers between North America, China, Japan, and the Oriental islands, put in. It is situated in the Bay of Yeddo, only a short distance from that second capital of the Japanese Empire and seat of the Tycoon — the civil Emperor, before the Mikado, the spiritual Emperor, absorbed his office into his own. The “Carnatic” anchored at the quay near the custom-house, amid a crowd of ships flying the flags of every nation.

Passepartout went timidly ashore on this so curious territory of the Sons of the Sun. He had nothing better to do than let chance be his guide and wander aimlessly through the streets of Yokohama. He found himself at first in a thoroughly European quarter, the houses with low fronts and adorned with verandas under which he caught glimpses of neat porticoes. This quarter, with its streets, squares, docks, and warehouses, filled all the space between the “promontory of the Treaty” and the river. Here, as in Hong Kong and Calcutta, swarmed mixed crowds of every race: Americans and English, Chinese and Dutch, mostly merchants ready to buy or sell anything. The Frenchman felt himself as much alone among them as if he had dropped into a tribe of Hottentots.

He had at least one resource: to call on the French and English consuls at Yokohama for help. But he balked at telling the story of his adventures, bound up as it was with his master’s; and before doing so, he resolved to exhaust every other option. As chance did not favour him in the European quarter, he ventured into the part inhabited by the native Japanese, determined, if need be, to push on as far as Yeddo.

The Japanese quarter of Yokohama is called Benten, after the goddess of the sea, who is worshipped on the surrounding islands. There Passepartout saw beautiful fir and cedar groves, sacred gates of a peculiar architecture, bridges half hidden among bamboo and reeds, temples shaded by huge cedars, holy retreats where Buddhist priests and followers of Confucius lived sheltered, and endless streets where a whole harvest of rose-cheeked, ruddy children, looking as if they had been cut from Japanese screens, played among short-legged dogs and yellowish cats.

The streets were crowded with people. Priests were passing in processions, beating their dreary tambourines; police and custom-house officers in pointed hats lacquered hard and wearing two sabres at their waists; soldiers in blue cotton with white stripes and carrying guns; the Mikado’s guards, wrapped in silken doublets, hauberks, and chain mail; and numbers of military men of every rank — for the military profession is as honoured in Japan as it is despised in China — went to and fro in groups and pairs. Passepartout also saw begging friars, long-robed pilgrims, and ordinary civilians, with their stiff, jet-black hair, big heads, long torsos, slim legs, short stature, and complexions ranging from copper to chalky white, but never the yellow of the Chinese, from whom the Japanese differ markedly. He did not fail to notice the curious vehicles — carriages and palanquins, sail-rigged barrows, and litters of bamboo; nor the women, whom he found not particularly handsome, taking little steps on their little feet, wearing canvas shoes, straw sandals, or clogs of carved wood, and showing narrow-looking eyes, flat chests, teeth fashionably blackened, and gowns crossed with silken scarves tied in a huge knot behind — an ornament which modern Parisian ladies seem to have borrowed from the women of Japan.

Passepartout wandered for several hours through this motley crowd, peering into the windows of the rich and curious shops, the jewellery houses gleaming with quaint Japanese ornaments, the restaurants hung with streamers and banners (which he was not allowed to enter), the tea-houses where the fragrant brew was drunk along with “saki,” a liquor distilled from fermented rice, and the comfortable smoking-houses where they were puffing not opium — which is almost unknown in Japan — but a very fine, stringy tobacco. He went on until he found himself in the fields, in the middle of vast rice plantations. There he saw dazzling camellias in full bloom, with flowers giving off their last colours and scents, not on bushes but on trees; and within bamboo enclosures, cherry, plum, and apple trees that the Japanese cultivate more for their blossoms than their fruit, and that grotesquely grinning scarecrows protected from sparrows, pigeons, ravens, and other voracious birds. Large eagles perched in the branches of the cedars; herons stood solemnly on one leg amid the foliage of the weeping willows; and on every side were crows, ducks, hawks, wild birds, and a multitude of cranes — which the Japanese hold sacred, taking them as symbols of long life and prosperity.
As he strolled along, Passepartout spotted some violets among the shrubs.
“Good!” he said. “That’ll be my supper.”
But on smelling them, he found that they had no scent.
“No luck there,” he thought.

The good fellow had taken care, of course, to eat as hearty a breakfast as possible before leaving the “Carnatic”; but after walking about all day, the demands of hunger were becoming impossible to ignore. He noticed that the butchers’ stalls held neither mutton, goat, nor pork; and, knowing too that it is a sacrilege to kill cattle, which are kept solely for farming, he concluded that meat was anything but plentiful in Yokohama — and he was not wrong. For lack of butcher’s meat, he could have wished for a haunch of wild boar or venison, a partridge, some quail, or some game or fish, which, along with rice, the Japanese eat almost exclusively. But he had to keep his spirits up and put off the meal he longed for until the next morning. Night came, and Passepartout went back into the native quarter, where he wandered through streets lit by lanterns of many colours, watching the dancers performing skilful steps and leaps, and the astrologers standing out in the open with their telescopes. Then he came to the harbour, lit up by the resin torches of the fishermen plying their trade from their boats.

At last the streets grew quiet, and the patrol — whose officers, in their splendid costumes and surrounded by their retinues, struck Passepartout as looking like ambassadors — replaced the bustling crowd. Every time a company passed, Passepartout chuckled and said to himself: “Good! another Japanese embassy off to Europe!”

chapters.title: Chapter 23. In which Passepartout’s Nose Becomes Outrageously Long
paragraphs: The next morning, poor jaded, famished Passepartout told himself that he had to get something to eat at all costs, and the sooner the better. He could, of course, sell his watch — but he would sooner starve. Now or never, he had to use the strong if not exactly melodious voice that nature had given him. He knew several French and English songs, and resolved to try them on the Japanese, who had to be lovers of music, since they were forever pounding on their cymbals, tam-tams, and tambourines, and were sure to appreciate European talent.

It was perhaps a little early in the morning to mount a concert, and the audience, prematurely roused from their sleep, might well decline to pay their entertainer with coins bearing the Mikado’s features. So Passepartout decided to wait several hours; and as he sauntered along, it occurred to him that he was rather too well dressed for a wandering artist. The idea struck him to swap his clothes for outfits more in keeping with his plan; and in the bargain he might get a little money to satisfy the immediate pangs of hunger. With his mind made up, it only remained to put it into action.

It was only after a long search that Passepartout found a native dealer in old clothes, whom he approached for an exchange. The man took a liking to the European costume, and before long Passepartout emerged from his shop rigged out in an old Japanese coat and a sort of lopsided turban faded by long use. Several small pieces of silver also jingled in his pocket.
“Good!” he thought. “I’ll pretend I’m at Carnival!”

His first concern, having thus been “Japanesed,” was to step into a modest-looking tea-house, where, over half a bird and a little rice, he breakfasted like a man for whom dinner was still an open question.

“Now,” he thought, when he had eaten his fill, “I mustn’t lose my head. I can’t trade this outfit for one even more Japanese. I must figure out how to leave this country of the Sun — of which I shall not keep the most delightful memories — as quickly as possible.”

It occurred to him to visit the steamers about to leave for America. He would offer himself as a cook or servant in exchange for his passage and meals. Once in San Francisco, he would find some way to go on. The catch was, how to cross the four thousand seven hundred miles of Pacific that lay between Japan and the New World.

Passepartout was not a man to let an idea go to waste, and he turned his steps towards the docks. But as he approached them, his plan, which had at first seemed so simple, began to look more and more daunting. What use would an American steamer have for a cook or servant, and what confidence would they place in him, dressed as he was? What references could he offer?
As he was mulling this over, his eyes fell upon a huge placard that a sort of clown was carrying through the streets. The placard, in English, read as follows:

ACROBATIC JAPANESE TROUPE, HONOURABLE WILLIAM BATULCAR, PROPRIETOR, LAST PERFORMANCES, PRIOR TO THEIR DEPARTURE TO THE UNITED STATES, OF THE LONG NOSES! LONG NOSES! UNDER THE DIRECT PATRONAGE OF THE GOD TINGOU! GREAT ATTRACTION!
“The United States!” said Passepartout. “That’s just what I want!”

He followed the clown, and soon found himself back in the Japanese quarter. A quarter of an hour later he stopped before a large shed, decorated with several clusters of streamers, whose exterior walls were painted to represent, in violent colours and without any perspective, a company of jugglers.

This was the Honourable William Batulcar’s establishment. That gentleman was a kind of Barnum, the director of a troupe of mountebanks, jugglers, clowns, acrobats, tightrope-walkers, and gymnasts who, according to the placard, was giving his last performances before leaving the Empire of the Sun for the States of the Union.
Passepartout went in and asked for Mr. Batulcar, who appeared in person without delay.
“What do you want?” he said to Passepartout, taking him at first for a native.
“Would you like a servant, sir?” asked Passepartout.

“A servant!” cried Mr. Batulcar, stroking the thick grey beard that hung from his chin. “I already have two who are obedient and faithful, who have never left me, and who serve me for their food — and here they are,” he added, holding out his two robust arms, ridged with veins as thick as the strings of a bass-viol.
“So I can be of no use to you?”
“None.”
“Confound it! I should so like to cross the Pacific with you!”
“Ah!” said the Honourable Mr. Batulcar. “You are no more Japanese than I am a monkey! Why are you dressed up like that?”
“A man dresses as he can.”
“True enough. You’re a Frenchman, aren’t you?”
“Yes; a Parisian, born and bred.”
“Then you must know how to pull faces?”
“Well,” replied Passepartout, a little put out that his nationality should prompt the question, “we Frenchmen do know how to pull faces, that’s true — but no better than the Americans do.”
“True. Well, if I can’t take you on as a servant, I can take you on as a clown. You see, my friend, in France they show off foreign clowns, and in foreign parts they show off French ones.”
“Ah!”
“You’re pretty strong, eh?”
“Especially after a good meal.”
“And you can sing?”
“Yes,” replied Passepartout, who had once been in the habit of singing in the streets.
“But can you sing standing on your head, with a top spinning on your left foot and a sabre balanced on your right?”
“Hmph! I think so,” answered Passepartout, recalling the exercises of his younger days.
“Well, that’s enough,” said the Honourable William Batulcar.
The contract was settled there and then.

Passepartout had at last found something to do. He was engaged to perform with the celebrated Japanese troupe. It was not a very dignified position, but within a week he would be on his way to San Francisco.

The performance, so noisily advertised by the Honourable Mr. Batulcar, was to begin at three o’clock, and soon the deafening instruments of a Japanese orchestra were sounding at the door. Passepartout, though he had had no chance to study or rehearse a part, was assigned to lend his sturdy shoulders to the great act of the “human pyramid,” performed by the Long Noses of the god Tingou. This “great attraction” was to close the show.

Before three o’clock the large shed was invaded by spectators — Europeans and natives, Chinese and Japanese, men, women, and children — who rushed onto the narrow benches and into the boxes facing the stage. The musicians took their place inside, and were vigorously playing on their gongs, tam-tams, flutes, clappers, tambourines, and huge drums.
The performance was much like any acrobatic display; but it must be admitted that the Japanese are the finest tightrope-walkers in the world.

One, with a fan and some scraps of paper, performed the graceful trick of the butterflies and the flowers; another traced in the air, with the fragrant smoke of his pipe, a series of blue words that made up a compliment to the audience; while a third juggled with lighted candles, which he snuffed out one after the other as they passed his lips and lit again without interrupting his juggling for an instant. Another produced the strangest combinations with spinning tops; in his hands the spinning tops seemed to have a life of their own in their endless whirling; they ran over pipe-stems, the edges of sabres, wires, and even hairs stretched across the stage; they spun around on the rims of large glasses, crossed bamboo ladders, scattered into every corner, and produced strange musical effects by combining their various pitches. The jugglers tossed them in the air, threw them like shuttlecocks with wooden battledores, and still they kept spinning; they put them into their pockets and took them out still whirling as before.
It is pointless to describe the astonishing performances of the acrobats and gymnasts. The turning on ladders, poles, balls, barrels, and the rest was carried out with wonderful precision.
But the main attraction was the show of the Long Noses, a spectacle Europe has yet to see.

The Long Noses make up a peculiar company, under the direct patronage of the god Tingou. Dressed in the fashion of the Middle Ages, they carried on their shoulders a splendid pair of wings; but what set them apart above all were the long noses fixed to their faces and the uses they made of them. These noses were made of bamboo, and were five, six, and even ten feet long — some straight, others curved, some ribboned, and some with imitation warts on them. It was on these appendages, strapped tightly over their real noses, that they performed their gymnastic feats. A dozen of these followers of Tingou would lie flat on their backs, while others, costumed as lightning-rods, came and frolicked about on their noses, leaping from one to another, and performing the most skilful jumps and somersaults.

For the closing scene, a “human pyramid” had been announced, in which fifty Long Noses were to represent the Car of Juggernaut. But instead of forming a pyramid by climbing on one another’s shoulders, the performers were to arrange themselves on top of the noses. As it happened, the performer who had until now formed the base of the Car had left the troupe, and since strength and skill were all that was needed for the role, Passepartout had been picked to take his place.

The poor fellow really did feel low when — melancholy memory of his youth! — he put on his costume, decked out with multicoloured wings, and strapped to his actual nose a false one six feet long. But he cheered up when he reflected that this nose was earning him something to eat.

He stepped onto the stage and took his place beside the others who were to form the base of the Car of Juggernaut. They all stretched out on the floor, their noses pointing to the ceiling. A second group of artists arranged themselves on top of these long appendages; then a third above them; then a fourth, until a human monument rising to the very cornices of the theatre had soon been built up on top of the noses. This drew loud applause, in the middle of which the orchestra was just striking up a deafening tune, when the pyramid wobbled, the balance was lost, one of the lower noses dropped out of the pyramid, and the human monument shattered like a castle of cards!

It was Passepartout’s fault. Abandoning his position, vaulting the footlights without the help of his wings, and clambering up to the right-hand gallery, he fell at the feet of one of the spectators, crying, “Ah, my master! my master!”
“You here?”
“Myself.”
“Very well; then let us go to the steamer, young man!”

Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Passepartout passed through the lobby of the theatre to the outside, where they ran into the Honourable Mr. Batulcar, furious with rage. He demanded damages for the “breakage” of the pyramid; and Phileas Fogg pacified him by handing him a fistful of banknotes.
At half-past six — the very hour of departure — Mr. Fogg and Aouda, followed by Passepartout, who in his haste had kept on his wings and his six-foot nose, stepped aboard the American steamer.

chapters.title: Chapter 24. During which Mr. Fogg and Party Cross the Pacific Ocean
paragraphs: What happened when the pilot-boat came in sight of Shanghai is easily guessed. The signals made by the “Tankadere” had been spotted by the captain of the Yokohama steamer, who, seeing the flag at half-mast, had turned his course towards the little craft. Phileas Fogg, after paying John Bunsby the agreed price for his passage, and rewarding the good fellow with an extra sum of five hundred and fifty pounds, climbed aboard the steamer with Aouda and Fix; and they set off at once for Nagasaki and Yokohama.

They reached their destination on the morning of the 14th of November. Phileas Fogg lost no time in going aboard the “Carnatic,” where he learned, to Aouda’s great delight — and perhaps to his own, though he betrayed no emotion — that Passepartout, a Frenchman, had indeed arrived on her the day before.

The San Francisco steamer was due to leave that very evening, and it became necessary to find Passepartout, if at all possible, without delay. Mr. Fogg appealed in vain to the French and English consuls, and after wandering the streets a long time, began to despair of finding his missing servant. Chance, or perhaps a kind of premonition, at last led him into the Honourable Mr. Batulcar’s theatre. He would certainly not have recognised Passepartout in the eccentric mountebank’s costume; but the latter, lying on his back, spotted his master up in the gallery. He could not help giving a start, which so shifted the angle of his nose that the “pyramid” came tumbling down on the stage.
All this Passepartout learned from Aouda, who recounted to him what had happened on the voyage from Hong Kong to Shanghai aboard the “Tankadere,” in the company of one Mr. Fix.

Passepartout did not change his expression at the name. He decided that the moment had not yet come to tell his master what had passed between the detective and himself; and in the account he gave of his absence, he simply made his excuses for having been overcome by drunkenness while smoking opium at a tavern in Hong Kong.

Mr. Fogg heard this narrative coldly, without a word; and then provided his servant with the funds needed for clothing more in keeping with his station. Within an hour the Frenchman had shed his nose, parted with his wings, and kept nothing about him that recalled the follower of the god Tingou.

The steamer about to depart from Yokohama for San Francisco belonged to the Pacific Mail Steamship Company and was called the “General Grant.” She was a large paddle-wheel steamer of two thousand five hundred tons; well equipped and very fast. The massive walking-beam rose and fell above the deck; at one end a piston-rod worked up and down; at the other a connecting-rod, transforming the straight-line motion into a circular one, drove directly the shaft of the paddles. The “General Grant” was rigged with three masts, giving her a large sail area, and so giving substantial help to her steam power. By making twelve miles an hour, she would cross the ocean in twenty-one days. Phileas Fogg was therefore justified in hoping that he would reach San Francisco on the 2nd of December, New York on the 11th, and London on the 20th — gaining several hours on the fatal date of the 21st of December.

There was a full complement of passengers on board: among them English, many Americans, a large number of coolies on their way to California, and several East Indian officers spending their leave on a tour of the world. Nothing of consequence happened during the voyage; the steamer, carried steadily on her large paddles, rolled little, and the “Pacific” almost lived up to its name. Mr. Fogg was as calm and taciturn as ever. His young companion felt herself drawn to him by ties other than gratitude; his silent but generous nature impressed her more than she realised; and it was almost unconsciously that she gave way to feelings which seemed not to affect her protector in the least. Aouda took the keenest interest in his plans, and grew impatient at any incident that threatened to delay the journey.

She often chatted with Passepartout, who could not fail to see the state of the lady’s heart; and being the most loyal of servants, he was tireless in his praise of Phileas Fogg’s honesty, generosity, and devotion. He took pains to ease Aouda’s doubts about a successful outcome to the journey, telling her that the most difficult part of it was past, that they were now beyond the fantastic countries of Japan and China and well on their way back to civilised places. A railway train from San Francisco to New York, and a transatlantic steamer from New York to Liverpool, would surely bring them to the end of this impossible journey round the world within the agreed time.

On the ninth day after leaving Yokohama, Phileas Fogg had covered exactly half the globe. On the 23rd of November the “General Grant” crossed the one hundred and eightieth meridian, putting them at the antipodes of London. Mr. Fogg had, it is true, used up fifty-two of the eighty days in which he was to complete the tour, and only twenty-eight were left. But although he was only halfway in terms of difference in meridians, he had really covered two-thirds of the whole journey; for he had been forced to make long detours from London to Aden, from Aden to Bombay, from Calcutta to Singapore, and from Singapore to Yokohama. Had he been able to follow the fiftieth parallel — London’s latitude — straight through, the whole distance would have been only about twelve thousand miles; whereas by the haphazard means of travel available, he would have to cover twenty-six thousand, of which on the 23rd of November he had already done seventeen thousand five hundred. And now the course ran straight, and Fix was no longer there to throw obstacles in their way!

It also happened, on the 23rd of November, that Passepartout made a joyful discovery. As will be remembered, the stubborn fellow had insisted on keeping his famous family watch on London time, and on treating that of the countries he passed through as quite false and unreliable. Now, on this day, although he had not moved the hands, he found that his watch agreed exactly with the ship’s chronometers. His triumph was hilarious. He would have loved to know what Fix would say if he were on board!

“That rogue told me all sorts of stories,” Passepartout kept saying, “about meridians, the sun, the moon! The moon, indeed! Moonshine, more like! If you listened to that lot, a fine sort of time you’d be keeping! I always knew the sun would one day fall in line with my watch!”

Passepartout did not know that, if the face of his watch had been divided into twenty-four hours, like the Italian clocks, he would have had no reason for triumph; for the hands of his watch would then, instead of indicating nine o’clock in the morning as they did, have shown nine o’clock in the evening — that is, the twenty-first hour after midnight, precisely the difference between London time and that of the one hundred and eightieth meridian. But even if Fix had been able to explain this purely physical fact, Passepartout would not have accepted it — even if he had understood it. What was more, had the detective been aboard at that moment, Passepartout would have taken him up on a very different subject, and in a very different manner.
Where was Fix at that moment?
He was, in fact, on board the “General Grant.”

On reaching Yokohama, the detective, leaving Mr. Fogg, whom he expected to run into again during the day, had gone straight to the English consulate, where he at last found the warrant of arrest. It had followed him from Bombay, and had come by way of the “Carnatic,” on which steamer he himself was supposed to have been. Fix’s disappointment can be imagined when he realised that the warrant was now useless. Mr. Fogg had left English ground, and it would now be necessary to obtain his extradition!

“Well,” thought Fix after a moment’s anger, “my warrant is no good here, but it will be in England. The rogue clearly means to return home, thinking he has shaken off the police. Good! I’ll follow him across the Atlantic. As for the money — heaven grant there may be some left! But the fellow has already spent more than five thousand pounds on travel, rewards, trials, bail, elephants, and all sorts of expenses. Still, after all, the Bank is rich!”

His course decided, he went aboard the “General Grant,” and was there when Mr. Fogg and Aouda arrived. To his utter amazement, he recognised Passepartout in spite of his theatrical disguise. He quickly hid himself in his cabin to avoid an awkward scene, and hoped — given the number of passengers — to remain unnoticed by Mr. Fogg’s servant.

On that very day, however, he met Passepartout face to face on the forward deck. The latter, without a word, made a rush for him, seized him by the throat, and, much to the amusement of a group of Americans who immediately began to bet on him, dealt the detective a perfect volley of blows, proving the great superiority of French over English pugilistic skill.
When Passepartout had finished, he felt relieved and comforted. Fix got up in a somewhat rumpled condition, and, looking at his adversary, said coldly, “Are you done?”
“For this time — yes.”
“Then let me have a word with you.”
“But I —”
“In your master’s interest.”
Passepartout seemed disarmed by Fix’s coolness, for he quietly followed him, and they sat down apart from the other passengers.
“You’ve given me a thrashing,” said Fix. “Good — I expected it. Now listen. Up to now I have been Mr. Fogg’s adversary. From this moment I am in his game.”
“Aha!” cried Passepartout. “You are convinced he is an honest man?”

“No,” Fix replied coldly. “I take him for a rascal. Hush! Don’t budge, and let me finish. As long as Mr. Fogg was on English ground, it was in my interest to hold him there until my warrant of arrest arrived. I did everything I could to detain him. I set the Bombay priests on his trail, I got you drunk at Hong Kong, I separated you from him, and I made him miss the Yokohama steamer.”
Passepartout listened with clenched fists.

“Now,” Fix went on, “Mr. Fogg seems to be heading back to England. Well, I’ll follow him there. But from here on, I’ll do as much to clear obstacles out of his way as I’ve done up to now to put them in it. I’ve changed my game, you see, simply because it suits me to change it. Your interest is the same as mine; for it is only in England that you’ll find out whether you are in the service of a criminal or an honest man.”
Passepartout listened very attentively to Fix, and was convinced he spoke in entirely good faith.
“Are we friends?” asked the detective.
“Friends? — no,” replied Passepartout. “Allies, perhaps. But at the slightest sign of treachery, I’ll wring your neck for you.”
“Agreed,” said the detective quietly.
Eleven days later, on the 3rd of December, the “General Grant” entered the bay of the Golden Gate, and reached San Francisco.
Mr. Fogg had neither gained nor lost a single day.

chapters.title: Chapter 25. In which a Slight Glimpse is Had of San Francisco
paragraphs: It was seven in the morning when Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Passepartout set foot on the American continent — if that name can be given to the floating quay where they disembarked. These quays, rising and falling with the tide, make loading and unloading easier. Alongside them lay clippers of every size, steamers of every nationality, and the multi-decked steamboats that ply the Sacramento and its tributaries. Piled there too were the products of a commerce that reaches to Mexico, Chili, Peru, Brazil, Europe, Asia, and all the Pacific islands.

Passepartout, in his joy at having reached the American continent at last, thought he would mark the moment by executing a perilous somersault in fine style; but, landing on some worm-eaten planks, he crashed straight through them. Embarrassed by the way in which he thus “set foot” on the New World, he let out a loud cry, which so frightened the countless cormorants and pelicans that perch on these movable quays that they flew off in a noisy panic.

Mr. Fogg, on reaching the shore, set about finding out at what hour the first train left for New York, and learned it was at six o’clock that evening; he therefore had a whole day to spend in the Californian capital. Hiring a carriage at a charge of three dollars, he and Aouda got in, while Passepartout climbed up beside the driver, and they set off for the International Hotel.

From his perch, Passepartout watched with great curiosity the wide streets, the low evenly aligned houses, the Anglo-Saxon Gothic churches, the great docks, the palatial wooden and brick warehouses, the many vehicles — omnibuses, horse-cars — and, on the pavements, not only Americans and Europeans but Chinese and Indians. Passepartout was astonished at everything he saw. San Francisco was no longer the legendary city of 1849 — a city of bandits, killers, and arsonists who had flocked there in crowds in pursuit of plunder; a paradise of outlaws who gambled with gold-dust, a revolver in one hand and a bowie-knife in the other: it was now a great commercial centre.

The lofty tower of its City Hall looked down on the whole panorama of streets and avenues crossing one another at right angles, with pleasant green squares scattered among them, while beyond lay the Chinese quarter, looking as if it had been shipped over from the Celestial Empire in a toy-box. Sombreros and red shirts and feathered Indians were rarely to be seen; instead, silk hats and black coats were worn everywhere by a multitude of briskly active, gentlemanly-looking men. Some of the streets — especially Montgomery Street, which is to San Francisco what Regent Street is to London, the Boulevard des Italiens to Paris, and Broadway to New York — were lined with splendid, spacious stores displaying in their windows the products of the entire world.
When Passepartout reached the International Hotel, it did not feel to him as if he had left England at all.

The ground floor of the hotel was taken up by a large bar — a sort of restaurant freely open to any passer-by — who could help himself to dried beef, oyster soup, biscuits, and cheese without taking out his purse. Payment was made only for the ale, porter, or sherry that was drunk. This seemed “very American” to Passepartout. The hotel’s refreshment rooms were comfortable, and Mr. Fogg and Aouda, settling themselves at a table, were generously served on tiny plates by Negroes of the darkest hue.

After breakfast, Mr. Fogg, with Aouda on his arm, set out for the English consulate to have his passport _visaed_. As he was leaving, he met Passepartout, who asked if it might not be a good idea, before boarding the train, to buy a dozen or so Enfield rifles and Colt revolvers. He had been listening to stories of attacks on the trains by the Sioux and Pawnees. Mr. Fogg thought this an unnecessary precaution, but told him to do as he thought best, and went on to the consulate.

He had not gone two hundred steps, however, when, “by the greatest chance in the world,” he ran into Fix. The detective seemed entirely taken aback. What! Had Mr. Fogg and he crossed the Pacific together without ever meeting on the steamer! At least Fix said he was honoured to set eyes again on the gentleman to whom he owed so much; and, since his business was calling him back to Europe, he would be delighted to continue the journey in such pleasant company.

Mr. Fogg replied that the honour would be his; and the detective — determined not to lose sight of him — asked permission to join them on their walk around San Francisco — a request Mr. Fogg readily granted.

They soon found themselves in Montgomery Street, where a great crowd had gathered; the pavements, the street, the horse-car rails, the shop doorways, the windows of the houses, and even the rooftops were full of people. Men were going about carrying large placards; flags and streamers floated in the wind; and loud cries were heard on every side.
“Hurrah for Camerfield!”
“Hurrah for Mandiboy!”
It was a political meeting; or so Fix guessed, who said to Mr. Fogg, “Perhaps we’d better not mix with the crowd. There may be danger in it.”
“Yes,” replied Mr. Fogg; “and blows, even political ones, are still blows.”

Fix smiled at the remark; and in order to be able to see without being jostled about, the party took up a position at the top of a flight of steps at the upper end of Montgomery Street. Opposite them, on the other side of the street, between a coal wharf and a petroleum warehouse, a large platform had been put up in the open air, towards which the current of the crowd seemed to be flowing.

What was this meeting for? What was the occasion of this excited gathering? Phileas Fogg could not imagine. Was it to nominate some senior official — a governor or a member of Congress? Not unlikely, so worked up was the crowd before them.

Just at this moment an unusual stir ran through the human mass. All hands were thrown up into the air. Some, tightly clenched, seemed to vanish suddenly amid the cries — an energetic way, no doubt, of casting a vote. The crowd swayed back, the banners and flags wavered, disappeared for an instant, then reappeared in tatters. The undulations of the human swell reached the steps, and all the heads bobbed on the surface like a sea whipped up by a squall. Many of the black hats vanished, and most of the crowd seemed to have lost some height.
“It is obviously a meeting,” said Fix, “and its subject must be a heated one. I shouldn’t be surprised if it were about the ‘Alabama,’ even though that question is settled.”
“Perhaps,” replied Mr. Fogg simply.
“At any rate, there are two champions squaring off — the Honourable Mr. Camerfield and the Honourable Mr. Mandiboy.”

Aouda, leaning on Mr. Fogg’s arm, watched the tumultuous scene with surprise, while Fix asked a man near him what it was all about. Before the man could reply, a fresh agitation broke out; hurrahs and excited shouts went up; the staffs of the banners began to be used as offensive weapons; and fists flew in every direction. Blows were exchanged from the tops of the carriages and omnibuses trapped in the crowd. Boots and shoes went whirling through the air, and Mr. Fogg thought he even heard the crack of revolvers mingling with the din; the rout pushed up towards the stairway, and spilled over onto the lowest step. One of the parties had clearly been driven back; but the bystanders could not tell whether Mandiboy or Camerfield had gained the upper hand.

“It would be wise for us to retreat,” said Fix, who was anxious that Mr. Fogg should come to no harm — at least until they were back in London. “If there’s any question about England in all this, and we were recognised, I fear it would go badly for us.”
“An English subject —” Mr. Fogg began.

He did not finish the sentence; for at that moment a terrific hubbub broke out on the terrace behind the flight of steps where they stood, and there were frantic shouts of, “Hurrah for Mandiboy! Hip, hip, hurrah!”

It was a band of voters coming to the rescue of their allies, attacking the Camerfield forces on the flank. Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Fix found themselves caught between two fires; it was too late to escape. The torrent of men, armed with loaded canes and sticks, was unstoppable. Phileas Fogg and Fix were roughly buffeted as they tried to protect their fair companion; Fogg, as cool as ever, tried to defend himself with the weapons nature has placed at the end of every Englishman’s arm — but in vain. A big brawny fellow with a red beard, a flushed face, and broad shoulders, who seemed to be the leader of the band, raised his clenched fist to strike Mr. Fogg and would have dealt him a crushing blow had not Fix rushed in and taken it in his place. An enormous bruise instantly appeared under the detective’s silk hat, which was completely caved in.
“Yankee!” exclaimed Mr. Fogg, casting a contemptuous look at the ruffian.
“Englishman!” the other shot back. “We shall meet again!”
“Whenever you please.”
“What is your name?”
“Phileas Fogg. And yours?”
“Colonel Stamp Proctor.”

The human tide then swept on, after knocking over Fix, who got quickly to his feet again, though with his clothes in tatters. Luckily he was not seriously hurt. His travelling overcoat had been split into two unequal parts, and his trousers looked like those of certain Indians, which fit less snugly than they are easy to put on. Aouda had escaped unharmed, and Fix alone bore the marks of the fray in his black and blue bruise.
“Thanks,” said Mr. Fogg to the detective, once they were clear of the crowd.
“No thanks needed,” replied Fix; “but let’s get going.”
“Where?”
“To a tailor’s.”

Such a visit was, in fact, well timed. The clothing of both Mr. Fogg and Fix was in rags, as though they themselves had taken an active part in the brawl between Camerfield and Mandiboy. An hour later, they were once more suitably dressed, and with Aouda they returned to the International Hotel.

Passepartout was waiting for his master, armed with half a dozen six-barrelled revolvers. When he caught sight of Fix, he knit his brows; but Aouda having, in a few words, told him about their adventure, his face resumed its usual placid expression. Fix was evidently no longer an enemy, but an ally; he was faithfully keeping his word.
Dinner over, the coach that was to take the travellers and their luggage to the station drew up at the door. As he was getting in, Mr. Fogg said to Fix, “You haven’t seen this Colonel Proctor again?”
“No.”
“I shall come back to America to find him,” said Phileas Fogg calmly. “It would not be right for an Englishman to allow himself to be treated like that without striking back.”
The detective smiled, but did not reply. It was clear that Mr. Fogg was one of those Englishmen who, while they will not tolerate duelling at home, fight abroad when their honour is attacked.

At a quarter to six the travellers reached the station, and found the train ready to depart. As he was about to board, Mr. Fogg called a porter and said to him: “My friend, was there not some kind of trouble today in San Francisco?”
“It was a political meeting, sir,” replied the porter.
“But I thought there was a great deal of disturbance in the streets.”
“It was only a meeting called for an election.”
“The election of a commander-in-chief, no doubt?” asked Mr. Fogg.
“No, sir; of a justice of the peace.”
Phileas Fogg boarded the train, which set off at full speed.

chapters.title: Chapter 26. In which Phileas Fogg and Party Travel by the Pacific Railroad
paragraphs: “From ocean to ocean” — so the Americans say; and these four words form the general name of the “great trunk line” that crosses the entire width of the United States. The Pacific Railroad is, however, really split into two distinct lines: the Central Pacific, between San Francisco and Ogden, and the Union Pacific, between Ogden and Omaha. Five main lines link Omaha with New York.

New York and San Francisco are thus joined by an unbroken ribbon of metal, no less than three thousand seven hundred and eighty-six miles long. Between Omaha and the Pacific the railway crosses a territory still infested by Indians and wild beasts, and a large tract that the Mormons, after being driven from Illinois in 1845, began to settle.
The journey from New York to San Francisco used to take, under the most favourable conditions, at least six months. It is now done in seven days.

It was in 1862 that, in spite of the Southern members of Congress, who wanted a more southerly route, it was decided to lay the road between the forty-first and forty-second parallels. President Lincoln himself set the terminus at Omaha, in Nebraska. Work began at once, and was pushed forward with true American energy; nor did the speed of construction harm the quality of the work. On the prairies, the road grew by a mile and a half a day. A locomotive, running on the rails laid the evening before, brought the rails to be laid the next day, and advanced over them as fast as they were put in place.

The Pacific Railroad is joined by several branches in Iowa, Kansas, Colorado, and Oregon. On leaving Omaha, it runs along the left bank of the Platte River as far as the junction of its northern branch; follows the southern branch; crosses the Laramie territory and the Wahsatch Mountains; rounds the Great Salt Lake; reaches Salt Lake City, the Mormon capital; plunges into the Tuilla Valley; crosses the American Desert, the Cedar and Humboldt Mountains, the Sierra Nevada; and descends, _via_ Sacramento, to the Pacific — its grade, even in the Rocky Mountains, never exceeding one hundred and twelve feet to the mile.
