Such was the road to be covered in seven days, which would let Phileas Fogg — at least so he hoped — catch the Atlantic steamer at New York on the 11th for Liverpool.

The car he was in was a sort of long omnibus on eight wheels, with no compartments inside. It had two rows of seats, set at right angles to the direction of the train on either side of an aisle leading to the front and rear platforms. These platforms ran the length of the train, and passengers could walk from one end of the train to the other. The train included saloon cars, balcony cars, restaurants, and smoking cars; only theatre cars were missing, and one day they will have those too.
Book and news vendors, sellers of food, drinks, and cigars — who seemed to have plenty of customers — circulated continually up and down the aisles.

The train left Oakland station at six o’clock. It was already night, cold and cheerless, the sky overcast with clouds that seemed to threaten snow. The train did not move quickly; counting the stops, it averaged no more than twenty miles an hour, which was, however, fast enough to bring it to Omaha within its scheduled time.

There was little conversation in the car, and soon many of the passengers were overcome by sleep. Passepartout found himself seated beside the detective; but he did not speak to him. After the recent events, their relations had grown somewhat cold; there could no longer be any mutual sympathy or intimacy between them. Fix’s manner had not changed; but Passepartout was very reserved, and ready to strangle his former friend at the slightest provocation.

Snow began to fall an hour after they started — fine snow, fortunately, that could not block the train; nothing could be seen from the windows but a vast white sheet, against which the smoke of the locomotive looked greyish.

At eight o’clock a steward entered the car and announced that it was time to go to bed; and within a few minutes the car was transformed into a dormitory. The backs of the seats were tilted down, neatly packed bedsteads were rolled out by an ingenious mechanism, berths were improvised in a moment, and each traveller soon had a comfortable bed at his disposal, screened from prying eyes by thick curtains. The sheets were clean and the pillows soft. It only remained to lie down and sleep — which everyone did — while the train sped on across the State of California.

The country between San Francisco and Sacramento is not very hilly. The Central Pacific, taking Sacramento as its starting point, runs eastward to meet the road from Omaha. The line from San Francisco to Sacramento runs north-east, along the American River, which empties into San Pablo Bay. The hundred and twenty miles between these cities were covered in six hours, and around midnight, while they were sound asleep, the travellers passed through Sacramento; so they saw nothing of that important place, the seat of the State government, with its fine quays, its broad streets, its noble hotels, squares, and churches.

The train, on leaving Sacramento, and passing the junction, Roclin, Auburn, and Colfax, entered the range of the Sierra Nevada. ’Cisco was reached at seven in the morning; and an hour later the dormitory was turned back into an ordinary car, and the travellers could take in the picturesque beauties of the mountain region they were steaming through. The track wound in and out among the passes, now hugging the mountainsides, now suspended over precipices, dodging sharp angles with bold curves, plunging into narrow defiles that seemed to have no outlet. The locomotive, its great funnel throwing a weird light, with its shrill bell and its cow-catcher thrust out like a spur, mingled its shrieks and bellowings with the noise of torrents and cascades, and wove its smoke through the branches of the gigantic pines.
There were few or no bridges or tunnels on the route. The railway curved around the sides of the mountains, making no attempt to violate nature by taking the shortest route from one point to another.
The train entered the State of Nevada through the Carson Valley around nine o’clock, still moving north-east; and at noon it reached Reno, where there was a twenty-minute stop for breakfast.

From here the road, running along the Humboldt River, headed north for several miles along its banks; then it turned eastward and followed the river until it reached the Humboldt Range, almost at the extreme eastern edge of Nevada.

Having breakfasted, Mr. Fogg and his companions returned to their places in the car, and watched the changing landscape unfold as they rolled past vast prairies, mountains lining the horizon, and creeks with their frothy, foaming streams. At times a great herd of buffaloes, massing together in the distance, looked like a moving dam. These countless herds of ruminating beasts often form an insurmountable obstacle to the trains; thousands of them have been seen crossing the track for hours on end, in compact ranks. The locomotive is then forced to halt and wait until the road is clear again.

This is exactly what happened to the train Mr. Fogg was on. Around twelve o’clock a herd of ten or twelve thousand head of buffalo blocked the track. The locomotive, slowing down, tried to clear a way with its cow-catcher; but the mass of animals was too great. The buffaloes plodded along at a calm pace, letting out a deafening bellow now and then. There was no point in interrupting them, for once they have set off in a particular direction, nothing can slow them down or turn them; it is a torrent of living flesh which no dam could hold back.

The travellers gazed at this curious spectacle from the platforms; but Phileas Fogg, who had more reason than anyone to be in a hurry, kept his seat, and waited philosophically until it pleased the buffaloes to clear the way.
Passepartout was furious at the delay they caused, and itched to empty his arsenal of revolvers into them.

“What a country!” he cried. “Mere cattle stop the trains and parade across as if they weren’t blocking traffic! Parbleu! I should like to know if Mr. Fogg foresaw _this_ mishap in his programme! And here’s an engineer who doesn’t even dare drive the locomotive into the herd!”

The engineer did not attempt to force the obstacle, and he was right not to. He would certainly have crushed the first buffaloes with the cow-catcher; but the locomotive, however powerful, would soon have been stopped, the train would inevitably have been thrown off the track, and would then have been helpless.

The best course was to wait patiently, and make up the lost time with greater speed once the obstacle was gone. The buffalo procession lasted three full hours, and it was night before the track was clear. The last ranks of the herd were just passing over the rails, while the first had already vanished below the southern horizon.
It was eight o’clock when the train passed through the defiles of the Humboldt Range, and half-past nine when it entered Utah, the region of the Great Salt Lake — the strange colony of the Mormons.

chapters.title: Chapter 27. In which Passepartout Undergoes, at a Speed of Twenty Miles an Hour, a Course of Mormon History
paragraphs: During the night of the 5th of December, the train ran south-east for about fifty miles; then climbed an equal distance to the north-east, towards the Great Salt Lake.

Around nine o’clock, Passepartout stepped out onto the platform for some air. The weather was cold, the sky grey, but it was not snowing. The sun’s disc, swollen by the mist, looked like an enormous ring of gold, and Passepartout was amusing himself by calculating its value in pounds sterling, when he was distracted from this interesting study by a strange-looking figure who appeared on the platform.

This personage, who had boarded the train at Elko, was tall and dark, with a black moustache, black stockings, a black silk hat, a black waistcoat, black trousers, a white cravat, and dogskin gloves. He might have been taken for a clergyman. He went from one end of the train to the other, fixing to the door of each car a hand-written notice.

Passepartout went up and read one of these notices, which announced that Elder William Hitch, a Mormon missionary, taking advantage of his presence on train No. 48, would give a lecture on Mormonism in car No. 117 from eleven to twelve o’clock; and that he invited all who wished to be instructed in the mysteries of the religion of the “Latter Day Saints” to attend.
“I’ll go,” Passepartout said to himself. He knew nothing of Mormonism beyond the practice of polygamy, which is its foundation.

The news spread quickly through the train, which held about a hundred passengers, of whom thirty at most, drawn by the notice, settled themselves into car No. 117. Passepartout took one of the front seats. Neither Mr. Fogg nor Fix cared to attend.

At the appointed hour Elder William Hitch rose, and, in an irritated voice, as if he had already been contradicted, said, “I tell you that Joe Smith is a martyr, that his brother Hiram is a martyr, and that the persecutions of the United States Government against the prophets will also make a martyr of Brigham Young. Who dares to say the contrary?”

No one ventured to contradict the missionary, whose worked-up tone made a curious contrast with his naturally calm face. No doubt his anger sprang from the hardships the Mormons were actually being put through. The government had just succeeded, with some difficulty, in bringing these independent fanatics under its rule. It had made itself master of Utah, and subjected that territory to the laws of the Union, after imprisoning Brigham Young on charges of rebellion and polygamy. The prophet’s disciples had since redoubled their efforts, and resisted, at least in words, the authority of Congress. Elder Hitch, as you see, was trying to win converts even on the railway trains.

Then, emphasising his words with his loud voice and frequent gestures, he related the history of the Mormons from Biblical times: how, in Israel, a Mormon prophet of the tribe of Joseph published the annals of the new religion, and bequeathed them to his son Mormon; how, many centuries later, a translation of this precious book, written in Egyptian, was made by Joseph Smith, junior, a Vermont farmer, who revealed himself as a mystical prophet in 1825; and how, in short, the heavenly messenger appeared to him in an illuminated forest and gave him the annals of the Lord.

Several listeners, not finding the missionary’s narrative very interesting, left the car at this point; but Elder Hitch, going on with his lecture, told how Smith, junior, with his father, two brothers, and a few disciples, founded the church of the “Latter Day Saints,” which, taken up not only in America but also in England, Norway, Sweden, and Germany, counts many artisans as well as men in the liberal professions among its members; how a colony was established in Ohio, a temple built there at a cost of two hundred thousand dollars, and a town founded at Kirkland; how Smith became an enterprising banker, and received from a humble mummy-showman a papyrus scroll written by Abraham and several famous Egyptians.

The Elder’s story became somewhat tedious, and his audience gradually thinned until it was down to twenty passengers. But this did not faze the enthusiast, who went on to the story of Joseph Smith’s bankruptcy in 1837, and how his ruined creditors gave him a coat of tar and feathers; his reappearance several years later, more honoured and more honourable than ever, at Independence, Missouri, as the head of a flourishing colony of three thousand disciples; and his pursuit from there by outraged Gentiles and retreat into the Far West.

Only ten listeners were left now, among them honest Passepartout, who was listening with all his ears. So he learned that, after long persecutions, Smith reappeared in Illinois, and in 1839 founded a community at Nauvoo, on the Mississippi, numbering twenty-five thousand souls, of which he became mayor, chief justice, and commander-in-chief; that in 1843 he put himself forward as a candidate for the Presidency of the United States; and that finally, lured into an ambush at Carthage, he was thrown into prison and assassinated by a band of masked men.

Passepartout was now the only person left in the car, and the Elder, looking him full in the face, reminded him that two years after the assassination of Joseph Smith, the inspired prophet, Brigham Young, his successor, left Nauvoo for the shores of the Great Salt Lake, where, in the heart of that fertile region, directly on the route of the emigrants crossing Utah on their way to California, the new colony, thanks to the polygamy practised by the Mormons, had flourished beyond all expectations.

“And this,” added Elder William Hitch, “this is why the jealousy of Congress has been turned against us! Why have the soldiers of the Union invaded the soil of Utah? Why has Brigham Young, our chief, been thrown into prison, in contempt of all justice? Shall we yield to force? Never! Driven from Vermont, driven from Illinois, driven from Ohio, driven from Missouri, driven from Utah, we shall yet find some independent territory on which to pitch our tents. And you, my brother,” the Elder went on, fixing his angry eyes on his last listener, “will you not pitch yours there too, under the shadow of our flag?”
“No!” answered Passepartout boldly, getting up in his turn and leaving the car, abandoning the Elder to preach to empty seats.

During the lecture the train had been making good progress, and around half past twelve it reached the north-west edge of the Great Salt Lake. From there the passengers could take in the vast expanse of this inland sea, also called the Dead Sea, into which an American Jordan empties. It is a picturesque stretch of water, framed by lofty crags in great strata encrusted with white salt — a superb sheet of water, once larger than it is now, its shores having advanced over time, thereby both reducing its breadth and increasing its depth.

The Salt Lake, seventy miles long and thirty-five wide, lies three miles eight hundred feet above the sea. Quite unlike Lake Asphaltite, whose depression lies twelve hundred feet below the sea, it contains a great deal of salt, and a quarter of the weight of its water is solid matter, its specific gravity being 1,170, and, after distillation, 1,000. Fish, of course, cannot live in it, and those that come down through the Jordan, the Weber, and other streams soon die.

The country around the lake was well cultivated, for the Mormons are mostly farmers; ranches and pens for domestic animals, fields of wheat, corn, and other cereals, lush prairies, hedges of wild rose, clumps of acacias and milk-wort would have been visible six months later. Now the ground was covered with a thin dusting of snow.

The train reached Ogden at two o’clock, where it stopped for six hours; Mr. Fogg and his party had time to pay a visit to Salt Lake City, connected with Ogden by a branch line; and they spent two hours in this strikingly American town, built on the pattern of other cities of the Union, like a chequerboard, “with the sombre sadness of right angles,” as Victor Hugo puts it. The founder of the City of the Saints could not escape that taste for symmetry which marks the Anglo-Saxons. In this strange country, where the people are certainly not up to the level of their institutions, everything is done “squarely” — cities, houses, and follies.

At three o’clock, then, the travellers were walking about the streets of the town set between the banks of the Jordan and the spurs of the Wahsatch Range. They saw few or no churches, but the prophet’s mansion, the court-house, and the arsenal — blue-brick houses with verandas and porches, surrounded by gardens bordered with acacias, palms, and locusts. A clay-and-pebble wall, built in 1853, encircled the town; and in the main street were the market and several hotels decked out with pavilions. The place did not seem heavily populated. The streets were almost deserted, except near the temple, which they only reached after passing through several quarters surrounded by palisades. There were many women, easily explained by the “peculiar institution” of the Mormons; but it should not be supposed that every Mormon is a polygamist. They are free to marry or not, as they please; but it is worth noting that it is mainly the female citizens of Utah who are eager to marry, since, according to the Mormon religion, single women are not admitted to its highest joys. These poor creatures seemed neither well off nor happy. Some — the better off, no doubt — wore short, open black silk dresses under a hood or modest shawl; others were dressed in Indian fashion.

Passepartout could not look without a certain alarm at these women charged, in groups, with making a single Mormon happy. His common sense pitied above all the husband. It struck him as a terrible thing to have to guide so many wives at once through the ups and downs of life, and to conduct them, as it were, in a body into the Mormon paradise, with the prospect of seeing them in the company of the glorious Smith — who was doubtless the chief ornament of that delightful place — for all eternity. He felt decidedly put off such a vocation, and imagined — perhaps mistakenly — that the fair ones of Salt Lake City were casting rather alarming glances at his person. Happily, his stay there was brief. At four the party were back at the station, took their places in the train, and the whistle sounded for departure. Just at the moment, however, when the locomotive wheels began to turn, cries of “Stop! stop!” were heard.

Trains, like time and tide, wait for no one. The man who had let out the cries was clearly a late-running Mormon. He was breathless from running. Luckily for him, the station had neither gates nor barriers. He raced down the track, jumped onto the rear platform of the train, and dropped, exhausted, into one of the seats.
Passepartout, who had been anxiously watching this amateur gymnast, went over to him with lively curiosity, and learned that he had taken flight after an unpleasant domestic scene.
When the Mormon had got his breath back, Passepartout ventured to ask him politely how many wives he had; for, judging by the way he had bolted, one might have thought he had twenty at least.
“One, sir,” replied the Mormon, raising his arms to heaven — “one, and that was enough!”

chapters.title: Chapter 28. In which Passepartout Does Not Succeed in Making Anybody Listen to Reason
paragraphs: The train, on leaving the Great Salt Lake at Ogden, ran north for an hour as far as Weber River, having now covered nearly nine hundred miles from San Francisco. From this point it turned east towards the jagged Wahsatch Mountains. It was on the stretch between this range and the Rocky Mountains that the American engineers met the most formidable difficulties in laying the road, and that the government granted a subsidy of forty-eight thousand dollars a mile, instead of the sixteen thousand allowed for work done on the plains. But the engineers, instead of violating nature, sidestepped its difficulties by winding around the rocks rather than cutting through them. Only one tunnel, fourteen thousand feet long, was bored to reach the great basin.

Up to this point the track had reached its highest elevation at the Great Salt Lake. From there it described a long curve, descending towards Bitter Creek Valley, only to climb again to the dividing ridge of the waters between the Atlantic and the Pacific. There were many creeks in this mountainous country, and Muddy Creek, Green Creek, and others had to be crossed on culverts.

Passepartout grew more and more impatient as they went on, while Fix longed to be out of this difficult region, and was more anxious than Phileas Fogg himself to put the danger of delays and accidents behind them and set foot on English soil.

At ten o’clock at night the train stopped at Fort Bridger station, and twenty minutes later it entered Wyoming Territory, following the valley of Bitter Creek all the way. The next day, the 7th of December, they stopped for a quarter of an hour at Green River station. Snow had fallen heavily during the night, but, mixed with rain, it had half melted and did not slow their progress. The bad weather, however, worried Passepartout; for a build-up of snow, by clogging the wheels of the cars, would surely have been fatal to Mr. Fogg’s tour.
“What an idea!” he said to himself. “Why did my master make this journey in winter? Couldn’t he have waited for the good season to improve his chances?”
While the good Frenchman was absorbed in the state of the sky and the drop in temperature, Aouda was suffering anxieties from a completely different cause.

Several passengers had got off at Green River and were walking up and down the platforms; and among them Aouda recognised Colonel Stamp Proctor — the same man who had so grossly insulted Phileas Fogg at the San Francisco meeting. Not wishing to be recognised, the young woman drew back from the window, very alarmed by what she had seen. She was attached to the man who, however coldly, gave her daily proofs of the most absolute devotion. She did not perhaps grasp the full depth of the feeling her protector inspired in her, which she called gratitude, but which — though she did not know it — was really more than that. Her heart sank when she recognised the man whom Mr. Fogg meant, sooner or later, to call to account for his conduct. Chance alone, clearly, had put Colonel Proctor on this train; but there he was, and at all costs Phileas Fogg must not catch sight of his adversary.
Aouda seized a moment when Mr. Fogg was asleep to tell Fix and Passepartout whom she had seen.
“That Proctor on this train!” cried Fix. “Well, set your mind at ease, madam; before he settles with Mr. Fogg, he has to settle with me! It seems to me I was the more insulted of the two.”
“And besides,” added Passepartout, “I’ll take charge of him, colonel or no colonel.”

“Mr. Fix,” Aouda went on, “Mr. Fogg will let no one avenge him. He said he would come back to America to find this man. If he were to spot Colonel Proctor, we could not prevent a collision that might have terrible consequences. He must not see him.”
“You are right, madam,” replied Fix; “a meeting between them might ruin everything. Whether he won or lost, Mr. Fogg would be delayed, and —”

“And,” added Passepartout, “that would play right into the hands of the gentlemen of the Reform Club. In four days we shall be in New York. Well, if my master does not leave this car for those four days, we may hope that chance will not put him face to face with this confounded American. We must, if at all possible, keep him from going outside.”

The conversation broke off. Mr. Fogg had just woken up and was looking out of the window. Soon afterwards Passepartout, without being overheard by his master or Aouda, whispered to the detective, “Would you really fight for him?”
“I would do anything,” Fix replied, in a tone that betrayed an iron will, “to get him back to Europe alive!”
Passepartout felt something like a shudder run through him, but his confidence in his master held firm.

Was there any way of keeping Mr. Fogg in the car, to avoid a meeting between him and the colonel? It ought not to be difficult, since the gentleman was naturally sedentary and not very curious. The detective, at least, seemed to have hit on a way; for after a few moments he said to Mr. Fogg, “These are long, slow hours, sir, that we are spending on the railway.”
“Yes,” replied Mr. Fogg; “but they pass.”
“You used to play whist,” Fix went on, “on the steamers.”
“Yes; but it would be difficult to do so here. I have neither cards nor partners.”
“Oh, we can easily buy some cards, for they are sold on all the American trains. And as for partners, if madam plays —”
“Certainly, sir,” Aouda replied quickly; “I know whist. It is part of an English education.”
“And I myself have some pretensions to playing a good game. Well, here are three of us, and a dummy —”
“As you please, sir,” replied Phileas Fogg, heartily glad to take up his favourite pastime again, even on the railway.
Passepartout was sent off in search of the steward, and soon returned with two packs of cards, some pins, counters, and a shelf covered with cloth.

The game began. Aouda played whist well enough, and even received some compliments on her play from Mr. Fogg. As for the detective, he was an outright expert, and a worthy match for his present opponent.
“Now,” Passepartout thought, “we’ve got him. He won’t budge.”

At eleven in the morning the train had reached the dividing ridge of the waters at Bridger Pass, seven thousand five hundred and twenty-four feet above sea level — one of the highest points the track reaches in crossing the Rocky Mountains. After about another two hundred miles, the travellers at last found themselves on one of those vast plains that stretch to the Atlantic, and which nature has made so well suited to the laying of an iron road.

On the slope of the Atlantic basin, the first streams, branches of the North Platte River, were already showing themselves. The whole northern and eastern horizon was bounded by the immense semi-circular curtain formed by the southern part of the Rocky Mountains, with Laramie Peak the highest. Between this and the railway stretched vast plains, plentifully watered. On the right rose the lower spurs of the mountain mass that runs south to the headwaters of the Arkansas River, one of the great tributaries of the Missouri.

At half-past twelve the travellers caught sight for an instant of Fort Halleck, which commands that section; and in a few more hours the Rocky Mountains would be crossed. There was reason to hope, then, that no accident would mark the journey through this difficult country. The snow had stopped falling, and the air had turned crisp and cold. Large birds, frightened by the locomotive, rose and flew off into the distance. No wild beast appeared on the plain. It was a desert in all its vast nakedness.

After a comfortable breakfast served in the car, Mr. Fogg and his partners had just resumed their whist when a violent whistling was heard, and the train stopped. Passepartout put his head out of the door, but saw nothing to explain the delay; no station was in sight.
Aouda and Fix feared that Mr. Fogg might take it into his head to get out; but the gentleman contented himself with saying to his servant, “See what is the matter.”
Passepartout rushed out of the car. Thirty or forty passengers had already got down, and among them Colonel Stamp Proctor.

The train had stopped before a red signal blocking the line. The engineer and conductor were arguing heatedly with a signalman whom the station-master at Medicine Bow, the next stop, had sent on ahead. The passengers gathered round and joined in the discussion, in which Colonel Proctor, with his insolent manner, was conspicuous.
Passepartout, joining the group, heard the signalman say, “No! you can’t go on. The bridge at Medicine Bow is shaky, and would not bear the weight of the train.”

This was a suspension bridge thrown over some rapids, about a mile from where they now were. According to the signalman, it was in ruinous condition, several of the iron wires being broken; and it was impossible to risk crossing. He was in no way exaggerating the bridge’s condition. It can be taken for granted that, reckless as Americans usually are, when they are cautious there is good reason for it.
Passepartout, not daring to tell his master what he had heard, listened with set teeth, motionless as a statue.
“Hum!” cried Colonel Proctor; “but we’re not going to stay here, I suppose, and take root in the snow?”
“Colonel,” replied the conductor, “we have telegraphed to Omaha for a train, but it is unlikely to reach Medicine Bow in less than six hours.”
“Six hours!” cried Passepartout.
“Certainly,” returned the conductor; “besides, it will take us that long to reach Medicine Bow on foot.”
“But it’s only a mile from here,” said one of the passengers.
“Yes, but it’s on the other side of the river.”
“And can’t we cross it in a boat?” asked the colonel.
“Impossible. The creek is swollen by the rains. It’s a rapid, and we shall have to make a ten-mile detour to the north to find a ford.”

The colonel let out a volley of oaths, cursing the railway company and the conductor; and Passepartout, who was furious, was not unwilling to make common cause with him. Here was an obstacle that all his master’s banknotes could not remove.

There was general dismay among the passengers, who, leaving the delay aside, saw themselves forced to trudge fifteen miles over a plain covered with snow. They grumbled and protested, and would surely have drawn Phileas Fogg’s attention had he not been entirely absorbed in his game.

Passepartout found he could not avoid telling his master what had happened, and, with his head down, he was turning back towards the car when the engineer, a true Yankee named Forster, called out, “Gentlemen, perhaps there is a way to get across after all.”
“Over the bridge?” asked a passenger.
“Over the bridge.”
“With our train?”
“With our train.”
Passepartout stopped short, listening intently to the engineer.
“But the bridge is unsafe,” urged the conductor.
“No matter,” replied Forster; “I think that by putting on the very highest speed we might have a chance of getting across.”
“The devil!” muttered Passepartout.

But a number of the passengers were immediately won over by the engineer’s proposal, and Colonel Proctor especially was delighted, finding the plan perfectly feasible. He told stories of engineers leaping their trains over rivers without bridges by putting on full steam; and many of those present declared themselves of the engineer’s mind.
“We’ve got fifty chances out of a hundred of making it,” said one.
“Eighty! ninety!”

Passepartout was astounded, and, though ready to try anything to get over Medicine Creek, thought the proposed experiment a little too American. “Besides,” he thought, “there’s a simpler way, and it doesn’t even occur to any of these people! Sir,” he said aloud to one of the passengers, “the engineer’s plan seems to me a little dangerous, but —”
“Eighty chances!” replied the passenger, turning his back on him.
“I know that,” said Passepartout, turning to another passenger, “but a simple idea —”
“Ideas are no use,” returned the American, shrugging his shoulders, “when the engineer assures us we can get across.”
“No doubt,” pressed Passepartout, “we can get across, but perhaps it would be more prudent —”
“What! Prudent!” cried Colonel Proctor, whom the word seemed to set off prodigiously. “At full speed, don’t you see, at full speed!”
“I know — I see,” Passepartout went on; “but it would be, if not more prudent — since that word displeases you — at least more natural —”
“Who! What! What’s the matter with this fellow?” several voices cried.
The poor fellow did not know whom to address.
“Are you afraid?” asked Colonel Proctor.
“I, afraid? Very well; I will show these people that a Frenchman can be as American as any of them!”
“All aboard!” cried the conductor.
“Yes, all aboard!” Passepartout repeated, and at once. “But they can’t keep me from thinking it would be more natural for us to cross the bridge on foot, and let the train come after!”

But no one heard this sage reflection, nor would anyone have admitted its justice. The passengers took their seats again in the cars. Passepartout sat down without saying anything about what had happened. The whist-players were quite absorbed in their game.

The locomotive whistled vigorously; the engineer, reversing the steam, backed the train almost a mile — drawing back, like a jumper, in order to take a longer leap. Then, with another whistle, he set off forward; the train picked up speed, and soon its speed became terrifying; a long screech burst from the locomotive; the piston worked up and down twenty strokes a second. They could feel that the whole train, rushing on at a hundred miles an hour, hardly rested on the rails at all.

And they made it! It was like a flash. No one saw the bridge. The train leapt, so to speak, from one bank to the other, and the engineer could not stop it until it had gone five miles beyond the station. But hardly had the train cleared the river when the bridge, utterly ruined, collapsed with a crash into the rapids of Medicine Bow.

chapters.title: Chapter 29. In which Certain Incidents are Narrated which are only to be Met with on American Railroads
paragraphs: The train continued on its way that evening without interruption, passing Fort Saunders, crossing Cheyne Pass, and reaching Evans Pass. Here the road reached the highest elevation of the journey, eight thousand and ninety-two feet above sea level. The travellers now had only to descend to the Atlantic by boundless plains, levelled by nature. A branch of the “grand trunk” line ran off southward to Denver, the capital of Colorado. The surrounding country is rich in gold and silver, and more than fifty thousand inhabitants have already settled there.

Thirteen hundred and eighty-two miles had been covered from San Francisco in three days and three nights; four more days and nights would probably bring them to New York. Phileas Fogg was not yet behind schedule.

During the night Camp Walbach was passed on the left; Lodge Pole Creek ran parallel to the road, marking the boundary between the territories of Wyoming and Colorado. They entered Nebraska at eleven, passed near Sedgwick, and called at Julesburg, on the southern branch of the Platte River.

It was here that the Union Pacific Railroad was inaugurated on the 23rd of October, 1867, by the chief engineer, General Dodge. Two powerful locomotives, carrying nine cars of invited guests — among them Thomas C. Durant, vice-president of the road — stopped at this point; cheers were given, the Sioux and Pawnees performed a mock Indian battle, fireworks were let off, and the first issue of the _Railway Pioneer_ was printed by a press brought along on the train. Thus was celebrated the inauguration of this great railroad, a mighty instrument of progress and civilisation, flung across the desert, and destined to link up cities and towns that do not yet exist. The whistle of the locomotive, more powerful than Amphion’s lyre, was about to bid them rise from American soil.

Fort McPherson was left behind at eight in the morning, and three hundred and fifty-seven miles still had to be covered before reaching Omaha. The road followed the capricious bends of the southern branch of the Platte River, along its left bank. At nine the train stopped at the important town of North Platte, built between the two arms of the river, which rejoin around it to form a single artery — a large tributary whose waters empty into the Missouri a little above Omaha.
The one hundred and first meridian was crossed.

Mr. Fogg and his partners had taken up their game again; no one — not even the dummy — complained of the length of the trip. Fix had begun by winning several guineas, which he now seemed about to lose; but he proved himself no less eager a whist-player than Mr. Fogg. During the morning, luck distinctly favoured that gentleman. Trumps and honours were showered on his hands.
Once, having decided on a bold stroke, he was about to play a spade when a voice behind him said, “I should play a diamond.”
Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Fix looked up, and saw Colonel Proctor.
Stamp Proctor and Phileas Fogg recognised each other at once.
“Ah! it’s you, is it, Englishman?” cried the colonel. “It’s you who are about to play a spade!”
“And who plays it,” replied Phileas Fogg coolly, throwing down the ten of spades.
“Well, I’d rather have it diamonds,” Colonel Proctor returned in an insolent tone.
He made a movement as if to seize the card that had just been played, adding, “You don’t understand the first thing about whist.”
“Perhaps I do — as well as any other man,” said Phileas Fogg, rising.
“You have only to try, son of John Bull,” replied the colonel.

Aouda turned pale, and her blood ran cold. She seized Mr. Fogg’s arm and gently pulled him back. Passepartout was ready to fling himself on the American, who was glaring insolently at his opponent. But Fix got up, went to Colonel Proctor, and said, “You forget that it is I you have to deal with, sir; for it was I you not only insulted but struck!”
“Mr. Fix,” said Mr. Fogg, “forgive me, but this affair is mine, and mine alone. The colonel has just insulted me again, by saying I should not play a spade, and he shall give me satisfaction for it.”
“When and where you like,” replied the American, “and with whatever weapon you choose.”

Aouda tried in vain to hold Mr. Fogg back; in vain did the detective try to make the quarrel his own. Passepartout wanted to throw the colonel out of the window, but a sign from his master checked him. Phileas Fogg left the car, and the American followed him onto the platform. “Sir,” said Mr. Fogg to his adversary, “I am in a great hurry to get back to Europe, and any delay whatever will be very much to my disadvantage.”
“Well, what’s that to me?” replied Colonel Proctor.
“Sir,” said Mr. Fogg, very politely, “after our meeting in San Francisco I resolved to return to America and find you, as soon as I had finished the business that called me back to England.”
“Really!”
“Will you set a meeting for six months from now?”
“Why not ten years from now?”
“I say six months,” returned Phileas Fogg; “and I shall be at the appointed place on time.”
“This is all just an evasion,” cried Stamp Proctor. “Now or never!”
“Very well. You are going to New York?”
“No.”
“To Chicago?”
“No.”
“To Omaha?”
“What difference does it make to you? Do you know Plum Creek?”
“No,” replied Mr. Fogg.
“It’s the next station. The train will be there in an hour, and will stop for ten minutes. In ten minutes a fair number of revolver-shots can be exchanged.”
“Very well,” said Mr. Fogg. “I will stop at Plum Creek.”
“And I reckon you’ll stay there too,” added the American insolently.

“Who knows?” Mr. Fogg replied, returning to the car as cool as ever. He set about reassuring Aouda, telling her that blusterers were never to be feared, and asked Fix to be his second at the coming duel — a request the detective could not refuse. Mr. Fogg took up the interrupted game again with perfect calm.

At eleven o’clock the locomotive’s whistle announced that they were nearing Plum Creek station. Mr. Fogg rose, and, followed by Fix, went out onto the platform. Passepartout went with him, carrying a pair of revolvers. Aouda stayed in the car, pale as death.

The door of the next car opened, and Colonel Proctor appeared on the platform, attended by a Yankee of his own stamp as his second. But just as the combatants were about to step down from the train, the conductor hurried up and shouted, “You can’t get off, gentlemen!”
“Why not?” asked the colonel.
“We are twenty minutes late, and we shall not stop.”
“But I am going to fight a duel with this gentleman.”
“I am sorry,” said the conductor; “but we shall be off at once. There’s the bell ringing now.”
The train started.

“I’m really very sorry, gentlemen,” said the conductor. “In any other circumstances I should have been happy to oblige you. But after all, since you haven’t had time to fight here, why not fight as we go along?”
“That mightn’t be convenient — for this gentleman,” said the colonel, in a jeering tone.
“It would be perfectly convenient,” replied Phileas Fogg.
“Well, we really are in America,” thought Passepartout, “and the conductor is a gentleman of the first order!”
Muttering to himself, he followed his master.

The two combatants, their seconds, and the conductor passed through the cars to the rear of the train. The last car was occupied by only a dozen passengers, whom the conductor politely asked if they would be so kind as to leave it free for a few moments, since two gentlemen had an affair of honour to settle. The passengers granted the request readily, and at once vanished onto the platform.

The car, which was some fifty feet long, was very convenient for their purpose. The adversaries could advance on each other in the aisle and fire at their leisure. Never was a duel more easily arranged. Mr. Fogg and Colonel Proctor, each provided with two six-barrelled revolvers, entered the car. The seconds, staying outside, shut them in. They were to begin firing at the first whistle of the locomotive. After an interval of two minutes, what remained of the two gentlemen would be taken out of the car.

Nothing could be more straightforward. Indeed, it was all so simple that Fix and Passepartout felt their hearts pounding fit to burst. They were listening for the agreed whistle, when suddenly savage cries rang out in the air, accompanied by gunshots that certainly did not come from the car where the duellists were. The reports were going on at the front and along the whole length of the train. Cries of terror came from inside the cars.
Colonel Proctor and Mr. Fogg, revolvers in hand, hurriedly left their prison, and rushed forward to where the noise was loudest. They saw then that the train was being attacked by a band of Sioux.

This was not the first attempt of these daring Indians, for more than once they had ambushed trains on the line. A hundred of them, in their usual style, had jumped onto the steps without stopping the train, with the ease of a clown mounting a horse at full gallop.
The Sioux were armed with guns, which produced the reports, to which the passengers — almost all of them armed — replied with revolver-shots.

The Indians had first mounted the engine and half stunned the engineer and stoker with blows from their muskets. A Sioux chief, wanting to stop the train but not knowing how to work the regulator, had opened the steam-valve wide instead of closing it, and the locomotive was plunging forward at terrific speed.

The Sioux had at the same time invaded the cars, skipping like enraged monkeys over the roofs, breaking open the doors, and fighting hand to hand with the passengers. Forcing their way into the baggage-car, they plundered it, throwing the trunks off the train. The cries and shots never let up. The travellers defended themselves bravely; some of the cars were barricaded, and stood under siege, like moving forts hurtling along at a hundred miles an hour.

Aouda behaved courageously from the start. She defended herself like a true heroine with a revolver, which she fired through the broken windows whenever a savage came into view. Twenty Sioux had been hit and fallen mortally wounded to the ground, and the wheels crushed those who fell on the rails as if they had been worms. Several passengers, shot or stunned, lay across the seats.

An end had to be put to the struggle, which had now lasted ten minutes, and which would end in the Sioux’s triumph if the train was not stopped. Fort Kearney station, where there was a garrison, was only two miles off; but once past it, the Sioux would be masters of the train between Fort Kearney and the next station.
The conductor was fighting beside Mr. Fogg when he was shot and fell. At the same moment he cried, “Unless the train is stopped within five minutes, we are lost!”
“It shall be stopped,” said Phileas Fogg, getting ready to rush out of the car.
“Stay, monsieur,” cried Passepartout; “I will go.”

Mr. Fogg had no time to stop the brave fellow, who, opening a door without being seen by the Indians, managed to slip under the car; and while the struggle went on and the bullets whizzed back and forth above him, he drew on his old acrobatic experience, and with astonishing agility worked his way under the cars, clinging to the chains, helping himself along by the brakes and the edges of the frames, crawling from one car to another with remarkable skill, and so reaching the front of the train.

There, hanging by one hand between the baggage-car and the tender, with the other he loosened the safety chains; but, given the pull on the couplings, he would never have managed to unscrew the coupling bar had not a violent jolt knocked it loose. The train, now detached from the engine, fell back a little, while the locomotive rushed forward at greater speed than ever.
Carried on by the momentum already gained, the train still rolled for several minutes; but the brakes were applied, and at last it came to a stop, less than a hundred feet from Kearney station.
The soldiers of the fort, drawn by the gunfire, came running up; the Sioux had not expected them, and decamped in a body before the train had quite stopped.
But when the passengers took stock of each other on the station platform, several were found to be missing — among them the brave Frenchman whose devotion had just saved them.

chapters.title: Chapter 30. In which Phileas Fogg Simply Does His Duty
paragraphs: Three passengers, Passepartout among them, had vanished. Had they been killed in the fighting? Had the Sioux carried them off? There was no way to tell.

Many were wounded, though none fatally. Colonel Proctor was among the worst hurt. He had fought bravely, and a bullet had gone into his groin. He was carried into the station with the other wounded passengers so that they could be given whatever care might help.

Aouda was safe, and Phileas Fogg, who had been in the thick of the fight, had not a scratch. Fix had a slight wound in the arm. But Passepartout was nowhere to be found, and tears ran down Aouda’s cheeks.

All the passengers had climbed down from the train, whose wheels were stained with blood. Ragged scraps of flesh hung from the rims and spokes. Red trails stretched across the white plain behind them as far as the eye could see. The last of the Sioux were disappearing to the south, along the banks of the Republican River.

Mr. Fogg stood motionless with his arms folded. He had a grave decision to make. Aouda, standing close by, looked at him without speaking, and he understood her look. If his servant was a prisoner, should he not risk everything to rescue him from the Indians? “I will find him, living or dead,” he told Aouda quietly.
“Ah, Mr.—Mr. Fogg!” she cried, clasping his hands and covering them with tears.
“Living,” Mr. Fogg added, “if we do not lose a moment.”

By this decision Phileas Fogg was inevitably giving himself up. He was pronouncing his own doom. A delay of one single day would make him miss the steamer at New York, and his bet would be lost beyond doubt. But he thought, “It is my duty,” and he did not hesitate.
The commanding officer of Fort Kearney was there. A hundred of his soldiers had taken up positions to defend the station in case the Sioux attacked it.
“Sir,” Mr. Fogg said to the captain, “three passengers are missing.”
“Dead?” asked the captain.
“Dead or taken prisoner. That is the question that has to be settled. Do you intend to pursue the Sioux?”
“That is a serious matter, sir,” the captain answered. “These Indians may fall back beyond the Arkansas, and I cannot leave the fort unprotected.”
“Three men’s lives are at stake, sir,” said Phileas Fogg.
“No doubt, but can I risk the lives of fifty men to save three?”
“I do not know whether you can, sir, but you ought to.”
“No one here,” the other replied, “has the right to instruct me in my duty.”
“Very well,” said Mr. Fogg coldly. “I shall go alone.”
“You, sir!” cried Fix, stepping forward. “You’re going alone after the Indians?”
“Would you have me let this poor fellow die, the man to whom everyone here owes his life? I shall go.”
“No, sir, you shall not go alone,” cried the captain, moved in spite of himself. “No! You are a brave man. Thirty volunteers!” he added, turning to the soldiers.
The entire company stepped forward at once. The captain only had to choose. Thirty men were picked, and an old sergeant was put in charge of them.
“Thank you, captain,” said Mr. Fogg.
“Will you let me go with you?” asked Fix.
“Do as you like, sir. But if you want to do me a favour, you will stay with Aouda. In case anything should happen to me—”

The detective’s face suddenly went pale. Part company with the man he had so doggedly followed step by step! Let him wander off into this wilderness! Fix looked searchingly at Mr. Fogg. Despite his suspicions, and despite the struggle going on inside him, he dropped his eyes before that calm, honest gaze.
“I’ll stay,” he said.

A few moments later Mr. Fogg pressed the young woman’s hand and handed her his precious carpet-bag. Then he set off with the sergeant and his little squad. Before leaving, though, he had told the soldiers, “My friends, I will share five thousand dollars among you if we save the prisoners.”
It was a little after noon.

Aouda withdrew to a waiting room. There she waited alone, thinking about Phileas Fogg’s simple, noble generosity and his quiet courage. He had given up his fortune and was now risking his life, all without hesitation, out of duty, and without a word.

Fix was not thinking such thoughts, and he could hardly hide his agitation. He paced up and down the platform feverishly, but soon got his outward calm back. Now he saw what a blunder he had made in letting Fogg go alone. What! The man he had just followed around the world, and now he had let him slip away from him! He began to blame and abuse himself, and, as if he were the chief of police, he gave himself a thorough scolding for his greenness.

“I’ve been an idiot!” he thought. “And this man will realise it. He’s gone, and he won’t come back! But how is it that I, Fix, with a warrant for his arrest in my pocket, have been so taken in by him? Clearly I am nothing but an ass!”

So the detective reasoned while the hours dragged by far too slowly. He did not know what to do. At times he was tempted to tell Aouda everything, but he had no doubt how the young woman would take his confession. What course should he follow? He thought of chasing Fogg across the great white plains, and it did not seem impossible that he might catch up with him. Footprints show easily in snow! But soon, under a fresh blanket, every track would be wiped out.
Fix lost heart. He felt an overwhelming urge to give up the game altogether. He could leave Fort Kearney station now and continue his journey home in peace.

Around two in the afternoon, while it was snowing hard, long whistles were heard approaching from the east. A great shadow came slowly forward, led by a wild glare of light, and looked even bigger through the mist, which made it seem unreal. No train was expected from the east, and there had not been time for the help requested by telegraph to arrive. The train from Omaha to San Francisco was not due until the next day. The mystery was soon cleared up.

The locomotive creeping toward them with deafening whistles was the one that had been uncoupled from the train and had carried on with such frightening speed, taking the unconscious engineer and stoker with it. It had run for several miles before its fire burned low for lack of fuel and the steam died down. About an hour later it had finally stopped some twenty miles beyond Fort Kearney. Neither the engineer nor the stoker was dead. After lying in a swoon for some time they had come to, and the engine had stood still. When the engineer found himself in the wilderness with a locomotive and no carriages, he understood what had happened. He could not imagine how the locomotive had come loose from the train, but he had no doubt that the train left behind was in trouble.

He did not hesitate over what to do. The sensible thing would have been to go on to Omaha, since going back to the train would be dangerous, with the Indians possibly still busy plundering it. Even so, he began to rebuild the fire in the furnace. The pressure rose again, and the locomotive went back, running in reverse, to Fort Kearney. This was what was whistling in the mist.
The travellers were glad to see the locomotive take its place at the head of the train once more. Now they could continue the journey that had been so dreadfully interrupted.
When Aouda saw the locomotive coming up, she hurried out of the station and asked the conductor, “Are you leaving?”
“Right away, madam.”
“But the prisoners, our unfortunate fellow travellers—”
“I can’t hold up the trip,” the conductor replied. “We are already three hours late.”
“And when will another train come through from San Francisco?”
“Tomorrow evening, madam.”
“Tomorrow evening! But then it will be too late! We must wait—”
“It’s impossible,” the conductor answered. “If you want to come, please get in.”
“I will not go,” said Aouda.

Fix had overheard this conversation. A little earlier, when there was no hope of continuing the journey, he had made up his mind to leave Fort Kearney. But now the train stood there ready to depart, and all he had to do was take a seat in a carriage, yet an irresistible force held him back. The station platform seemed to burn his feet, and he could not move. The battle in his mind started up again. Anger and failure choked him. He wanted to fight on to the end.

Meanwhile the passengers and some of the wounded, among them Colonel Proctor, who was badly hurt, had taken their places on the train. The roar of the overheated boiler could be heard, and steam was escaping from the valves. The engineer blew the whistle, the train pulled out, and soon it vanished, its white smoke mingling with the swirls of thickly falling snow.
The detective had stayed behind.

Several hours went by. The weather was bleak and bitterly cold. Fix sat motionless on a bench in the station, and he might have been taken for someone asleep. Aouda, in spite of the storm, kept coming out of the waiting room and walking to the end of the platform. She peered into the blizzard as if she could pierce the mist that closed in the horizon around her, and she listened for some welcome sound. She heard and saw nothing. Then she would go back in, chilled to the bone, only to come out again a few minutes later, always in vain.

Evening came, and the little band had not returned. Where could they be? Had they found the Indians and were they fighting them, or were they still wandering in the mist? The commander of the fort was worried, though he tried to hide his fears. As night drew near the snow fell less thickly, but the cold became intense. Complete silence lay over the plains. Not a bird flew, and not a beast passed to disturb the perfect stillness.

All night long Aouda, filled with dark forebodings and a heart tight with anguish, wandered along the edge of the plains. Her imagination carried her far away and showed her countless dangers. What she suffered through those long hours cannot be described.
Fix stayed rooted to the same spot, but he did not sleep. Once a man came up and spoke to him, and the detective only answered by shaking his head.

So the night passed. At dawn the pale, half-dimmed disc of the sun rose over a misty horizon, but by now it was possible to make out objects two miles away. Phileas Fogg and the squad had gone south, and in the south there was still nothing but emptiness. It was then seven o’clock.
The captain, who was truly alarmed, did not know what to do.

Should he send another detachment to rescue the first? Should he sacrifice more men with so little chance of saving those already sacrificed? His hesitation did not last long, though. He called one of his lieutenants and was about to order a scouting party when gunshots rang out. Was it a signal? The soldiers rushed out of the fort, and half a mile away they saw a small band coming back in good order.
Mr. Fogg was marching at their head, and right behind him came Passepartout and the other two travellers, rescued from the Sioux.

They had met the Indians and fought them ten miles south of Fort Kearney. Shortly before the detachment arrived, Passepartout and his companions had begun struggling with their captors, and the Frenchman had knocked down three of them with his fists, when his master and the soldiers hurried up to help.

Everyone was welcomed with joyful cries. Phileas Fogg handed out the reward he had promised the soldiers, while Passepartout, with good reason, muttered to himself, “I must admit that I cost my master dearly!”

Fix said nothing. He looked at Mr. Fogg, and it would have been hard to work out the thoughts that were battling inside him. As for Aouda, she took her protector’s hand and held it in hers, too moved to speak.
Meanwhile Passepartout was looking around for the train. He expected to find it there, ready to leave for Omaha, and he hoped that the lost time could be made up.
“The train! The train!” he cried.
“Gone,” said Fix.
“And when does the next train come through here?” asked Phileas Fogg.
“Not until this evening.”
“Ah!” answered the imperturbable gentleman quietly.

chapters.title: Chapter 31. In which Fix, the Detective, Considerably Furthers the Interests of Phileas Fogg
paragraphs: Phileas Fogg was now twenty hours late. Passepartout, who had unintentionally caused the delay, was frantic with despair. He had ruined his master!
Just then the detective came up to Mr. Fogg and, studying his face closely, said:
“Tell me seriously, sir: are you in a great hurry?”
“Entirely seriously.”
“There is a reason for my question,” Fix continued. “Must you absolutely reach New York on the 11th before nine in the evening, when the Liverpool steamer is due to sail?”
“It is absolutely essential.”
“And without this interruption by the Indians, you would have arrived in New York on the morning of the 11th?”
“Yes, with eleven hours remaining before the steamer’s departure.”
“Good! That puts you twenty hours behind. Subtract twelve from twenty, and eight remain. Eight hours must be made up. Would you like to attempt it?”
“By walking?” Mr. Fogg asked.
“No, by sledge,” Fix answered. “A sailing sledge. Someone has offered to take us that way.”
It was the same man who had approached Fix during the night, when the detective had declined his proposal.

Phileas Fogg paused before answering. Fix pointed out the man pacing in front of the station, and Fogg walked over to him. A moment later he and the American, whose name was Mudge, entered a hut just below the fort.

Inside, Mr. Fogg inspected an unusual vehicle. It consisted of a frame resting on two long beams that curved slightly upward in front like sledge runners. Five or six people could sit on it. A tall mast, secured to the frame by metal stays, carried a large brigantine sail. An iron stay supported a jib, and at the rear a kind of rudder controlled the direction. In effect, it was a sledge fitted out like a sloop. When winter snow blocks the trains, such vehicles race over the frozen plains between stations. With more sail than a cutter and a following wind, they skim across the prairies at speeds that match, or even exceed, those of express trains.

Mr. Fogg quickly struck a bargain with the owner of this land-going craft. A fresh wind blew favourably from the west, the snow had frozen hard, and Mudge was confident he could reach Omaha in a few hours. From there, eastbound trains ran frequently to Chicago and New York. They might still recover the lost time; an opportunity like this was not to be passed over.

Wishing to spare Aouda the discomfort of travelling exposed to the weather, Mr. Fogg suggested leaving her at Fort Kearney with Passepartout. The servant would undertake to escort her to Europe by an easier route and in better conditions. But Aouda would not part from Mr. Fogg. Her decision delighted Passepartout: nothing could persuade him to leave his master alone with Fix.

The detective’s thoughts were hard to guess. Had Phileas Fogg’s return shaken his certainty, or did he still see him as an exceptionally cunning villain who expected to be perfectly safe in England after circling the globe? Perhaps his opinion had softened somewhat. He nevertheless remained determined to do his duty and get the whole party back to England as quickly as possible.

By eight the sledge was ready. The passengers climbed aboard and wrapped their travelling cloaks tightly around themselves. Up went the two great sails, and the wind drove the sledge over the hard snow at forty miles an hour.

In a straight line, Fort Kearney lies no more than two hundred miles from Omaha. With a steady wind they could cover that distance in five hours. Provided nothing went wrong, they might be there by one o’clock.

What a ride! Huddled together, the travellers were too cold to speak, and their speed made the cold sharper still. The sledge skimmed along as lightly as a boat across waves. When the wind swept low across the ground, the sails seemed almost to lift it clear of the earth. At the rudder, Mudge held a straight course, correcting the craft’s tendency to lurch with a turn of his hand. Every sail was set, the jib positioned so it would not block the wind from the brigantine. A topmast was raised, and a second jib caught the breeze, adding its pull to the rest. Their speed could not be measured precisely, but they were certainly making at least forty miles an hour.
“Provided nothing gives way,” Mudge said, “we shall make it!”
Mr. Fogg had given Mudge a personal interest in arriving at Omaha within the promised time by offering him a generous bonus.

They crossed the prairie in a straight line. Flat as the sea, it resembled an immense frozen lake. The railway through this region curved from southwest to northwest, passing Great Island, Columbus—an important Nebraska town—Schuyler, and Fremont on its way to Omaha. Throughout, it followed the Platte River’s right bank. The sledge cut across this curve, taking the chord of the arc described by the tracks. Mudge had no fear of being stopped by the Platte: it was frozen over. Their route therefore presented no obstacles. Phileas Fogg had only two things to worry about: damage to the sledge, or a change in the wind—or its dying away altogether.

Instead of weakening, the wind blew hard enough to threaten to bend the mast. The metal stays held it firm, vibrating like the strings of an instrument beneath a violin bow. An intense, mournful music accompanied the sledge as it glided on.
“The notes of those strings form a fifth and an octave,” Mr. Fogg remarked.

He said nothing else throughout the journey. Aouda, snugly wrapped in furs and cloaks, was protected as well as possible from the freezing wind. Passepartout’s face glowed red as the sun setting through mist, and every breath of the biting air cost him an effort. Yet his naturally buoyant spirits were reviving. If they could not reach New York on the morning of the 11th, they would arrive that evening; there was still a chance of beating the Liverpool steamer’s departure.

Passepartout even felt a strong impulse to shake hands with his ally Fix. After all, the detective had found the sledge, their only hope of reaching Omaha in time. Some instinct held him back, however, and he maintained his usual reserve. One thing he would never forget was his master’s unhesitating sacrifice to rescue him from the Sioux. Mr. Fogg had put both his life and his fortune at risk. No! His servant could never forget such a deed!

While these very different thoughts occupied the travellers, the sledge flew over the vast white carpet. They did not even notice the creeks beneath them; fields and watercourses alike had vanished under the snow. The plain was utterly deserted, a great uninhabited island between the Union Pacific line and the branch connecting Kearney with Saint Joseph. Not a village, station, or fort came into sight. Occasionally they swept past a ghostly tree, its white skeleton rattling and twisting in the wind. Sometimes wild birds rose in flocks, or lean, starving, savage prairie-wolves chased them, howling. Passepartout held his revolver ready to shoot any that approached too closely. Had the sledge broken down then, the beasts would have put them in dreadful danger. But it maintained its steady course, soon outpaced the wolves, and left the howling pack safely behind.

Around noon, landmarks told Mudge that they were crossing the Platte River. He kept this to himself, but knew Omaha was now less than twenty miles away. Within an hour he left the rudder and furled the sails. Driven by the momentum the wind had given it, the sledge still travelled another half-mile with no sail spread.
Finally it stopped. Pointing to a cluster of snow-covered roofs, Mudge announced, “Here we are!”
They had arrived! Reached the station with its numerous daily trains connecting them to the Atlantic coast!

Passepartout and Fix sprang down, stretched their stiff limbs, and helped Mr. Fogg and Aouda off the sledge. Phileas Fogg paid Mudge a handsome reward, and Passepartout shook his hand warmly. They then made for Omaha station.
This important Nebraska town marks the end of the Pacific Railroad proper. From Omaha, the Chicago and Rock Island Railroad runs due east through fifty stations to connect with Chicago.

A train was on the point of departure when the party arrived. They had barely time to climb aboard. Omaha itself remained unseen, but Passepartout admitted there was little reason for regret: sightseeing was not the object of this journey.

The train sped across Iowa through Council Bluffs, Des Moines, and Iowa City. During the night it crossed the Mississippi at Davenport, entering Illinois by way of Rock Island. At four the next afternoon, the 10th, they reached Chicago. Already risen from its ruins, it stood prouder than ever beside beautiful Lake Michigan.

New York was still nine hundred miles from Chicago, but Chicago had no shortage of trains. Mr. Fogg transferred immediately, and the locomotive of the Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne, and Chicago Railway raced away as though it understood that he had not a moment to spare. Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey flashed past. They rushed through towns bearing ancient names, some already supplied with streets and tracks but as yet without houses. At last the Hudson appeared. At a quarter past eleven on the evening of the 11th, the train pulled into the station on the river’s right bank, directly opposite the Cunard pier.
The “China,” bound for Liverpool, had sailed forty-five minutes earlier!

chapters.title: Chapter 32. In which Phileas Fogg Engages in a Direct Struggle with Bad Fortune
paragraphs: With the “China” gone, Phileas Fogg’s last hope seemed to have sailed away as well. None of the remaining steamers suited his plans. The French Transatlantic Company’s “Pereire” did not depart until the 14th, though that company’s excellent ships could rival any for comfort and speed. The Hamburg vessels sailed to Havre rather than directly to Liverpool or London; the extra journey from Havre to Southampton would defeat his final efforts. The Inman steamer left the next day and could not cross the Atlantic soon enough to save the bet.
His “Bradshaw,” listing each day’s transatlantic sailings, supplied Mr. Fogg with all this discouraging information.

Passepartout was devastated. Missing the ship by just forty-five minutes overwhelmed him. It was his own fault: instead of assisting his master, he had continually placed difficulties in his way! He reviewed every mishap of the journey, added up the money wasted or spent on his account, and thought of the huge stake which, together with the cost of this fruitless expedition, would leave Mr. Fogg utterly ruined. Bitter accusations against himself filled his mind. His master, however, offered no reproach. Leaving the Cunard pier, he merely said, “Tomorrow we shall consider the best course. Come along.”

They crossed the Hudson on the Jersey City ferry and took a carriage to the St. Nicholas Hotel in Broadway. Rooms were booked. For Phileas Fogg, sleeping soundly, the night passed quickly; for Aouda and the others, too troubled to rest, it seemed interminable.

The following day was December 12th. Between seven that morning and a quarter to nine on the evening of the 21st, nine days, thirteen hours, and forty-five minutes remained. Had Phileas Fogg caught the “China,” one of the Atlantic’s fastest steamers, he could have reached Liverpool and then London within the agreed limit.

Mr. Fogg went out alone, instructing Passepartout to wait for him and to tell Aouda to be ready to leave at a moment’s notice. At the Hudson waterfront he searched among the ships moored or anchored in the river for any preparing to sail. Several displayed departure signals and were getting under way with the morning tide. In this vast, splendid port, scarcely one day in a hundred passes without ships leaving for every part of the globe. Most, however, were sailing ships and therefore useless to Phileas Fogg.

He appeared almost ready to abandon hope when he spotted a well-shaped screw-driven merchant vessel anchored off the Battery, no more than a cable’s length away. Smoke billowing from her funnel showed that she was preparing to depart.

Phileas Fogg hailed a boat and was soon aboard the “Henrietta,” an iron-hulled ship with wooden upper works. On deck he asked for the captain, who promptly appeared: a fifty-year-old sea-wolf with large eyes, red hair, a thick neck, a growling voice, and a complexion like oxidised copper.
“Are you the captain?” Mr. Fogg asked.
“Yes, I am her captain.”
“My name is Phileas Fogg, from London.”
“And mine is Andrew Speedy, from Cardiff.”
“Are you about to put to sea?”
“In one hour.”
“Your destination is—”
“Bordeaux.”
“What cargo are you carrying?”
“None. We sail with ballast only.”
“Are any passengers travelling with you?”
“No passengers. I never take them. They get in the way.”
“Does your ship make good speed?”
“Eleven to twelve knots. The ‘Henrietta’ is well known.”
“Would you take me and three companions to Liverpool?”
“Liverpool? Why not ask for China?”
“Liverpool is what I said.”
“No!”
“No?”
“No. I am sailing for Bordeaux, and Bordeaux is where I shall go.”
“Would money make any difference?”
“None.”
The captain’s tone left no room for any further argument on that point.
“But the ‘Henrietta’s’ owners—” Phileas Fogg began again.
“I am her owner,” the captain replied. “This vessel is my property.”
“I will pay to charter her.”
“No.”
“I will purchase the ship from you.”
“No.”

Not the slightest disappointment appeared on Phileas Fogg’s face, but the difficulty was serious. New York was not Hong Kong, and the “Henrietta’s” captain was a different proposition from the captain of the “Tankadere.” Until now money had removed every obstacle. At last it was powerless.

Some way of crossing the Atlantic by ship still had to be found, unless they resorted to a balloon—an adventurous idea, and impracticable besides. Phileas Fogg seemed to have thought of something. “Very well,” he said to the captain. “Will you take me to Bordeaux?”
“No, not even if you offered two hundred dollars.”
“I am offering two thousand dollars.”
“For each?”
“For each.”
“There are four in your party?”
“Four.”

Captain Speedy scratched his head. Eight thousand dollars without altering course: that was surely worth overcoming his dislike of passengers of every description. Besides, at two thousand dollars a head they ceased to be passengers and became valuable cargo. “I sail at nine,” he said simply. “Can your whole party be ready?”
“We shall all be aboard at nine,” Mr. Fogg replied with equal simplicity.

It was half past eight. With his unfailing composure, Mr. Fogg left the “Henrietta,” jumped into a cab, hurried to the St. Nicholas, and came back with Aouda, Passepartout, and even the inseparable Fix, all in very little time. They were aboard as the “Henrietta” prepared to lift her anchor.
Learning what this final passage would cost, Passepartout let out a long “Oh!” that ran through his entire vocal range.

Fix privately concluded that the Bank of England would recover very little from this affair. By the time they reached England, more than seven thousand pounds would have gone—even if Mr. Fogg refrained from scattering handfuls of banknotes into the sea!

chapters.title: Chapter 33. In which Phileas Fogg Shows Himself Equal to the Occasion
paragraphs: An hour later, the “Henrietta” passed the lighthouse at the Hudson’s mouth, rounded Sandy Hook, and headed out to sea. Through the day she followed Long Island’s coast, passed Fire Island, and sped eastward.

At noon the following day, a man climbed to the bridge to establish the ship’s position. Captain Speedy, one might suppose? Nothing of the kind. It was Phileas Fogg, Esquire. Captain Speedy, meanwhile, was locked in his cabin, shouting at the top of his voice in a rage both understandable and excessive.

The explanation was simple. Phileas Fogg wanted Liverpool, and the captain refused to take him there. He therefore booked passage to Bordeaux. During his thirty hours aboard, he used his banknotes so skilfully that the sailors and stokers, a crew hired for the occasion and on poor terms with their captain, came over to his side to a man. That was why Phileas Fogg now commanded the ship, why Captain Speedy was confined to his cabin, and why the “Henrietta” was sailing for Liverpool. Watching Mr. Fogg handle her, one could hardly doubt that he had been a sailor.

We shall soon see how the affair ended. Aouda was worried but kept silent. Passepartout found his master’s manoeuvre magnificent. The captain had promised “between eleven and twelve knots,” and the “Henrietta” was living up to his words.

If, then—and there were still several ifs—the sea stayed reasonably calm, the wind did not swing east, and neither vessel nor machinery suffered an accident, the “Henrietta” could cover the three thousand miles between New York and Liverpool in the nine days from December 12th to December 21st. Admittedly, once they arrived, this business aboard the ship, added to the Bank of England affair, might cause Mr. Fogg more trouble than he anticipated or wanted.

The first days passed well enough. The sea was fairly favourable, the wind held steadily in the northeast, and with sails raised the “Henrietta” drove through the water like a proper transatlantic liner.

Passepartout was ecstatic. His master’s latest feat thrilled him; he gave no thought to its consequences. The crew had never encountered anyone so cheerful or so handy. He made close friends among the sailors and astonished them with his acrobatics. To him they handled the ship like gentlemen, while the stokers tended the furnaces like heroes. His talkative good spirits spread through the whole company. Past annoyances and delays were forgotten. He thought only of the goal, now so close, and sometimes his impatience boiled over as though fired by the “Henrietta’s” furnaces. Often, too, he circled round Fix and watched him with sharp suspicion. But he said nothing to the detective: their former friendship was over.

Fix, it must be admitted, could make no sense of events. Seizing the “Henrietta,” buying off the crew, handling the ship like an experienced seaman—all these things bewildered and astonished him. What was he to think? A man who began by stealing fifty-five thousand pounds might well finish by stealing a ship. It was natural enough for Fix to suspect that, under Fogg’s command, the “Henrietta” was heading not for Liverpool but for some safe refuge where the thief, now turned pirate, could quietly disappear. This was at least a plausible theory, and the detective began seriously to regret ever having embarked on the business.

Captain Speedy continued howling and growling in his cabin. Passepartout had to bring him his meals and, brave though he was, approached the task with extreme caution. Mr. Fogg seemed scarcely aware that a captain was aboard at all.

On the 13th they skirted the Banks of Newfoundland, a dangerous region known for frequent fogs and fierce gales, especially in winter. The previous evening the barometer had suddenly dropped, warning of a change in the weather. Overnight the temperature shifted, the cold deepened, and the wind turned southeast.

This was an unfortunate turn of events. To avoid being driven off course, Mr. Fogg furled the sails and increased steam power. Even so, the sea slowed the vessel: long waves struck her stern, and violent pitching hampered her progress. The wind gradually rose into a tempest, and there was reason to fear that the “Henrietta” might be unable to stay upright among the waves.

Passepartout’s face grew as gloomy as the sky, and for two days he lived in constant fear. But Phileas Fogg was a courageous seaman who knew how to make headway in rough water. He kept his course without even reducing steam. When the “Henrietta” could not climb a wave, she drove through it, her deck flooded but her passage safe. Sometimes a mountain of water lifted the stern so high that the screw emerged and thrashed in the air. Still the ship went straight on.

The wind, however, never became as violent as they had feared. This was no storm hurtling along at ninety miles an hour. It remained strong, but the real misfortune was its stubborn southeast direction, which left the sails useless.

December 16th marked seventy-five days since Phileas Fogg’s departure from London, and the “Henrietta” had suffered no serious delay. Nearly half the crossing was complete, and they had left the most dangerous waters behind. In summer their success would have been almost certain; in winter they remained at the mercy of the season. Passepartout said nothing, but secretly kept hoping. If the wind would not serve them, he reassured himself, there was always steam.

That day the engineer came up on deck and entered into an earnest conversation with Mr. Fogg. For no reason he could explain—perhaps a premonition—Passepartout felt uneasy. He would have sacrificed one ear to hear with the other what was being said. At last he caught a few words and distinctly heard his master ask, “Are you quite certain of this?”

“Quite certain, sir,” the engineer answered. “Remember, we have been firing every furnace hard from the start. We carried enough coal to steam at low power from New York to Bordeaux, but not enough to steam at full power from New York to Liverpool.” “I shall consider the matter,” said Mr. Fogg.

Passepartout understood immediately and was seized with terrible anxiety. They were running out of coal! “Ah, if my master can solve this one,” he muttered, “he will be a famous man!” He could not resist telling Fix what he had heard.
“So you actually believe we are heading for Liverpool?”
“Of course.”
“Idiot!” the detective replied, shrugging and turning away from him.

Passepartout nearly answered this insult with force; he could not imagine why Fix had called him such a thing. Then he reflected that the unfortunate detective must feel bitterly disappointed and wounded in his pride after so clumsily pursuing a false lead round the world. He restrained himself.

What would Phileas Fogg do now? It was hard to guess. Yet he seemed to have settled on a plan, for that evening he called the engineer and instructed him, “Keep every furnace fed until the coal is gone.”

Soon torrents of smoke poured from the “Henrietta’s” funnel. She continued at full steam, but on the 18th, exactly as he had warned, the engineer reported that the remaining coal would be exhausted before the day ended.
“Do not allow the fires to sink,” Mr. Fogg replied. “Keep them burning to the very end. Let the valves be filled.”

Near noon, after checking their position, Phileas Fogg summoned Passepartout and told him to fetch Captain Speedy. The good fellow might as well have been ordered to release a tiger. Heading towards the poop, he told himself, “He will be absolutely wild!”

A few moments later a bomb came onto the poop-deck, swearing and shouting.
