The bomb was Captain Speedy, and it clearly threatened to explode. “Where are we?” was the first coherent question his fury allowed him. Had he been prone to apoplexy, the poor man could never have survived such a fit of rage.
“Where have we got to?” he demanded again, purple in the face.
“Seven hundred and seven miles short of Liverpool,” Mr. Fogg answered, utterly composed.
“You pirate!” Captain Speedy shouted.
“Sir, I asked to see you—”
“Pickaroon!”
“—sir,” Mr. Fogg continued, “because I wish to buy your ship.”
“No! By every devil, no!”
“But I shall have to burn her.”
“Set fire to the ‘Henrietta’!”
“Yes, her upper works at least. We have used the last of the coal.”
“Burn my ship!” Captain Speedy cried, barely able to get the words out. “A ship worth fifty thousand dollars!”

“I offer sixty thousand,” Phileas Fogg replied, holding out a roll of banknotes. Andrew Speedy was transformed. Sixty thousand dollars is a sight few Americans can contemplate without emotion. In an instant the captain forgot his fury, his confinement, and every grievance against his passenger. The “Henrietta” was twenty years old; this was an excellent bargain. The bomb, after all, would not explode. Mr. Fogg had removed the match.
“I keep the iron hull, though,” the captain said, his voice softening.
“The iron hull and her engine. Do we have an agreement?”
“Agreed.”
Andrew Speedy seized the notes, counted them carefully, and put the money into his pocket.

Throughout this exchange Passepartout was white as a sheet, while Fix looked ready to suffer an apoplectic fit. Almost twenty thousand pounds had now been spent, and Fogg was leaving the hull and engine—nearly the ship’s entire value—with the captain! Still, fifty-five thousand pounds had been stolen from the Bank.

Once Andrew Speedy had pocketed the cash, Mr. Fogg explained, “There is no need for surprise, sir. Unless I reach London by a quarter to nine on the evening of December 21st, I lose twenty thousand pounds. I missed my steamer in New York, and since you refused to carry me to Liverpool—”
“A wise refusal!” Andrew Speedy cried. “It has earned me at least forty thousand dollars!” Then, more calmly, he added, “I’ll tell you something, Captain—”
“Fogg.”
“There is a touch of the Yankee in you, Captain Fogg.”
Having offered what he considered a tremendous compliment, he turned to go. Mr. Fogg stopped him. “The vessel is mine now?”
“Certainly, from the keel to the mastheads. All the wooden parts, that is.”
“Very good. Pull out the interior seats, bunks, and frames, and use them as fuel.”

Dry timber was needed to maintain sufficient steam pressure. That day they sacrificed the poop, cabins, bunks, and spare deck. On December 19th, the following day, the masts, rafts, and spars fed the flames. The crew worked energetically to keep the furnaces burning. Passepartout hacked, chopped, and sawed with all his strength. A frenzy of destruction took hold of everyone.

On the 20th the railings, fittings, most of the deck, and the upper sides vanished, leaving the “Henrietta” a flat hulk. But that day also brought the Irish coast and Fastnet Light into view. By ten that evening they were off Queenstown. Only twenty-four hours remained for Phileas Fogg to reach London, yet even at full steam it would take all that time merely to reach Liverpool. And their steam was on the point of failing altogether!
“Sir,” Captain Speedy said, now deeply concerned for Mr. Fogg’s enterprise, “I am truly sorry for you. Everything is going against you. We have only reached the waters off Queenstown.”
“Ah,” said Mr. Fogg. “Those lights we can see belong to Queenstown?”
“Yes.”
“Could we go into the harbour?”
“Not for three hours. We need high tide.”
“Wait,” Mr. Fogg replied calmly. His face gave no hint that a final inspiration had suggested one more attempt to overcome his bad luck.

Queenstown is the Irish port where transatlantic steamers put the mail ashore. Express trains, kept ready to leave, carry it to Dublin; from Dublin the fastest boats take it on to Liverpool. This route brings the mail in twelve hours ahead of the Atlantic steamers.

Phileas Fogg intended to gain those same twelve hours. Rather than reach Liverpool aboard the “Henrietta” the following evening, he would be there at noon. That would leave him time to get to London before a quarter to nine that night.

At one in the morning, with the tide high, the “Henrietta” entered Queenstown Harbour. Captain Speedy gave Phileas Fogg a vigorous handshake. Fogg then left him on the stripped hulk, which was still worth half the sum he had received for it.

The travellers went ashore immediately. Fix felt a powerful temptation to arrest Mr. Fogg there and then, but held back. Why? What conflict was taking place inside him? Had he revised his judgment of “his man”? Did he realise he had made a serious mistake? Whatever the reason, he did not leave Fogg’s side. At half past one they all boarded a train just ready to depart. Dawn found them in Dublin, where they promptly embarked on a steamer that seemed to disdain climbing the waves and always cut straight through them instead.
At twenty minutes to twelve on December 21st, Phileas Fogg finally stepped onto the Liverpool quay. London was only six hours away.
At that very moment Fix approached, laid a hand on his shoulder, and produced his warrant. “You are indeed Phileas Fogg?” he asked.
“I am.”
“In the Queen’s name, I place you under arrest!”

chapters.title: Chapter 34. In which Phileas Fogg at Last Reaches London
paragraphs: Phileas Fogg was a prisoner. Locked inside the Custom House, he was to be sent to London the following day.

At the sight of his master’s arrest, Passepartout would have attacked Fix if several policemen had not restrained him. Aouda was stunned by this sudden, incomprehensible turn of events. Passepartout explained why the brave and honourable Fogg had been taken for a thief. She recoiled at so monstrous an accusation. When she realised there was nothing she could do to save her protector, she broke into bitter tears.
Fix, for his part, had made the arrest because duty required it, whether or not Mr. Fogg was guilty.

Then Passepartout realised that he himself had caused this fresh disaster! Had he not kept Fix’s purpose secret from his master? Why had he said nothing after the detective revealed his identity and mission? Forewarned, Mr. Fogg could surely have proved his innocence and convinced Fix of his error. At the very least, the detective would not have travelled at his master’s expense and on his heels, only to arrest him the instant he reached English soil. Passepartout wept until he could no longer see and felt like putting a bullet through his head.
Despite the cold, he and Aouda waited beneath the Custom House portico. Neither could bring themselves to leave; both longed to see Mr. Fogg again.

He truly was ruined, just as success had seemed within reach. This arrest was fatal. He had arrived in Liverpool at twenty minutes to twelve on December 21st and had until a quarter to nine that evening to reach the Reform Club—nine and a quarter hours. The Liverpool-to-London journey took six.

Anyone entering the Custom House then would have seen Mr. Fogg sitting perfectly still on a wooden bench, calm and apparently free from anger. He had not resigned himself to defeat, but even this final blow drew no outward sign of feeling from him. Was he consumed by one of those hidden rages, made more terrible by restraint, which burst out with irresistible violence at the last moment? No one could say. He sat quietly waiting—but for what? Did he still have hope? With the prison door shut upon him, could he still believe he would succeed?

Whatever his thoughts, Mr. Fogg carefully placed his watch on the table and followed the moving hands. He spoke not a word, though his expression was unusually rigid and stern. In either case his position was dreadful. It came to this: if Phileas Fogg was honest, he was ruined; if dishonest, he was caught.

Did he consider escape? Did he look for some way out of his confinement, some opening he could use? Perhaps: once he got up and walked slowly round the room. But the door was locked and thick iron bars guarded the window. He sat again and took his journal from his pocket. Beside “21st December, Saturday, Liverpool,” he wrote “80th day, 11.40 a.m.” Then he waited.
The Custom House clock sounded one. Mr. Fogg noticed that his own watch was running two hours fast.
Two hours! If he could board an express at that moment, he could still reach London and the Reform Club by a quarter to nine that evening. A faint crease crossed his forehead.
At thirty-three minutes past two he heard an unusual commotion outside, followed by doors opening hurriedly. Passepartout’s voice reached him, then Fix’s. For an instant Phileas Fogg’s eyes lit up.
The door opened wide. Passepartout, Aouda, and Fix came into view and hurried towards him.
Fix was breathless, his hair dishevelled, scarcely able to speak. “Sir,” he stammered, “sir—please forgive me—a most unfortunate resemblance—the thief arrested three days ago—you are free!”

Phileas Fogg was free! He stepped up to the detective and looked straight into his face. Then, in the only swift movement he had ever made or would ever make, he drew back his arms and, with mechanical precision, knocked Fix to the floor.
“A fine hit!” Passepartout cried. “Parbleu! Now that is what I call putting English fists to good use!”

Fix lay on the floor without a word. He had received no more than he deserved. Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Passepartout immediately left the Custom House, climbed into a cab, and within minutes arrived at the railway station.
Phileas Fogg asked whether an express for London was about to depart. It was now twenty minutes to three. The express had left thirty-five minutes earlier. He therefore ordered a special train.
Several fast locomotives were available, but railway arrangements meant that the special could not depart before three o’clock.
At three, having promised the driver a generous reward, Phileas Fogg finally started for London, accompanied by Aouda and his loyal servant.

They had to complete the journey in five and a half hours. With a clear line throughout, that would have been easy, but unavoidable delays intervened. As Mr. Fogg stepped onto the platform at the terminus, every clock in London was striking ten minutes to nine.[1]
After travelling right round the world, he was five minutes late. The wager was lost!
[1] A rather extraordinary peculiarity on the part of London’s clocks!—TRANSLATOR.

chapters.title: Chapter 35. In which Phileas Fogg Does Not Have to Repeat His Orders to Passepartout Twice
paragraphs: The next morning, Saville Row’s residents would have been surprised to learn that Phileas Fogg was home. Doors and windows remained shut; from outside, nothing appeared to have changed.
On leaving the station, Mr. Fogg told Passepartout to buy provisions and quietly made his way back to the house.

He endured the catastrophe with his customary composure. Ruined! And through a detective’s blunder! After steadily completing that immense journey, overcoming a hundred obstacles, facing so many dangers, and still finding time to do good along the way, he had failed within reach of success through a sudden event he could neither foresee nor resist. It was terrible! Of the great sum carried with him, only a few pounds remained. His fortune now consisted solely of the twenty thousand pounds deposited at Barings, and that money belonged to his Reform Club friends. The trip had cost so much that even victory would hardly have made him richer. Probably riches had never been his aim: he was a man who wagered for honour rather than profit. But this particular wager had left him penniless.
Nevertheless, Mr. Fogg had settled on his next course. He knew exactly what remained to be done.
Aouda was given a room in the Saville Row house. Her protector’s misfortune filled her with grief, and a few remarks he made suggested that some serious purpose occupied his thoughts.
Passepartout knew that Englishmen in the grip of a fixed idea sometimes took the desperate course of suicide. He therefore watched his master closely, taking care to hide that he was doing so.

The good fellow’s first act had been to go upstairs and extinguish the gas in his room, still burning after eighty days. A bill from the gas company awaited him in the letter-box. He considered it high time to end this expense that he was condemned to pay.
The night went by. Mr. Fogg went to bed, but did he sleep? Aouda never closed her eyes. Like a faithful dog, Passepartout kept watch outside his master’s door until morning.

In the morning Mr. Fogg called him and ordered breakfast for Aouda, and tea with a chop for himself. He asked her to excuse his absence from both breakfast and dinner: he would be occupied all day arranging his affairs. That evening, he would request a few minutes of conversation with her.

Orders received, Passepartout could only obey. Yet he looked at his impassive master and could hardly bring himself to leave. His heart was heavy, his conscience tortured by remorse. More bitterly than ever, he blamed himself for this irreparable disaster. Yes! Had he warned Mr. Fogg and exposed Fix’s intentions, his master would certainly not have paid the detective’s passage to Liverpool; and then—
At last Passepartout could restrain himself no longer.
“Master! Mr. Fogg!” he cried. “Why don’t you curse me? It was my fault that—”
“I hold no one responsible,” Phileas Fogg answered with complete calm. “Go!”
Passepartout went out and found Aouda, to whom he passed on his master’s message.
“Madam,” he added, “I can do nothing—nothing at all! I cannot influence my master. But perhaps you might—”

“How could I influence him?” Aouda answered. “No one has any influence over Mr. Fogg. Has he ever realised how deeply grateful I am? Has he ever understood my heart? My friend, we must not leave him alone for a moment! You say he intends to speak to me this evening?”
“Yes, madam, probably about making arrangements for your safety and comfort here in England.”
“We shall see,” said Aouda, suddenly lost in thought.
All that Sunday the Saville Row house seemed deserted. For the first time since taking up residence there, Phileas Fogg did not leave for his club when the Westminster clock struck half past eleven.

Why visit the Reform? His friends were no longer expecting him. Since he had failed to enter the saloon by a quarter to nine the previous evening—Saturday, December 21st—he had lost. He did not even need to collect the twenty thousand pounds from his bankers. His opponents already held his cheque; they had only to complete it and send it to Barings, and the money would be transferred to their accounts.

With no reason to go out, Mr. Fogg stayed at home. He shut himself in his room to put his affairs in order. Passepartout went endlessly up and down the stairs, finding the hours unbearably long. He listened at the door and peered through the keyhole as if entitled to do so, fearing some dreadful event at any instant. Occasionally he thought of Fix, but without anger now. Like everyone else, Fix had misjudged Phileas Fogg; in pursuing and arresting him he had merely done his duty. Whereas he, Passepartout . . . The thought pursued him, and he continually cursed his own miserable stupidity.
Too unhappy to remain by himself, he knocked at Aouda’s door and entered. Without speaking, he sat in a corner and gazed sorrowfully at her. She was still absorbed in thought.
At about half past seven that evening, Mr. Fogg sent to ask whether Aouda would see him. A few moments later they were alone together.
Phileas Fogg drew up a chair by the fireplace and sat opposite her. His face betrayed no feeling. The returned Fogg was exactly the Fogg who had left: the same composure, the same unruffled reserve.
For several minutes he sat without speaking. Then he looked at Aouda. “Madam,” he said, “can you forgive me for bringing you to England?”
“Forgive you, Mr. Fogg!” Aouda answered, trying to steady her beating heart.

“Please hear me out,” Mr. Fogg continued. “When I chose to take you far from the country where you faced such danger, I was wealthy. I intended to set aside part of my fortune for you, so that your life could be happy and free. Now I am ruined.”
“I know, Mr. Fogg,” Aouda replied. “And I must ask your forgiveness in return: for coming with you and—who can say?—perhaps delaying you, and so helping to bring about your ruin.”
“Madam, you could not stay in India. Your safety required us to take you so far away that the people pursuing you could never reach you.”
“Then, Mr. Fogg,” Aouda said, “saving me from a dreadful death was not enough. You also felt obliged to provide for my comfort in another country?”
“Yes, madam. Circumstances have defeated me, but I still ask you to accept the little that remains at my disposal.”
“And what is to become of you, Mr. Fogg?”
“For myself, madam,” the gentleman answered coldly, “there is nothing I require.”
“But how do you regard the future that lies before you, sir?”
“In precisely the way I always have.”
“At least,” Aouda said, “a man like you should never be left in poverty. Your friends—”
“Madam, I have no friends.”
“Your family—”
“I no longer have any family.”

“Then I feel for you, Mr. Fogg. Loneliness is a sad condition, with no loving heart to hear your troubles. Yet they say that even suffering can be patiently endured when two sympathetic souls share it.”
“So people say, madam.”
“Mr. Fogg,” Aouda said, standing and taking his hand, “would you like both family and a friend? Will you take me as your wife?”

Mr. Fogg rose as well. An unfamiliar light shone in his eyes, and his lips trembled slightly. Aouda looked into his face. The honesty, uprightness, resolve, and tenderness in that gentle gaze—the gaze of a noble woman ready to risk everything to save the man to whom she owed everything—first startled him, then reached his heart. For a moment he closed his eyes as though to escape her look. Opening them again, he said simply, “I love you! Yes, by everything sacred, I love you, and I am wholly yours!”
“Ah!” Aouda exclaimed, drawing his hand against her heart.
They called Passepartout, who appeared at once. Mr. Fogg still held Aouda’s hand. The servant understood immediately, and his broad, round face shone like the tropical sun at midday.
Mr. Fogg asked whether it was too late that evening to send word to the Reverend Samuel Wilson of Marylebone parish.
With his warmest smile, Passepartout replied, “It is never too late.”
The time was five minutes past eight.
“Shall I arrange it for tomorrow, Monday?”
“For tomorrow, Monday,” Mr. Fogg said, looking towards Aouda.
“Yes, tomorrow, Monday,” she answered him.
Passepartout rushed away as quickly as his legs would take him.

chapters.title: Chapter 36. In which Phileas Fogg’s Name is Once More at a Premium on ’change
paragraphs: We must now describe the shift in English public opinion when news emerged that the real bank thief, a man called James Strand, had been arrested in Edinburgh on December 17th. Three days earlier, Phileas Fogg had been a criminal pursued relentlessly by the police. Now he was once again an honourable gentleman, carrying out his eccentric world journey with mathematical precision.

Newspapers returned to discussing the wager. As if by magic, everyone who had bet for or against him recovered their interest. “Phileas Fogg bonds” could be traded again, fresh wagers multiplied, and his name once more commanded a premium on the Exchange.

His five Reform Club friends spent those three days in feverish uncertainty. Could Phileas Fogg, whom they had almost forgotten, really appear before them again! Where was he now? December 17th, the date of James Strand’s arrest, was the seventy-sixth day after Fogg’s departure, yet they had heard nothing from him. Was he dead? Had he given up, or was he still following the agreed itinerary? Would he stand in the doorway of the Reform Club’s saloon on Saturday, December 21st, at a quarter to nine in the evening?

London society’s anxiety during those three days defies description. Telegrams went to America and Asia seeking news of Phileas Fogg. Messengers visited Saville Row morning and evening. Nothing. Even the police had no information about Fix, the detective so unfortunately engaged on a false trail. Still, the number and size of wagers increased. Like a racehorse, Phileas Fogg was approaching the final turn. His bonds were quoted no longer at a hundred below par, but at twenty, ten, and five. Even old, paralysed Lord Albemarle backed him at even odds.

On Saturday evening enormous crowds filled Pall Mall and the surrounding streets, like an army of brokers permanently encamped around the Reform Club. Traffic could scarcely move. Everywhere people argued, debated, and struck financial deals. The police struggled to hold the crowds back, and as Phileas Fogg’s deadline approached, the excitement reached its peak.

His five opponents had assembled in the club’s great saloon: bankers John Sullivan and Samuel Fallentin; engineer Andrew Stuart; Bank of England director Gauthier Ralph; and brewer Thomas Flanagan. Every one of them waited anxiously.
When the clock showed twenty past eight, Andrew Stuart stood up. “Gentlemen,” he said, “in twenty minutes the period Mr. Fogg and we agreed on will be over.”
“When did the last Liverpool train get in?” Thomas Flanagan asked.
“At twenty-three minutes past seven,” Gauthier Ralph answered. “The next one is not due until ten past twelve.”
“Well, gentlemen,” Andrew Stuart continued, “had Phileas Fogg been on the 7:23, he would be here already. We may therefore consider ourselves the winners.”

“Wait, let us not jump to conclusions,” Samuel Fallentin replied. “You know how eccentric he is. His punctuality is famous: never early, never late. It would not surprise me if he appeared at the very last minute.”
“Why,” Andrew Stuart said nervously, “even if he walked in, I would hardly believe it was him.”

“The truth is,” Thomas Flanagan added, “that Mr. Fogg’s scheme was absurd from the start. Punctuality could not prevent the inevitable delays. Only two or three lost days would have wrecked the whole journey.”
“And remember,” John Sullivan put in, “we have heard absolutely nothing from him, although telegraph lines follow his entire route.”

“He has lost, gentlemen,” Andrew Stuart declared. “Lost a hundred times over! Besides, the ‘China’ arrived yesterday—the only steamer from New York that could have brought him here in time. I have inspected her passenger list: Phileas Fogg’s name is absent. Even assuming he has been wonderfully lucky, he can hardly have reached America. I expect him to be at least twenty days late, and Lord Albemarle to be poorer by a cool five thousand pounds.”
“That is perfectly clear,” Gauthier Ralph replied. “All that remains is to present his cheque at Barings tomorrow.”
Just at that moment, the club clock’s hands reached twenty minutes to nine.
“Five minutes left,” Andrew Stuart observed.
The five men exchanged glances. Their suspense was becoming acute, but none wished to reveal it. They readily agreed when Mr. Fallentin suggested a rubber of whist.
“I would not sell my four-thousand-pound share of this bet,” Andrew Stuart said as he sat down, “for three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine.”
The clock now showed eighteen minutes to nine.
They picked up their cards, yet their eyes kept returning to the clock. However confident they felt, surely no minutes had ever dragged so slowly!
“Seventeen minutes to nine,” Thomas Flanagan announced while cutting the pack Ralph had handed him.

Silence followed. The great saloon lay perfectly still, though the crowd’s murmur drifted in from outside, broken occasionally by a piercing shout. With mathematical regularity the pendulum marked each second, and every player listened and counted intently.
“Sixteen minutes to nine!” John Sullivan called, unable to keep the emotion from his voice.
One minute remained before victory. Andrew Stuart and his companions stopped playing, laid down their cards, and counted off the seconds.
Forty seconds: nothing. Fifty seconds: still no one.
At the fifty-fifth second a great shout rose in the street, followed by clapping, cheers, and a few angry growls.
All five players sprang from their chairs.

At the fifty-seventh second the saloon door opened. Before the pendulum could mark the sixtieth, Phileas Fogg stood there. An excited crowd had forced its way through the club entrance behind him. In his usual calm voice, he said, “Here I am, gentlemen!”

chapters.title: Chapter 37. In which it is Shown that Phileas Fogg Gained Nothing by His Tour Around the World, Unless it Were Happiness
paragraphs: Yes, Phileas Fogg himself.

The reader will recall that at five minutes past eight that evening—roughly twenty-five hours after the travellers returned to London—Mr. Fogg sent Passepartout to arrange for the Reverend Samuel Wilson to conduct a certain wedding ceremony, which was to take place the following day.

Delighted with his errand, Passepartout soon reached the clergyman’s house, only to find him out. He waited a full twenty minutes. By the time he left the reverend gentleman, it was twenty-five minutes to nine. And what a state he was in! Bareheaded, his hair in disarray, he tore down the street faster than anyone had ever seen a man run, bowling over pedestrians and sweeping along the pavement like a waterspout.
Three minutes later he reached Saville Row and stumbled into Mr. Fogg’s room once more.
Words would not come.
“What has happened?” Mr. Fogg asked him.
“Master!” Passepartout gasped. “The marriage—it’s impossible—”
“Impossible?”
“Not possible—tomorrow.”
“Why is that?”
“Because tomorrow—is Sunday!”
“It is Monday,” Mr. Fogg replied.
“No—today is Saturday.”
“Saturday? That’s impossible!”
“Yes, yes, yes, yes!” Passepartout shouted. “You are a whole day out! We reached home twenty-four hours early, but now only ten minutes remain!”
He had caught his master by the collar and was hauling him along with a force impossible to resist.

Abducted in this fashion, Phileas Fogg had no time to think. He left the house, leapt into a cab, and promised the driver a hundred pounds. After running over two dogs and overturning five carriages, they arrived at the Reform Club.
The clock showed a quarter to nine as he entered the great saloon.
Phileas Fogg had completed his circuit of the world within eighty days!
His twenty-thousand-pound wager was won by Phileas Fogg!

How could a man so scrupulous and precise have miscounted an entire day? Why did he believe he had returned on Saturday, December 21st, when the date was really Friday the 20th, only the seventy-ninth day since he left London?
There is a very simple explanation for the mistake.

Without realising it, Phileas Fogg had gained a day while travelling. He had done so simply by going continually _eastward_; had he travelled in the opposite direction, _westward_, he would instead have lost a day.

Going east, he travelled towards the sun, shortening his days by four minutes for every degree he crossed in that direction. The earth’s circumference contains three hundred and sixty degrees; multiply three hundred and sixty by four minutes and the result is exactly twenty-four hours—the day he had gained unknowingly. Put another way, as Phileas Fogg travelled east he watched the sun cross the meridian _eighty_ times, while his London friends saw it cross only _seventy-nine_ times. That was why they expected him at the Reform Club on Saturday, rather than on Sunday as he believed.
Passepartout’s celebrated family watch, still faithfully keeping London time, would have exposed the mistake if only it had shown the date as well as hours and minutes!

Phileas Fogg had therefore won twenty thousand pounds, although his expenses of nearly nineteen thousand left little financial profit. Victory, however, had been his aim, not money. He divided the remaining thousand pounds between Passepartout and the unfortunate Fix, towards whom he felt no resentment. For the sake of order, though, he deducted from Passepartout’s portion the bill for the gas that had burned in his room throughout nineteen hundred and twenty hours.
That evening, as calm and unruffled as ever, Mr. Fogg asked Aouda, “Do you still wish our marriage to take place?”
“Mr. Fogg,” she answered, “surely I should be asking you. You were penniless then; now you are wealthy once more.”
“Forgive me, madam, but that wealth is yours. Without your proposal, my servant would never have visited the Reverend Samuel Wilson. I would not have discovered my mistake, and—”
“My dear Mr. Fogg!” the young woman exclaimed.
“My dear Aouda!” Phileas Fogg answered.
Naturally, the wedding took place forty-eight hours later. Passepartout, radiant and resplendent, gave the bride away. Had he not rescued her, and did that not entitle him to the honour?
At first light the next morning, Passepartout knocked energetically on his master’s door. Mr. Fogg opened it. “What is the matter, Passepartout?” he asked.
“The matter, sir? I have only this moment discovered—”
“What?”
“That we could have travelled round the whole world in just seventy-eight days.”
“Certainly,” Mr. Fogg answered, “if we had not crossed India. But without crossing India, I would not have saved Aouda. She would not be my wife, and—”
Mr. Fogg closed the door quietly.

Phileas Fogg had won his bet and circled the globe in eighty days. He had used every form of transport to achieve it: steamers, trains, carriages, yachts, merchant ships, sledges, and elephants. Throughout, this eccentric gentleman had shown his astonishing powers of composure and precision. But what of it? What had all that effort really gained him? What had he brought home from so long and exhausting a journey?
Nothing, you say? Perhaps: nothing except a charming woman who, strange though it may seem, made him the happiest man alive!
Would you not, in truth, go round the world for less?
